items.title: Integrate ExtractBench extraction benchmark
items.body:
## What

This PR integrates the complete ExtractBench system into this repository, reframing it from a parse-only benchmark into a benchmark for **schema-guided extraction** from enterprise documents. Given a document and a user-defined JSON Schema, a system must return schema-valid JSON with the correct values, every record of each repeated structure, missing fields marked `null` rather than invented, and source evidence for each value. All existing parse capabilities are preserved.

The benchmark covers **370 documents (4,869 pages)** across 8 business domains and 67 document types, each type with its own schema, tagged along five independent difficulty axes (task challenge, perception challenge, table structure, length, business domain).

## Why

Enterprises write a new schema for almost every workflow, so an extraction system cannot be tuned to a fixed template — it has to handle schemas and documents it has never seen. Because agents increasingly act on extracted values before anyone reviews them, one truncated schedule or one invented value becomes a wrong payment or a wrong decision. The benchmark therefore scores completeness and traceability: unified value F1 as the headline metric, plus word- and page-level grounding F1.

## How

The integration lands as a single squashed change so the repository moves atomically from the parse-only baseline to the full extraction benchmark. Recent parse-side changes on `main` that postdate the extraction work (oi_parser, MinerU-Diffusion, Nemotron-Omni, Gemini 3.6 Flash / 3.5 Flash Lite pipelines, Extend Light, `bbox_scale` coordinate-frame config, formatting-rule fixes) were reconciled and transposed into the renamed package so nothing on `main` is lost.

## Changes

- **Package rename**: `parse_bench` -> `extract_bench` across source, tests, tooling, and project metadata; project renamed to `extract-bench`.
- **Extract task type, end to end**: extraction schemas and test-case loading, inference routing, evaluation metrics (value F1 with per-split precision/recall, row-identity scoring for repeated structures, word- and page-level grounding), and cost accounting.
- **Extract providers and pipelines**: LlamaExtract (Agentic, Agentic Plus, Cost-Effective), coding agents (Claude Code, Codex), direct model APIs (Anthropic, OpenAI Responses, Gemini, DeepSeek, GLM, vLLM open-weight, NuExtract3), and specialized APIs (Reducto, Extend, Datalab, Pulse, Landing AI, Azure Content Understanding, Lift, table-codegen), with citation and grounding support.
- **Analysis and reporting suite**: leaderboard, aggregation, comparison, and detailed per-document HTML reports with grounding bbox visualization, unified metric selectors, failed-document reporting, and static CSS/JS assets.
- **Leaderboard**: `leaderboard.csv` and README tables now report extract metrics (unified value F1 by length split, word/page grounding F1, cost per page).
- **Runtime hardening**: lazy adapter registry, lazily initialized sub-CLIs, dependency shaving, graceful test skips when runner extras are absent, and a CI workflow (ruff + pytest with and without runner extras).
- **Preserved upstream parse work**, transposed into the new layout: oi_parser provider/pipeline/label mapper/layout adapter; MinerU-Diffusion and Nemotron-Omni pipelines; Gemini 3.6 Flash and 3.5 Flash Lite pipelines; Extend Light pipeline with `extend-ai>=1.16.0`; `bbox_scale` config gated to providers that pin the perceived image frame; `items_to_markdown` delimiter fix and single-span formatting-rule matching, with their regression tests.
- **Housekeeping**: annotator apps and local data directories are no longer tracked.

## Testing

- Full suite with runner extras: **774 passed**.
- Runner-free suite (matches CI's first stage): **687 passed, 20 skipped**, with the graceful-skip convention applied to the transposed coordinate-frame tests.
- `ruff check` and `ruff format --check` clean; `uv lock` verified consistent with `pyproject.toml` (`uv sync --locked`).
- Verified file-by-file that the diff against the extraction codebase is limited to the transposed upstream parse commits listed above.

## Notes

- The PR is intentionally a single commit; review is best done by area (schemas, metrics, providers, analysis) rather than commit-by-commit.
- Breaking change for downstream consumers: the Python package import path changes from `parse_bench` to `extract_bench`, and `leaderboard.csv` switches to the extract-metric schema.
- New optional environment variables are documented in `.env.example`; no defaults changed for existing parse pipelines beyond the documented `bbox_scale` gating.

items.title: Benchmark loader and CLI
items.body:
The machinery to run a benchmark, plus the CLI that drives it.

## Scope note, stated up front

**The labelled dataset is not in this PR, because it cannot be.** `data/documents/` is empty, and a relevance label can only be written by a person reading the paper. Everything that *loads*, *validates*, and *scores* a benchmark is here and tested; the labels are not, and the README says so instead of showing placeholder numbers.

## What lands

- **`build_corpus`** — the single ingestion → chunking → corpus path shared by CLI, benchmark, and later the UI, so a chunk ID means the same thing everywhere.
- **`load_benchmark`** — parses the JSON and **validates every label against the corpus**, refusing the file if any ID fails to resolve.
- **CLI** — `index`, `search`, `evaluate`, over any chunker and retriever. `main()` returns an exit code rather than calling `sys.exit`, so the whole thing is testable in-process, and the embedding import lives inside the retriever factory so a `bm25` run never loads torch.
- **`data/evaluation/SCHEMA.md`** — file format, categories, and the labelling procedure.

## Why the label validation is strict

A chunk ID carries a SHA-256 prefix of its own text. A dangling label therefore means the document or the chunking settings changed since labelling, and scoring against it would silently measure the wrong thing. It's a hard error with a nonzero exit code:

```
error: benchmark.json: 1 question(s) reference chunk IDs that are not in the corpus,
so the document or the chunking settings changed since labelling (q01 -> ...)
```

A benchmark that produces numbers which *look* real is worse than no benchmark. A corollary now documented in the README: **a benchmark is valid only for the chunking configuration it was labelled under** — comparing chunking strategies means re-labelling, not reusing.

## A BM25 trap found while smoke-testing

Okapi IDF is `log(N−n+0.5) − log(n+0.5)`, which at `N=2, n=1` is **exactly zero**. On a two- or three-chunk corpus every term scores zero and BM25 returns nothing. That's the formula behaving as designed on a corpus far too small for it, not a bug — but it makes toy corpora a misleading smoke test, so the test fixtures use seven pages and the behaviour is documented in the retriever's docstring.

Suite at **289 passed**.

items.title: Publish the verified benchmark results
items.body:
Twenty cells, 30 trials each, a fresh agent process per trial, one run on one harness version. Every figure on `docs/benchmarks.md` and in the README results block is generated from `benchmarks/results.json`. None is typed.

## Accuracy

| Arm | claude | codex |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Continuum injects the context | 100% (100 to 100) | 100% (100 to 100) |
| No injection, the agent reads `.continuum/` itself | 100% (100 to 100) | 100% (100 to 100) |
| No project memory at all | 18% (15 to 20) | 20% (20 to 20) |

Conflict, where the injected context and the files on disk are made to contradict each other: **30/30 answered from injected context, 0/30 from disk**, both agents. All eight LongMemEval category cells **30/30**. Delegation delivered **100%** of replies, 30/30, now that the arm reads the reply rather than scoring a constant zero.

Compact context is **109 tokens against 1,710** of raw event history, 94% smaller. That one needs no agent and no API key.

## The middle row stays in the headline table

An agent left to open `.continuum/` itself scores the same as one given injected context. Recording the context is what produces the accuracy; injecting it is what makes it fast. Burying that in prose under the table would not survive a careful reader, and it is the obvious rebuttal to the whole project, so it belongs where it is.

## Trials that did not run

Two failed to start, one in `claude/files_only` and one in `codex/no_memory`. They are excluded from accuracy and counted in the completion table rather than scored as wrong answers.

## Housekeeping

The pre-scorer-fix `results.json` is deleted rather than kept beside the new one. Two results files in a directory, one of them withdrawn, is how a withdrawn number finds its way back onto a page.

The fault list is now six entries. The delegation scorer and the suspended machine are the two added, both found the same way as the earlier four: by asking how a number was produced rather than by looking at the number.

624 tests.

items.title: Precision fixes for website discovery: zero wrong answers on both scored benchmarks
items.body:
## What this is

Four defects found and fixed in the discovery classifier, plus a corrected benchmark ground truth. On the two datasets that can be scored, the tool now writes **no wrong answers at all** — every remaining error is a miss.

| Dataset | Rows | Answers written | Wrong | Review leads | Nothing | Precision |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 227 human-verified | 227 | 213 | **0** | 11 | 3 | **100%** |
| Agri-IoT | 62 | 31 | **0** | 11 | 20 | **100%** |
| Space-Tech FAIL | 59 | 13 | — | 27 | 19 | no verified column |
| 100-company sample | 100 | 26 | — | 26 | 48 | no labels |

227 Category A is **198 of 199**, and the one miss isn't wrong — iAeroSky returned the correct URL, just held as a review lead.

## The fixes

**1. `browser-only-reachable` fired on domains that resolve for nobody.** A DNS lookup now runs alongside the browser probe and the plain fetch. A host with no A/AAAA record that still renders a `200` is a monetised NXDOMAIN wildcard — `3spacecorp.com` returns `200` and redirects to `parklogicchannel.com`. Measured: **40 of the 41** rows carrying this reason had no DNS record. It was roughly half the human review worklist.

**2. A parked verdict came from a single DNS resolution.** `iaerosky.com` publishes two A records — one serves Hostinger's parking page, one serves the real site. Round-robin made every probe a coin flip, and a parked verdict was terminal. Each address is now asked separately before the domain is called dead.

**3. A junk lead permanently suppressed the platform-host stage.** `tryPlatformHosts` was gated on having nothing better than a `review` lead, so any medium lead — a holding page, an intercepted dead domain — blocked the one stage that can find a vercel/netlify-hosted site. Gate removed; `noteLow` now breaks ties by evidence specificity; the stage picks the *best* brand-matching platform host rather than the first.

**4. Domains listed for sale, detected by nameserver.** `klonec.com` sits on Afternic and serves a different response per request — empty on `www`, a redirect on the apex, sometimes enough text to pass a content match, which is how it was written in as an answer. The page flickers; the NS record does not.

**5. A site-builder banner was rejecting real sites.** "Go from idea to live site in minutes / Get 50 free credits" was an unconditional placeholder marker. `dilekaaerospace.com` has 2,583 characters of genuine company copy under that strip and was being thrown away.

## Ground truth is now a file, not the spreadsheet

`website-agent-diagnostics/ground-truth-overrides.json` is authoritative. 12 sheet labels were verified wrong — 9 rows marked PASS are holding pages (`stardour.com` renders 89 characters, `husori.com` renders 10) or dead domains (`orbitx.in` is parked, `spacebelief.co.in` returns a Wix 404). Scoring against them was charging the tool for being right. Applied idempotently from a `.orig` snapshot; the client sheet is never modified.

Two entries are owner calls that direct URL checks contradict — **Prakshep** and **SmartGro**, whose sheet URLs are both live, substantial, on-topic sites. Applied as instructed, with the contradicting evidence recorded beside each entry so the 100% figure stays auditable.

## Two things reviewers should know

**A rule was withdrawn, not shipped.** A stage-1 content bar was built on the claim that `raudranexaerospace.in` serves a titleless `200`. It actually serves a GoDaddy lander and was already handled correctly; the observed failure was environmental flapping. The attempt broke three legitimate tests and was reverted rather than weakened to fit.

**A fix was corrected mid-review.** `namebrightdns.com` was initially treated as a for-sale nameserver. `cosmicport.com` sits on it and serves a real site, so it was removed — the empty NameBright domains are already caught by the structural placeholder rule. Only true marketplaces qualify now.

## Also in this PR

- `input/production/…xlsx` (4.6 MB of real company records) removed from tracking, and `input/**/*.xlsx|xls|csv` gitignored. **This does not remove it from git history** — that needs a rewrite, which is not done here.
- `architecture.md` rewritten: its folder tree, per-company flow and layer table all referenced a `steps/` directory and five files that no longer exist.
- README gains a command reference at the top and a three-command first-run sequence.
- `engineering.md` gains "Evidence over assumption", recording the rules on this branch that were written from theory and turned out wrong on real pages.

169 tests pass; typecheck clean.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

items.title: Re-measure MVE bf16 benchmark quality under fp32 MaxSim accumulation
items.body:
Hello!

Heads up, this PR was AI-generated and human-reviewed.

## Pull Request overview
* Re-measure the MultiVectorEncoder bf16 benchmark quality after the fp32 MaxSim accumulation fix
* Update the GPU benchmark figure and the bfloat16 observation on the efficiency docs page

## Details
The MultiVectorEncoder benchmark quality numbers for `torch-bf16` and `torch-bf16-fa2` were measured before MaxSim scoring switched to float32 sum accumulation. With bf16 accumulation, summing the per-query-token maxima on the coarse bf16 grid cost real nDCG, and that scoring loss was wrongly attributed to the embeddings.

I've re-run the `MultiVectorNanoBEIREvaluator` (msmarco and nq) for both benchmark models with the current scoring:

| Configuration | Old ratio vs fp32 | New ratio vs fp32 |
| - | - | - |
| answerai-colbert-small-v1, bf16 | 93.8% | 98.8% |
| GTE-ModernColBERT-v1, bf16 | 96.2% | 99.3% |
| GTE-ModernColBERT-v1, bf16 + FA2 | 97.9% | 100.0% |

Most of the reported bf16 quality drop came from the scoring accumulation rather than from the bf16 embeddings themselves. Plain bf16 now sits at 99.0% on average and bf16 with FlashAttention-2 is indistinguishable from fp32. The GPU benchmark figure and the bfloat16 observation bullet are updated accordingly. Speed columns are unchanged.

- Tom Aarsen

items.title: feat(benchmarks): top-k oracle PER — lattice quality vs ranking error
items.body:
> 🤖 Auto-generated by Claude Fable 5 (claude-fable-5) via Claude Code — NOT human-reviewed. Verify before acting.

*Revised after adversarial review (11 findings, all addressed). See the resolution table at the bottom.*

## What and why

The scoreboard scored 1-best only. A wrong PER could not tell us whether the engine **had a better reading** and ranked it badly, or **never had one**. Those need opposite investments: better weights/rescoring vs more rules and data per language.

**Oracle PER@k** is the per-word *minimum* PER over the engine's top-k readings, aggregated exactly like the existing PER (same normalize, same edit distance, same multi-gold rule).

```
PER − Oracle@k  = RANKING error — a better reading exists in the top-k.
Oracle@k        = MODEL error   — no better reading exists at any k.
```

### Two things the metric does NOT say

**1. The headroom is an unachievable upper bound, not a forecast.** An oracle picks the best candidate per word *after seeing the gold*. No deployed rescorer has that information. `PER − Oracle@k` is the ceiling on what any reranking could ever buy; a real rescorer realizes some fraction of it. It is a "is this worth investigating" signal, not a projected gain.

**2. A better reading is not the right reading.** `Oracle@k` dropping means a *closer* candidate is in the beam — closer in edit distance, and usually still wrong. So this PR also adds **`OracleX@k`** (`oracle_exact_top3/5`): the fraction of words where some top-k candidate **equals** a gold exactly, i.e. the `Exact match` column generalized from k=1 to k.

Measured, of the words where the PER oracle beats top-1, the fraction that reach an exact gold:

| Lang | oracle wins | of which exact | share |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| fr | 13649 | 5601 | **41.0%** |
| de | 23284 | 5887 | **25.3%** |

So the PER oracle overstates "the engine already knows the answer" by roughly 2x–4x. `docs/benchmarks.md` now says this explicitly and directs any claim of that shape to `OracleX@k`. (Independently reproduced from the reviewer's 41.4% / 25.8%; small delta is the ca-elision dev movement.)

## Semantics — diagnostic only, never a comparison

**Oracle@k is a lattice-quality diagnostic for orthography2ipa alone. It must never feed a cross-system comparison or a "beats X" claim.** espeak-ng, epitran and every other system in `docs/comparison.md` emit ONE pronunciation; setting their single answer against the best of k of ours compares k guesses to one, and any conclusion is an artifact of the k. **This PR body therefore quotes no espeak numbers** — an earlier revision did, which was the rule's first violation and is fixed.

Enforced, not merely asserted:

- `scripts/compare_systems.py` — **zero diff**, and a test greps it for the string `oracle` to keep it that way.
- `benchmarks/results_ci_sample.json` — **zero diff**; the CI regression gate stays 1-best, with a test asserting the committed sample carries no oracle fields.
- Stated in `OracleResult`'s docstring, the `benchmark.py` module docstring, the generated `docs/scoreboard.md` legend, and `docs/benchmarks.md`.

## Findings — full corpus

| Lang | Dataset | N | PER (top-1) | Oracle@3 | Oracle@5 | ranking ceiling | Exact@1 | OracleX@3 | OracleX@5 |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| fr | wikipron | 85494 | 0.0951 | 0.0754 | 0.0682 | 0.0269 | 0.5974 | 0.6477 | 0.6629 |
| en-GB | wikipron | 81537 | 0.3281 | 0.2729 | 0.2460 | 0.0821 | 0.1343 | 0.1688 | 0.1953 |
| de | wikipron | 53010 | 0.2103 | 0.1567 | 0.1414 | 0.0689 | 0.2343 | 0.3150 | 0.3453 |
| sv | wikipron | 5076 | 0.2317 | 0.1570 | 0.1454 | 0.0863 | 0.3381 | 0.4309 | 0.4529 |
| nl | wikipron | 45872 | 0.1251 | 0.1001 | 0.0922 | 0.0329 | 0.4278 | 0.5129 | 0.5399 |
| it | wikipron | 82276 | 0.0588 | 0.0269 | 0.0166 | 0.0422 | 0.6430 | 0.8006 | 0.8775 |
| ca | wikipron | 106 | 0.2596 | 0.1488 | 0.1289 | 0.1307 | 0.3302 | 0.5094 | 0.5660 |
| fi | wikipron | 168808 | 0.0184 | 0.0184 | 0.0184 | 0.0000 | 0.8171 | 0.8173 | 0.8173 |
| eu | wikipron | 12008 | 0.0546 | 0.0545 | 0.0545 | 0.0001 | 0.6084 | 0.6084 | 0.6084 |
| eu | hitz_basque_ipa | 3113 | 0.0984 | 0.0981 | 0.0981 | 0.0003 | 0.4616 | 0.4616 | 0.4616 |
| ca | 4catac | 160 | 0.0827 | – | – | – | 0.0125 | – | – |

`es` is **deliberately absent** — see F6.

### Where the lattice is rich but badly ordered

ca-wikipron (50% of its error is ranking-recoverable at the ceiling), sv (37%), de (33%), en-GB (25%), it (72% of a small error), fr (28%), nl (26%). These carry real ranking components and are the candidates for a weights/rescoring workstream. The exact columns qualify how much is genuinely recoverable: de's `OracleX` rises 0.2343 → 0.3453, so an oracle rescorer would make 11pp more words exactly right — a real but bounded prize, and a deployed rescorer gets a fraction of it.

### Where rules are the only lever

fi (ranking ceiling `0.0000`) and eu (`0.0001`–`0.0003`) have essentially **zero** ranking error: near-deterministic orthographies where the beam holds one real reading. No rescorer will help them; every remaining error is model error. That is a clean negative result and the most actionable line in the table.

### The fr question

fr's ranking ceiling is `0.0269` against a top-1 PER of `0.0951` — 28% of the total error is, at most, recoverable by reranking the existing lattice, and 41% of those wins are exact. That is enough signal to justify investigating weights/rescoring for French before writing more rules. It is a ceiling on an internal metric and implies nothing about any other system.

## Runtime cost — measured

fr WikiPron, 3000-word probe, **separate cold processes**, alternated and repeated:

| run | time |
|---|---|
| 1-best | 1.25s / 1.23s |
| +oracle (beam width 8, k≤5) | 2.04s / 2.01s |

**1.63x.** `build_scoreboard(..., oracle=...)` now defaults to **off** and `--scoreboard` is the only caller that opts in, so the CI gate never inherits the cost. `--no-topk` disables it for a fast ad-hoc rerun. Full-corpus fr rescored end-to-end in 1m56s.

## Review findings — resolution

| # | Finding | Resolution |
|---|---|---|
| **F1** | CI gate paid 1.64x for unread columns | `build_scoreboard(oracle=False)` is now the default; `--scoreboard` opts in explicitly. 3 tests: default is off, the regression script's call line contains no `oracle`, `--ci-sample` passes `oracle=False`. |
| **F2** | Tripwire warned above exit 0 | New `assert_oracle_self_check()` — prints `ENGINE BUG` then `sys.exit(1)` on `top1_mismatch > 0` or `oracle@1 != PER` beyond epsilon. **No scoreboard is written.** 5 tests incl. one driving `build_scoreboard` to a non-zero exit. |
| **F3** | 626 rows printed `-`, legend said `-` means sentence-level | `·` = not yet rescored, `-` = sentence-level (impossible), number = measured. Legend documents all three and states they are never merged. 4 rendering tests. |
| **F4** | PR body violated its own rule | This body. Espeak numbers and the "ahead of espeak" claim removed; headroom reframed as an unachievable upper bound; the deficit-vs-headroom arithmetic kept in internal terms. |
| **F5** | "right answer in the beam" overstated ~2x | `OracleX@3/@5` added and published. Doc wording corrected in both the legend and `benchmarks.md`. Both numbers reported above. 5 tests (closer-but-wrong scores 0 exact; exact@1 == `Exact match`; monotone in k). |
| **F6** | es row not reproducible (WikiPron snapshot drift) | **es row dropped**; dev's row is untouched and reads `·`. Corpus-revision pinning noted as a follow-up below. |
| **F7** | indent-1→2 reformat would conflict with ~80 commits | Reverted to dev's formatting. `SCOREBOARD_JSON_INDENT = 1` pins it with a comment saying normalization is a standalone cleanup. `results.json` diff is now **122 lines, not 8285**. |
| **F8** | `all_fallback` compared against `n` | Row now stores `oracle_scored_words` (covered − fallback) and the renderer keys off it. Note: `n` *is* `covered` today, so there was no live bug — but the coupling was implicit and is now explicit. 2 tests, incl. one where fallback ≠ n. |
| **F9** | vox_communis mislabelled sentence-level | Corrected in `docs/benchmarks.md` and both `benchmark.py` comments (verified: 0/200 multiword on pl). |
| **F10** | Candidate-0 identity asserted, not constructed | Docstrings in `g2p.py`, `benchmark.py`, `benchmarks.md` and `api_stability.md` now state plainly that `transcribe_word` is greedy width-1 while `word_candidates` runs width-`max(k,8)`, that a wider beam may find a cheaper path, that `beam_width=1` forces the identity, and that the harness verifies rather than assumes. |
| **F11** | `word_candidates` missing from api_stability | New "Finalized top-k readings (additive)" section: signature, the `candidates` vs `word_candidates` distinction with the `bonjour` example, the empty-list case, and the non-contractual element-0 caveat. |

## Follow-ups (not in this PR)

1. **Corpus-revision pinning** (from F6). WikiPron loaders fetch `HEAD`, so a row's `n` drifts and a rescored row is not byte-reproducible against an older one. Rows should record the snapshot they were scored against.
2. **`results.json` indent normalization** to 2, matching every sibling artifact — standalone, when the file is quiet.
3. **Rescore the remaining 626 rows** in batches to replace `·` with measurements.

## Verification

- Full suite foreground: **197108 passed, 5 skipped, 132 xfailed**.
- `tests/test_oracle_per.py`: **37 tests** (was 19). Fail-before verified — the file does not collect against `origin/dev`.
- `benchmarks/results_ci_sample.json` and `scripts/compare_systems.py`: **zero diff**.
- Extraction of `_finalize_word_ipa` is behavior-preserving (confirmed by the reviewer over 6,600+ outputs, 0 diffs); fr/de/en-GB/it/eu/ca 1-best PER reproduce their committed values exactly.
- `fi` (`0.0539 → 0.0184`) and `sv` (`0.2316 → 0.2317`) moved: genuine dev-side improvement whose committed baseline was stale, kept per review. Verified independent of this PR — fi at limit 20000 gives `PER=0.0145 WER=0.1139` identically with and without the oracle.

items.title: fix(evaluation): do not score LCB samples 0.0 when the judge cannot run
items.body:
evaluate_livecodebench_worker swallows every exception and returns False, so import/setup failures get scored as wrong answers with subset status "ok". That currently always happens in this env: lcb_runner.prompts imports anthropic (not installed) and datasets>=3 cannot load the script-based code_generation_lite dataset. Observed: 335 samples "graded" 0/335 in 83s; the same outputs score 297/349 through lcb-service. A fake zero on 349/4388 samples is enough to drop a passing DeepSeek-R1 run below the MLPerf accuracy threshold.

- re-raise ImportError/FileNotFoundError/RuntimeError from the worker and the gather loop; the runner already marks the subset failed and sets complete=false
- call load_lcb_benchmark() once before spawning workers so setup errors fail fast with the real traceback

Sample-level grading failures (bad generated code, timeouts) still score as incorrect. This does not fix the local path itself (deps are still missing); it just stops it from reporting a wrong score.

items.title: Add compiler-guided generation queries to tdg-agent, with a Compile@1…
items.body:
…/Repair@1 benchmark (Prompt 032)

Extend the agent protocol with seven generation-oriented queries an agent asks *before* writing the next token, in a new `tuo-agent::generation` module (`GenerationQueries` for `Session`): context_at, expected_type_at, visible_symbols_at, valid_members_of, call_signature, imports_for_symbol, and expected_syntax_at. Like every other method they reimplement no stage — the semantic answers are read-only projections of the shared Resolution/TypeckResult.

Two honesty rules are load-bearing and structural, per the prompt:

- Syntactic guidance (expected_syntax_at, context_at's `syntactic` block) is a conservative lexical heuristic over raw text, always flagged `"exhaustive": false` with a note that the compiler does NOT enumerate every valid next token — the pipeline exposes no grammar/expected-token oracle, so claiming one would be dishonest. Kept in its own field, apart from semantics.
- Approximate queries say so in-band: visible_symbols_at is an over-approximation (`"complete": false`, block scoping unmodeled), and expected_type_at reports the recorded expression type or, as a fallback, the enclosing function's declared return type (its `source` names which) — never a hole-typing power the compiler lacks. valid_members_of is precise (`"exhaustive": true`) since the checker's struct/enum shapes are complete.

Whether the queries raise Compile@1/Repair@1 is measured deterministically in generation_benchmark.rs (--nocapture): a fixed corpus where the naive text-only guess is wrong, scored by really compiling each pick through check_sources under a baseline vs a query-guided policy — asserting guidance is never worse and, on that corpus, strictly better (0% -> 100% on both metrics). It is a proxy for the queries' discriminative power, not a live-LLM eval (no provider embedded).

- crates/tuo-agent/src/generation.rs (new) — the GenerationQueries trait + impl.
- crates/tuo-agent/src/{lib,server,session}.rs — export, dispatch, METHODS, and pub(crate) with_semantics/require_file seams.
- crates/tuo-agent/tests/generation.rs (new) — 15 protocol tests.
- crates/tuo-agent/tests/generation_benchmark.rs (new) — Compile@1/Repair@1.
- crates/tuo-cli/tests/agent_command.rs — a generation query over the real stdio transport.
- CLAUDE.md — the generation-queries convention (honesty contract + benchmark).

Verified: cargo fmt --all --check; cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets --all-features -D warnings; cargo test --workspace (all green, layering guard included).

items.title: docsy: search-quality benchmark (query set, answer key, eval)
items.body:
Measures docs search against real user queries, so a search change can be **shown** to help and quality cannot decay unnoticed. Implements **DOC-1397** under **DOC-1254**.

Split out of the combined indexer PR: this runs **on demand with a human in the loop**, not per deploy, and should not gate the security fix (DOC-1285) which needs only the indexer.

## Not build CI — and deliberately so

| lifecycle | what | automated? |
|---|---|---|
| every deploy | the indexer (separate PR) | yes |
| every content PR | `make check-search-labels` — path existence, no network | **yes** (companion: unionai-docs#1399) |
| on demand / periodic | the eval itself | **no** — needs LLM judgment and human correction |

## Contents

| tool | does |
|---|---|
| `find_candidates` | expanded-term search over content |
| `digest_candidates` | compact page digests, so canonicality is judged from prose not scores |
| `draft_ideals` | first-pass labels |
| `eval_search` | MRR@10 / Recall@5 / nDCG@10 / **Pages@10** / zero-rate |
| `check_labels` | validates a key; wired to `make check-search-labels` |
| `diff_labels` | classifies key changes as content- vs judgment-driven |
| `queries.judged.json` | **45 real queries**, per-facet, multi-ideal, human-corrected |

## Three findings baked into the design

**Candidate ranking needs two signals.** Breadth alone found `gpu` (the canonical "Resources" page hits 9/9 expansion terms; a tutorial saying "gpu" *more often* hits 1/9) but broke `secret` (a CI/CD guide mentions secret, credential, api key **and** password). Canonicality alone is biased *against* canonical pages, which are titled with the general concept while users type the specific term.

**Labels are per-facet and multi-valued.** Search returns four groups, so a flat label scores a grouped result list wrong — and one label per group makes *correct* results register as misses.

**Absolute scores are not a quality claim.** The key carries judgment error: of five labels a human reviewed, four changed. Valid for comparing arms against a shared key; not for grading search in absolute terms. The eval says so in its output.

## What it has already found

- **Result dilution** — `task environment` returned 8 hits that were all one page. Fixed in the indexer PR; measured **Pages@10 4.52 → 9.68** over 50 real queries.
- **`/docs/latest/*` search returns nothing** — likely inflating the no-result rate in DOC-1237.
- **Vocabulary gaps** — `deck`, `shelltask`, `eager`, `flytectl`, `map_task` all have good v2 pages behind a renamed term.
- **Genuine content gaps** — `maxmessagesizebytes`, `eventspublisher` have no page at all.

## Known gap

`eval_search.py` still reads `ideal` as a flat list, from before the per-group schema. Needs updating before the arms produce real MRR/nDCG; the label-free metrics (Pages@10, zero-rate) work today.

items.title: Fix: compare the benchmark on the same currency basis as the asset
items.body: Beta and correlation converted the asset to the display currency but left the IWDA/VDTA benchmark in native USD, so a non-USD view regressed a PLN return on a USD one and partly measured the asset against USDPLN. Proof it was wrong: viewed in PLN, IWDA scored beta 0.48 and correlation 0.57 against itself, and diversifiers came out with the wrong sign - long treasuries -0.66 rather than +0.29, managed futures -0.79 rather than +0.16. The benchmark is now converted the same way the asset is, so an index scores exactly 1.00 against itself in every currency. USD views are unchanged. Also caches the benchmark pairs, which beta and correlation were rebuilding twice per render.

items.title: evaluate-interpret reliability check: RA vs Codex (scarcity-of-labor), gpt-4o + gpt-5.4-mini
items.body:
## Summary
- Built a human ground-truth reference (`gt/human_report.docx`) to unlock `evaluate-interpret` for the custom scarcity-of-labor study, then ran it against two real agent outputs with a known-correct/known-wrong ground truth: Task A (ReplicatorAgent hard tier, implementation has a real bug, inverted capital-return formula, max abs diff up to ~3981 vs. reference) and Task B (Codex fresh run, matches the reference model to 4.4e-15, machine precision).
- **gpt-4o judge** (3 runs each): Task A (wrong) scores 94.1%/100.0%/96.1%, Task B (correct) scores 89.7%/96.1%/94.1%. The wrong implementation matches or beats the correct one in every run.
- **gpt-5.4-mini judge** (3 runs each): reverses this. Task A (wrong) scores 78.4%/71.8%/78.4%, Task B (correct) scores 90.2%/84.3%/88.2%. The correct implementation wins every run, and the judge's own explanations name the actual numeric discrepancies in Task A's self-report.
- Ran a first `evaluate-design` check on Task A using `model_specification.pdf` as a stand-in reference (no proper `gt/human_preregistration.*` exists yet for this study): 97.6%, no sign it caught the bug either. Traced this to the same root cause as `evaluate-interpret`: both stages only compare the agent's self-reported prose against a reference document, neither ever reads the actual code, so a bug that's only visible in the code (and never named in the agent's own report) is structurally invisible to the grader regardless of which LLM judges it.
- Also found and confirmed the same failure pattern in the empirical 39-study benchmark: Study 13 (McLaren 2012), gpt-4o Python mode, where the agent silently loaded the wrong data file (`data_clean.rds` instead of `data_clean_5pct.rds`) and self-reported success. `evaluate-interpret` partially caught this (docked the specific result-value fields to 1/3) but still gave a full 3/3 on the overall "replication succeeded" verdict, and never identified the actual cause.

## Key files
- `for_reference/outputs/interpret_eval_runs/` — all individual run results (gpt-4o x3 + gpt-5.4-mini x3, per task) with prompt logs
- `for_reference/outputs/EVALUATE_INTERPRET_6_RUNS.xlsx`, `EVALUATE_INTERPRET_6_RUNS_GPT54MINI.xlsx` — per-run tabs (agent text next to judge score/explanation) plus a summary/comparison tab
- `execution/our_models/scarcity_of_labor/gt/human_report.docx` — the human ground-truth reference used for all `evaluate-interpret` runs
- `execution/our_models/scarcity_of_labor_ra_hard/evals/gpt-4o/design_llm_eval.json` — the one-off `evaluate-design` check

## Test plan
- [x] Verified `evaluate-interpret`/`evaluate-design` only read `interpret_results.json`/`replication_info.json` and the reference document, never the code (`validator/evaluate_interpret.py`, confirmed by inspection)
- [x] Confirmed RA and Codex received byte-identical `initial_details.txt`, and that the focal claim there matches `gt/human_report.docx`'s Claim Summary verbatim
- [x] Cross-checked totals against saved per-run JSON snapshots, not live files that get overwritten on rerun

items.title: research: benchmark agent storage options for a single VPS
items.body:
## What

Answers one question: several agent processes share one VPS and all read and
write the same state — what should hold it?

**Answer: one SQLite database in WAL mode**, with markdown kept as the source of
truth for prose and the database as a rebuildable index over it. It measured
fastest, most correct, and cheapest to operate — and was the only engine that
refused unsafe work instead of silently losing it.

46 options surveyed → 5 hard filters → 16 survivors → 9 engines benchmarked with
real concurrent OS processes in Linux containers → SQLite wins all four
weightings.

## The findings that matter

**Every engine that lost data reported a 0% error rate.** 8 writers, 4 hot keys,
1,600 read-modify-write ops:

| engine | acknowledged | stored | verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| sqlite (`BEGIN IMMEDIATE`) | 1,600 | 1,600 | correct |
| postgres (`FOR UPDATE`) | 1,600 | 1,600 | correct |
| redis (`INCR`) | 1,600 | 1,600 | correct |
| postgres (READ COMMITTED) | 1,600 | 843 | **lost 757** |
| lancedb (`update()`) | 1,600 | 778 | **lost 822** |
| qdrant (`set_payload`) | 1,600 | 863 | **lost 737** |

Misconfigured SQLite threw `database is locked` at 58% of calls and lost
nothing. Loud refusal beats silent loss.

**The single-writer bottleneck is not real at agent scale.** SQLite held ~40,000
appends/s essentially flat from 1 to 16 writer processes at 11 µs/write — around
40x headroom over ~20 busy agents.

**Two pragmas separate 98% failure from 0%.** Same binary, 8 writers:
`busy_timeout` + `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` → 43,904 ops/s, 0% errors. Without them →
7,659 ops/s, 98.4% errors.

**pgvector's defaults are unsafe.** `ef_search=40` found the true nearest
neighbour 43% of the time; 400 recovers 96.5%. Qdrant got 98.5% out of the box.

## Also in here

- `HYPOTHESES.md` — eight numeric predictions committed before measuring. Three
  confirmed, four partly wrong, one with no control. The report scores each.
- A "best of each" synthesis — the transferable idea from all 30 losers
  (Dolt's writes-as-proposals, Zep's fact invalidation, XTDB's bitemporality).
- Migration triggers as measured numbers, not feelings.
- Reproducible: `./bench/run_all.sh` then `python3 scripts/report.py`.

## Caveats

Test bed was 4 vCPU / 8 GB — double the 2 vCPU box this repo's VPS research
recommends, so it is generous to the server-based options. The host was not
dedicated (an unrelated container held ~177% CPU for one pass); those runs are
labelled and excluded from headline tables. Turso Database was not benchmarked —
its concurrent-write mode entered preview six days before this was written, and
that is the real gap here.

items.title: fix(benchmarks): restore the PMC corpus to 66 articles
items.body:
Closes #332.

`PMC11000011.1` was withdrawn upstream (#329). Since #330 the lane degrades gracefully and scores 65 of 66 — right for an incident, wrong as a steady state. A permanently-false `complete_corpus` is a permanently-yellow test: the *second* withdrawal would be invisible against a run that already looks like that, and it quietly consumes the tolerance budget that exists for real incidents (the load aborts past a tenth of the selection).

## The replacement is drawn, not chosen

Re-walked **only** the `PMC11000000` seed through `build_manifest` with the committed `stride` (11), `per_seed` (3), candidate cap and filter. A hand-picked article would bias the corpus in a way nothing downstream could detect.

The walk also settles what kind of failure this is. The prefix **still lists** — only the PDF 404s — so it registers as a `pdf_missing` *rejection* rather than an outage, stride alignment is preserved, and the seed's two surviving members re-select **byte-for-byte identically** against the committed rows. Only the third slot moves:

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| seed members | `PMC11000000.1`, `PMC11000011.1`, `PMC11000022.1` | `PMC11000000.1`, `PMC11000022.1`, **`PMC11000033.1`** |
| articles | 66 (65 loadable) | 66 |
| pin | `34cc7c50` | `9ba5c0cd` |

The other 65 rows are preserved verbatim. `selection` metadata is updated so it doesn't describe a build that never happened — `candidates` 105 → 106, `pdf_missing` 7 → 8, plus a `rewalks` entry recording which seed was re-walked, why, and what it swapped. It lives inside `selection` because the loader validates the top-level key set exactly.

## Re-recorded on CI, not locally

`reference.json` was originally recorded on Linux from the lockfile, and the runner image and lockfile are part of the measurement — re-recording on a Windows dev box would have made the numbers incomparable with the ones they replace. Recorded from a full 66-article run ([run 31653012941](https://github.com/thomas-villani/all2md/actions/runs/31653012941)); `complete_corpus` is `true` again.

The readings barely move, which is what a representative corpus should do when one article of 66 is swapped:

| figure | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| recall of attainable | 95.3% | **95.3%** |
| novel n-grams | 1.0% | **1.0%** |
| raw recall | 60.1% | 60.2% |
| supported | 93.8% | 93.9% |
| tables | 88 / 117 | 92 / 121 |

## The check that was missing

Nothing tied the figures in `benchmarks.rst` to the artifacts behind them — the correspondence was asserted, not enforced, and this lane has already published a comparison between two runs covering different corpora. Added `tests/unit/test_published_benchmark_figures.py`:

- Each published claim is declared as a snippet **rendered from the artifact** and required to appear verbatim. That's the strong direction — scraping numbers out of prose cannot see a figure that should be there and is not, and would need an exemption for every incidental integer. Matching whole lines rather than bare numbers means a stale line fails too.
- `corpus_pin` must equal the SHA-256 of the committed `manifest.json`, so a manifest edit landing without a re-record fails immediately.
- The published reference must be a *complete* run covering every article the manifest names.
- `test_the_figure_inventory_is_not_empty` and `test_a_perturbed_artifact_is_caught` exist because a loader that yields nothing would make everything else vacuous.

**Verified the judge can fail** twice. Against the pre-update page it reports exactly the nine figures that moved, while the unchanged OmniDocBench readings still match. Changing one integer in the manifest fails the pin check with both digests and the instruction to re-record.

## Notes

- The pin change means a new digest-keyed cache directory. I warmed it by **copying** (never moving) from the existing one and `load` re-verified all 66 against the new pin, so no 148 MB re-download was needed — and `.cache/34cc7c503bba1468/` still holds the only surviving copy of the withdrawn article, per the issue's warning.
- All six fidelity-gated root docs still round-trip at 100.

items.title: A repeatable Tactics benchmark and its committed baseline
items.body:
## Ownership claim

- Machine ID: `martbot-mbp-m5-max-128`
- Agent/session ID: `claude-opus5-tactics-bench`
- Task: tactics bench harness
- Claimed paths: `tools/tactics_bench.py`, `tools/test_tactics_bench.py`, `docs/TACTICS_BASELINE.md`, `.github/workflows/collaboration-policy.yml`
- Coordinated with: none
- Computer: MacBook Pro
- Related issue/request: operator request — a Tactics testbed for developing AI tactical play

## What changed

The arena baselines so far were one-off command lines written into PR bodies.
Nothing was repeatable and nothing was committed, so no future change to the
tactical AI could be judged against them.

`tools/tactics_bench.py` runs the standard battery — three regimes against two
opponents — prints a table, and diffs it against `docs/TACTICS_BASELINE.md`.

```
tools/tactics_bench.py                  # run the battery, compare to baseline
tools/tactics_bench.py --only attrition # one regime while iterating
tools/tactics_bench.py --write-baseline # record a new baseline
```

Every run writes to its own scratch ratings file under a temporary directory
that is removed afterwards, so a benchmark never adds rated evidence to the
shipped Tactics ledger.

### The document leads with the mistake it exists to prevent

`advanced_v1` is a frozen copy of the live controller, and nearly everything
separating them is empire-level machinery an arena never exercises — so that
column sits near 50% whatever the tactical AI does. **A near-50% result there
is the expected null, not a finding**, and I read it as one earlier in this
work before checking against a genuinely different opponent. `basic` is the
informative opponent, and it is the `basic` column that moves.

### The recorded baseline

| regime | advanced vs basic | advanced vs advanced_v1 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 city per side | 97.5% | 77.5% (62.5–87.7) |
| no cities | 2.5% | 47.5% (32.9–62.5) |
| no cities, random era | 20.0% | 52.5% (37.5–67.1) |

The inversion between the first two rows is the whole finding: the advanced
controller is overwhelmingly better with a city to take and overwhelmingly
worse when the only thing to do is fight. Running the battery as a battery also
produced a figure the ad-hoc runs had missed — across random eras it recovers
to 20%, so the collapse is worst in the Ancient era, which is exactly the one a
fixed-era sweep measures.

## Validation

- [x] Branch started from current `origin/main`
- [x] Ownership/overlap is coordinated above — no open PR claims these files
- [x] Latest `origin/main` merged before ready — branch cut from current `origin/main` (f004df8b) this session
- [x] `git diff --check origin/main...`
- [x] `cargo test --profile ci --locked` — exit 0, all 8 suites (no Rust changed; run as the guard against an accidental engine edit)
- [x] Relevant focused tests — `python3 -m unittest` over the full policy list including the new suite: 241 tests, OK. The new cases cover the parsing, which is where a benchmark goes quietly wrong: a leaderboard row and a standardized pair-score line share a prefix, and reading one as the other reports the order-sensitive figure as the order-independent one
- [x] Soak run for engine changes, or reason it is not applicable — not applicable: a benchmark tool, a generated document and one CI line; no engine, rules or client change. The tool itself was run end to end, writing the baseline and then re-running `--only attrition` to exercise the comparison path, which read `+0.0` against the recorded figures
- [x] No unrelated formatting, generated output, or runtime artifacts

The test suite is added to the policy workflow's test list. Without that line CI
would never run it — the same gap that left `test_civvis_desktop_apps.py` red
for three days.

## Notes for integration

Squash merge only. Delete the branch after merge.

The baseline is the shipped controllers as of `f004df8b`. Regenerate and quote
the diff in any PR that moves tactical play.

items.title: feat: M-2 — projection accuracy scoreboard (the benchmark harness)
items.body:
The referee for the whole projections project: every stored week-horizon projection set scored against the actual weekly team totals already stored in `league_week_scoreboards` — per source × week × category. This is the merge gate for the FCP model (M-3's baseline comparison; M-7 merges only if it beats v1 here) and works today for BBM vs ESPN-15.

**Metrics** (per category, across the league's fantasy teams): MAE, MAE% (miss as a share of the category's actual level, so categories are comparable), signed bias (positive = over-projection), and Spearman rank correlation. GP is scored as a bonus category when the league tracks it — separates "wrong about schedules/availability" from "wrong about rates". Per-source aggregates across all scored weeks.

**The missing-data problem this also fixes:** ESPN week projections were live-only (the virtual set) — nothing ever recorded what ESPN projected at the time, so past weeks were permanently unscorable. The refresh worker now snapshots one ESPN-15 week set per (league, week), saved with `activate=False` so benchmark data never hijacks the user's chosen projection source. Failure-isolated phase; no-op on re-runs within a week.

**Roster mapping:** projected team totals need to know who was on which fantasy roster that week. ESPN snapshots embed it (`roster_team`); global uploads (BBM) borrow the same week's ESPN snapshot roster map. No roster source → reported unscoreable, never guessed. All unscoreable (source, week) pairs come back with a reason: week in progress (partial actuals excluded via a new cheap `get_current_snapshot_week` lookup), no stored actuals, no roster mapping, no team overlap.

**Surface:** `GET /leagues/{slug}/projection-accuracy` + internal page at `/leagues/:slug/accuracy` — source-vs-source summary table (MAE% + ρ per category), scored-week detail with team coverage and unassigned-player counts, plain-language unscoreable list.

**Granularity note (scope honesty):** v1 scores at the fantasy-team-week level because that's what stored actuals contain. The spec's player-level MAE/rank-correlation needs per-player weekly actuals (nba_api game logs on the M-1 pipeline) — deliberate follow-up, noted in the module docstring.

**Tests:** 31 backend + 4 frontend. Per the spec, the harness itself is tested against a synthetic season with known answers: perfect projection → MAE 0 / ρ 1.0; constant +5 offset reproduces exactly as MAE 5 / bias +5; inverted projection → ρ −1. Plus attempt-weighted FG% (never averaged percentages), store snapshot semantics (activate=False leaves the active set untouched; `league_slug` round-trips; pre-M-2 manifests load fine), orchestration (borrowed rosters, per-league scoping, newest-set-wins, current-week exclusion), and worker snapshot idempotence. Full suites green: 518 backend clean-env, 62 frontend, tsc clean.

No migrations. Zero changes to existing consumers — the store changes are additive (`activate` defaults to True, `league_slug` defaults to None).

items.title: fix(benchmarks): PLAN-0104 Step 1 — repair stale SQL_EXPECT and make its guard read the artifact
items.body:
## What

**PLAN-0104 Step 1.** Repairs two factually-wrong `SQL_EXPECT` gold tokens in the text-to-SQL comparison arm, and — the load-bearing half — makes the guard that was supposed to catch them actually able to fail. 2 files, +74/−3.

## The two tokens, and why nothing caught them

`SQL_EXPECT["nl-02"]` was `["11"]` and `["nl-05"]` was `["1"]`, against real values of **13** and **2**. PLAN-0070 added two synthetic readings (one warn-severity) and this constant was never updated. Because `score_sql` requires every expected token to appear in the stringified result, `"11"` can never appear in `"13"` — **both cases scored `wrong` on every run of this arm, silently.**

The reason it survived is the interesting part. `test_gold_values_cross_check_against_real_sql` has carried the docstring *"The SQL_EXPECT tokens are the true answers (validates the gold set)"* since session 58 — and its body **never referenced `SQL_EXPECT` at all**. It asserted `13`, `2`, `96.5`, `5`, `41.3` as literals beside the constant. Those assertions pin the *data*, which is genuinely useful, but nothing ever compared the constant *to* the data, so drift between them could not redden.

**A guard that reads its own copy of the answer cannot fail.**

## The fix keeps both layers rather than swapping one for the other

1. **Layer 1 (kept).** The literal assertions stay — they redden if `synthetic.py` moves.
2. **Layer 2 (new).** A hand-written correct SQL per question (`CANONICAL_SQL`) is executed, and the **real result rows are fed through the production `score_sql`**, asserting `correct`. A stale token now fails.

Layer 2 covers **every scored qid**, not the five the old test happened to touch, and asserts that coverage explicitly (`set(CANONICAL_SQL) == set(SQL_EXPECT) - HONESTY_QIDS`) so an uncovered qid cannot go stale the way nl-02 and nl-05 did. The honesty probe (nl-12) is scored from the error path, never from rows.

## Non-vacuity probe — run, and the RED seen, before any of this was trusted

Replanting `"nl-02": ["13"]` → `["11"]` (from a `/tmp` copy, **never restored from git**):

```
AssertionError: nl-02: SQL_EXPECT=['11'] does not match the real result [(13,)]
                — the gold token is stale, or the synthetic data moved
assert 'wrong' == 'correct'
tests/benchmark/test_nl_query_text_to_sql.py:147
```

The probe was designed so its result is informative, not merely red: **layer 1 stays green through this mutation** — execution reaches line 147 — which demonstrates that the OLD guard could not have caught this defect and that the new layer is what does. Restoration verified byte-identical; suite green again after.

## Deliberately NOT changed — `nl-03`, surfaced for Cray

Its token list omits `event-reading-08`, which `gold.yaml` lists among its three expected ids. **This is a different defect class.** `score_sql` matches a *subset*, so nl-03's present tokens are correct and it still scores `correct` — the oracle is **weaker than it should be, not wrong**. Adding the token would make the benchmark **stricter**: a model whose SQL filters by unit would flip nl-03 from `correct` to `wrong`. That changes what the measured numbers mean, which is a measurement decision rather than a typo fix, so it is not taken unilaterally.

Also noted and not acted on: `score_sql` matches tokens as **substrings**, so an expected `"1"` would match a result of `"21"`. Changing that alters the benchmark's semantics and is out of scope here.

## Verification — on the committed tree, `git diff --stat HEAD` empty

| Gate | Result |
|---|---|
| full `tests/` | **4028 passed, 8 skipped** (469s) |
| `mypy --strict services/` | Success, no issues in 134 source files |
| `ruff check .` | All checks passed |
| `ruff format --check .` | clean |

⚠️ ruff was run against `git archive HEAD` extracted to a temp dir — CI's actual view — because a bare `ruff check .` in the working directory also lints untracked local scratch files.

## Why this Step ran first

Step 7's live evidence run scores against this arm. Left stale, two of the twelve cases would have scored wrong on the very run the PLAN needs as its proof.

items.title: Add search, indexes and explain; add an MCP benchmark arm; fix two scoring bugs
items.body:
Completes steps 6 and 7 of the design brief: the three remaining commands, and a third benchmark arm so the published table covers psql, MCP and `pg-axi` together.

## Commands

`search <pattern>`, `indexes [table]` and `explain "<sql>"`, bringing the CLI to the six commands in the brief.

Three decisions worth a reviewer's attention, since none were specified:

- **`explain` does not execute by default.** `--analyze` opts into real execution and wraps it in a transaction that is always rolled back. Explaining a `DELETE` must not delete anything. CI asserts this rather than trusting it.
- **`search` returns no row counts.** Mixing an estimate here against the exact counts the summary gives would be a quiet inconsistency; `table <name>` is one step away with the real number.
- **Primary keys and unique constraints are never listed as unused**, even at zero scans, because dropping them is not an option the reader has.

## Benchmark: three arms

| arm | success | avg input | avg turns | avg cost |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| psql | 98% (137/140) | 4,469 | 3.34 | $0.0059 |
| MCP (DBHub 1.2.0) | 95% (133/140) | 4,989 | 3.22 | $0.0065 |
| **pg-axi** | **100% (140/140)** | **3,629** | **3.05** | **$0.0048** |

14 tasks, 10 repeats, 420 runs under one set of conditions. 19% fewer input tokens than psql (95% CI -30% to -5%), 27% fewer than MCP (CI -43% to -10%).

DBHub was chosen because it is the Postgres MCP example in Anthropic's own Claude Code documentation. The obvious candidate, `@modelcontextprotocol/server-postgres`, is deprecated and archived with a published unpatched SQL-injection writeup.

### The accuracy result

On "which table has the most rows" the answer is `payment`, 16,049.

| arm | `payment` | `rental` |
|---|---|---|
| psql | 7/10 | 3/10 |
| MCP | 3/10 | **7/10** |
| **pg-axi** | **10/10** | 0/10 |

`payment` is partitioned, so `pg_stat_user_tables` shows the parent empty and `rental` looks largest. MCP does worst because `search_objects` is the natural tool to reach for and lists tables without row counts, routing the agent into the statistics views. `pg-axi` folds partitions into their root and counts exactly.

MCP also takes the single biggest win on the board, `email-columns` at 2,638 tokens against 5,435 and 7,000. That is in the README next to its failures.

## Two scoring bugs, both fixed

Found while investigating a `pg-axi` "failure":

- **`staff-count` demanded the word "staff"** while its prompt asked only for a count, so the correct answer `2` was scored wrong three times in ten. That penalty falls hardest on whichever arm encourages brevity, which is the arm under test.
- **`hasNumber` used `includes`**, so "12 staff" would have passed a check expecting 2. A wrong answer scored as a pass, worst where the expected numbers are small.

Now matched on digit boundaries and covered by `test/bench-checks.test.ts`. The harness had tests for the CLI but none for the code that decides pass or fail. All stored runs were re-scored offline against the corrected checks; only the definitive run changed, and only in `pg-axi`'s favour.

## Harness changes

- `Arm` now exposes a list of tools rather than one. An MCP server declares its own surface and usually exposes several; that is a real difference between these interfaces, not something to normalise away. Tool descriptions are passed through unmodified.
- `bench/trace.ts` had its own copy of the agent loop and system prompt. It is the tool used to establish the turn-count finding, so drift would have meant explaining a run that never happened. It now drives the real loop through a trace hook.
- Turn count added to the report. The whole finding is about turns and only tool calls were being shown.
- Arms are built lazily, so an arm nobody asked for never spawns a process. The MCP server version is pinned.

## A hypothesis that did not survive

The turn-count finding suggested `pg-axi`'s own next-step lines might be causing serial round trips. Tested with three variants of the disclosure block against 280 runs: turn count is flat at 2.97 / 2.99 / 2.97, moving by 0.00 turns paired across tasks. Disclosure costs about 46 input tokens per run, 1.3%, which is just the size of the block. Shipped behaviour unchanged.

## Reviewer notes

- The earlier README claimed 19% off a single 5-repeat run. Across three runs that figure ranged 7% to 20%, driven by one high-variance task. The table now carries bootstrapped intervals and says so explicitly.
- Raw results for every published figure are committed under `bench/results/`, force-added past the gitignore.
- Benchmark spend for this PR was about $7 of the $30 cap, on Claude Haiku 4.5 via Bedrock.
- Not done: step 8, packaging and npm publish.

items.title: feat(health): run the healthcare benchmarks on the Whissle key alone
items.body:
## The problem

Two of the three health adapters demanded an external OpenAI / Anthropic / Bedrock key for LLMs that are **not the thing being measured**:

| adapter | LLMs it needed besides the agent under test | previously required |
|---|---|---|
| PatientAgentBench | patient simulator, K=2 jury, sandbox (EHR) generator | `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` or AWS Bedrock creds |
| AgentClinic | patient, measurement reader, moderator, decline classifier | already Whissle-default, but the moderator was undefended |
| MedAgentBench | **none** | nothing |

`.env` has only `WHISSLE_API_KEY` and `WHISSLE_BASE`, so every full matrix run was blocked on credentials for the measuring apparatus rather than on the agent.

## The fix

Route those support LLMs through Whissle's own à-la-carte model API (`POST /api/models/chat`) by default — the same endpoint `src/tau2/flow/usersim.py` has been driving the flow-sim user simulator *and* its task-success and goal-drift judges with all along. That single choice is why the flow-sim effort runs on nothing but `WHISSLE_API_KEY`, and it now does the same for health.

Routing is **selectable, not hard-wired**:

```
--judge-provider whissle|openai|anthropic     # default: whissle
--judge-model <model>                          # override the external model
--support-llm litellm:<model>                  # raw escape hatch, unchanged
```

The external path is fully intact and fails fast with the exact missing env var — it is the configuration a *published* number should use.

### What each adapter needed

**`src/tau2/health/model_router.py`** (new, shared) — provider selection, fail-fast key check, cost ledger, the independence caveat text, and the constrained-decode helper. **Retry/error handling is delegated to `usersim.WhissleModel`, not reimplemented.** That class already owns the one correct policy for this endpoint (retry 5xx and empty completions with a long backoff, never retry a 4xx), learned when transient empty completions were silently killing ~40% of flow-sim sessions. Both benchmarks now inherit it by construction rather than by a third copy.

**PatientAgentBench** — the real work. It is CC-BY-NC-4.0 and explicitly takes no PRs, so nothing here forks or patches their tree. `patientagent/judge_model.py`:

1. **adds** three keys (`whissle-judge` / `whissle-patient` / `whissle-sandbox`) to their `MODEL_STORE` dict — no upstream entry is touched;
2. **wraps** `config.create_chat_model`, documented upstream as "the single factory for all LLM creation in the project". Configs whose provider is `whissle-model-api` get our `BaseChatModel`; every other provider falls through to their untouched code. Their six consumers do `from ...config import create_chat_model` at import time, so the wrapper is rebound in each already-imported module too — otherwise an already-loaded evaluator would still demand AWS creds.

A minimal `BaseChatModel` is sufficient and verified: nothing on the patient/jury/sandbox path calls `bind_tools` or `with_structured_output` — they all `invoke(messages)` and parse text.

**AgentClinic** — the moderator now answers **exactly** `yes`/`no`. Upstream's grading rule is a literal string test; upstream could rely on that because it pinned one model to one prompt. Routed through any other backend, a reply of `"Yes."` scores a *correct* diagnosis wrong and the benchmark starts measuring the grader's punctuation instead of the doctor. The constraint is **decode-side only**:

- the system and user prompts stay byte-for-byte upstream (a test pins that `compare_results` and `moderate` send an identical first prompt);
- decorated replies canonicalize to the bare token;
- a genuinely non-conforming reply is retried with a one-word instruction appended to a *follow-up user message*;
- a reply that still never conforms falls back to upstream's strict rule and is **flagged, never guessed**.

Every run reports `moderator_retried`, `moderator_normalized` and `moderator_unconstrained`, so grader formatting can never move a number invisibly.

**MedAgentBench — needed nothing, and nothing changed.** Grading is fully programmatic: `grader.py` answers a strict boolean per task against constants stated in the task's own `context`/`instruction` (NDC/SNOMED/LOINC codes, dosing rules, referral text), with `--refsol` swapping in upstream's official module. There is no patient simulator and no LLM-as-a-judge. The practical consequence is now documented in `MEDAGENTBENCH.md`: a MedAgentBench number carries **no judge-independence caveat at all, because no model produced it**.

## The independence caveat, as worded

Written verbatim into `model_router.INDEPENDENCE_CAVEAT`, into `AGENTCLINIC.md` and `PATIENTAGENTBENCH.md`, and printed in every run report:

> Judge independence: this run's simulators and graders were routed through Whissle's own model API (`POST /api/models/chat`). That is a real frontier model, not a self-grading shortcut — the agent under test and the judge are different models on different prompts — and it is the right default for internal diagnostics, regression tracking and before/after comparisons, where what matters is that the measuring stick is held constant. It is NOT an independent judge: the same vendor supplies both the agent and the grader. A number published against the paper's leaderboard is materially stronger when the judge is re-run on an independent provider (`--judge-provider openai` or `anthropic`). Do not present a Whissle-judged number as if it were independently graded.

External-judge runs get the counterpart note instead. Every report records `judge_provider`, `judge_model` and `judge_independent`; `summary.json` carries them at the top level *and* in a `judge` block. Two further honesty measures:

- **K = 1, not 2, on the Whissle route.** The paper averages two evaluators. Two calls to the same endpoint is one grader sampled twice, not a jury, so the default is a single evaluator and the report prints `K = 1 (the paper uses K=2)`. Claiming K=2 would fake evaluator agreement.
- **A run with no judge record renders as "Judge provider: unrecorded — do not publish these numbers; re-run."** The report refuses to guess.

## Cost, kept visible

`/api/models/chat` bills our own wallet and these harnesses make many judge calls, so total calls + USD (per run and per case) are printed in both summaries and stored in both `summary.json`s.

## A bug this shook out

`/api/models/chat` caps output at **~512 tokens by default and truncates silently** — the caller sees a `200` with a cut-off body. PatientAgentBench's sandbox generator emits a multi-kB JSON document, so *every* session failed with `Unterminated string` and the first smoke run scored 0/3 with no error from the endpoint. `WhissleModel` gained an **opt-in** `max_tokens`; existing callers send a byte-identical body, so flow-sim numbers cannot shift under this change.

## Validation

**Offline: 60 new tests against a mocked model endpoint**, plus the existing suites green (`181 passed` in the tau2 venv, `28 passed` in the PatientAgentBench venv). Coverage:

- routing selection: `whissle` default, `openai`/`anthropic`, `litellm:<model>` passthrough, unknown provider rejected, external provider without its key fails fast;
- the inherited retry policy: empty completion retried, 5xx retried, connection error retried, **4xx not retried**, exhaustion raises;
- the moderator's exact-`yes` constraint: 8 decorated forms canonicalize without a retry, a verbose reply is retried (and the nudge lands on the follow-up *user* message while the system prompt stays upstream's), `no` is not coerced to `yes`, an unconstrainable reply is flagged not guessed;
- the `max_tokens` fix, and that flow-sim's request body is unchanged;
- provider, independence flag, caveat text and cost present in **both** adapters' reports; unrecorded-judge report refuses to publish;
- the no-fork integration: registry keys added without mutating theirs, `install()` idempotent, our provider intercepted, a `bedrock` config still takes *their* path, the factory rebound in already-imported consumer modules, and a real `BaseRubric` built on the Whissle route with `_bedrock_client is None`.

One pre-existing test changed on purpose: `test_moderator_strictness_is_recorded_not_hidden` encoded the old behaviour (`"Yes."` → scored wrong). It is now `test_moderator_decode_is_constrained_to_the_exact_token`, plus a new test for the never-conforms case.

**Live smoke — `WHISSLE_API_KEY` only, with `OPENAI_API_KEY` / `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` / `AWS_*` explicitly unset from the environment:**

| adapter | N | result | judge spend | previously |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| AgentClinic (MedQA, `--limit 5`, 12 inferences/case) | **N = 5** cases, 0 infra_fail | accuracy **100% (5/5)**, 0 declined, avg 6.6 inferences/case | 33 calls, **$0.0016** (6.6 calls/case) | ran, but the moderator was one `"Yes."` away from scoring a correct case wrong |
| PatientAgentBench (`sample_benchmark.json`, `--limit 3`, harness mode, 8 turns) | **N = 3** sessions, 0 excluded | weighted aggregate **3.77** — task completion 4.00 [100%], clinical safety 3.67 [67%], workflow accuracy 4.00 [100%], triage 3.33 [100%], helpfulness 3.33 [100%], conversational 4.67 [100%] | 30 calls, **$0.0065** (10/session) | **could not run at all** without `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` / AWS creds |

Both N are deliberately tiny — these are *runnability* proofs, not measurements. At N=3 and N=5 the CIs span most of the scale (clinical safety: [1.05, 6.28]) and nothing here should be quoted as a result. Artifacts for both are committed under `results/whissle/`.

Honest note on the AgentClinic smoke: the moderator happened to reply `"Yes"` (case only), which upstream's own `.lower()` already absorbed, so the constraint changed none of these five verdicts — `moderator_normalized` correctly reports 0. It is defence against the `"Yes."` form, not a number-mover here.

MedAgentBench was not smoked because nothing about it changed and it needs a FHIR server, not a key.

items.title: fix(benchmark): remove unpassable expectations from Automatic Complex suite
items.body:
## Why

The Automatic Complex suite (29 tests) had a very low success rate. Simulating an *ideal* model run against every test — the exact tool calls each instruction asks for — showed **9 of 29 tests failing on fully correct behaviour**, so the suite was capped at ~69% before model quality was measured at all.

## Root causes

| # | Defect | Tests affected |
|---|--------|----------------|
| 1 | Expectations demanded parameters whose value **is the tool's own schema default** (`blastType: 'blastn'`, `includeCoordinates`, `format: 'pdb'`, `representation: 'cartoon'`, `readingFrame: 1`, `includeLocal`). Models omit them, the tool behaves identically, but every concrete parameter was required to be present. | 6 |
| 2 | The workflow matcher took the **first call matching a tool name**, so a workflow with two `toggle_track` steps scored two parameter mismatches when the model toggled the tracks in the other order. | 1 |
| 3 | `ui_auto_01` counted tabs **only from array-shaped results**, but the runner always passes a parsed response object — every correct run reported 0 tabs opened. | 1 |
| 4 | Organism expectations rejected the abbreviation models emit (`'E. coli'` vs `'Escherichia coli'`, 44% string similarity). | 1 |
| 5 | Unsatisfiable expectations: the unregistered tools `navigate_to` / `quick_db_for_current_genome`, and `format: 'fasta'`, which is not in that parameter's enum (`standard\|wrapped\|single_line`). | — |

Two further defects that don't surface on ideal runs: tracker records were read from the **whole benchmark session**, so an earlier test's call could be matched with the wrong parameters, and the fixed 120 s match window was shorter than the 180 s timeouts of the BLAST/export tests, clipping their opening steps.

## Fixes

- `schemaDefault(value)` in `BenchmarkEvaluatorBase` — satisfied when omitted, still compared when sent — applied to the 13 affected expectations.
- Parameter-aware candidate selection in `matchWorkflowCallsToExpected`, plus `orderInsensitiveTools` on the genuinely independent steps.
- Tab counting from the executed-call record (tracker as fallback); organism-name normalization; removed the dead tools and the invalid enum value.
- Tracker records scoped to the test under evaluation; match window derived from the test's own timeout.

## The opposite defect, found via negative controls

Single-tool tests **never checked parameters** — the base evaluator read them from the top level of the parsed response — so a gel run with the wrong ladder *and* wrong percentage scored 5/5. Concrete parameters must now match, as the workflow path already required. Fuzzy string matching is also limited to values ≥12 chars: `blastp` is 83% similar to `blastn` and was passing as a match.

## Verification

- **29/29** tests pass on ideal behaviour, and still pass when the model adds exploratory calls or uses snake_case parameters.
- **11 negative controls** (wrong gene, wrong organism, wrong ladder, protein-vs-nucleotide BLAST, half-finished workflows, failed calls) all still fail.
- New guard `test/unit/automatic-complex-golden-path.test.js` pins both directions and cross-checks every expectation against the tool registry, so unknown tools, unknown parameters, invalid enum values and unwrapped schema defaults fail CI.
- Full suite green: **1383 tests / 131 files**. Prettier clean.

## Scope note

This removes the cases where correct behaviour was scored as failure, so the ceiling is now 100%. The *actual* rate depends on model performance — there were no recorded benchmark results in the repo to measure against.

items.title: feat: cooperative benchmarking with privacy-safe server-side averages (#75)
items.body:
## Summary

Implements **Cooperative Benchmarking** (Issue #75) — giving **Cooperative** users access to the benchmarking dashboard so they can compare themselves against **National / Regional / Sector** averages, **without exposing other cooperatives' raw financial data**.

The core change is architectural: average computation moves **from the browser to the backend**, and the cooperative response type becomes **structurally incapable** of containing another cooperative's raw rows.

---

## Motivation / Problem

Previously `/app/benchmarking` was admin-only (`ministry`, `federation`, `apex`). The frontend called `GET /api/v1/analytics/national-overview`, which returned **every cooperative's raw KPI row**, and computed averages **in the browser**.

Extending this to cooperative users broke one of two invariants:
- **Data leak** — a coop user would receive competitors' raw financials.
- **Broken math** — scoping the array to the caller's own row makes the "national average" equal their own score.

**Root cause:** averages lived in the wrong layer (client-side over raw data), forcing the client to receive raw data to compute them.

---

## Changes

### Backend (Rust / Axum)
- **Refactor:** extracted reusable `compute_coop_rows()` from `get_national_overview` (pure refactor — admin behavior unchanged).
- **New endpoint:** `GET /api/v1/analytics/benchmark` — computes averages over the **full population server-side** and returns only the caller's own row + aggregate averages.
- **DTOs:** `BenchmarkResponse`, `BenchmarkInsufficientData`, `BenchmarkParams` — the response type has **no `cooperatives[]` field**, making the privacy guarantee structural.
- **DRY:** shared `scoped_average()` helper for regional / sector / sector+regional slices.
- **Differential-privacy guard:** `MIN_CONTRIBUTORS = 3` withholds averages over tiny populations.
- **Routes + OpenAPI:** registered the endpoint and schemas; added `tests/handlers_benchmark.rs`.

### Frontend (React / TanStack)
- **Hook:** `useBenchmark` calling the new endpoint via the generated OpenAPI client.
- **Route guard + nav:** added `"cooperative"` role to `/app/benchmarking` and the sidebar.
- **Role-aware widget** (`CooperativeComparison.tsx`):
  - Coop users → benchmark endpoint; own coop locked; peer dropdown shows **only averages** (never other coops).
  - Admins → national-overview; can still compare any two coops.
  - Four comparison targets: National, Regional, Sector (national), Sector (regional).
  - **Apex/Fed sector scope:** sector averages computed over their own scoped coops (level-scoped) with a lower `MIN_CONTRIBUTORS_APEX_FED = 2` threshold.
  - **Sector context surfaced** via a badge next to the selected coop and a subtitle under the comparison target (labels read simply "Sector Average").
  - **Honest empty states:** amber notice instead of a misleading `0` when an average is withheld.
- **i18n:** all new strings added across `en`, `fr`, `pt`, `ss`.

### Docs
- `docs/benchmarkdesign.md` — full design + implementation record.
- `docs/testingUide.md` — platform hierarchy & submission workflow testing guide.

---

## Testing

- **Backend:** `cargo fmt` ✅, `cargo clippy` ✅, `cargo test` — 253 tests pass (incl. new benchmark handler tests).
- **Frontend:** `tsc --noEmit` ✅, changed files lint-clean ✅, 184 unit tests pass.
- **OpenAPI:** regenerated backend + frontend client.
- **Manual (dev DB):** seeded approved 2025 submissions for 4 finance coops (varied, realistic SACCO values) and verified the Sector / Sector (regional) charts render at the apex/fed level once the contributor threshold is met, and that the "Not enough cooperatives…" notice appears below the threshold.

---

## Notes

This branch also carries several previously-merged fixes (Keycloak dynamic URL/redirects, landing page, member-list crash safeguard, i18n init, deployment env fixes) that were integrated from other branches. If a more focused review is preferred, those can be split out separately.

Closes #75

items.title: P1.6 Ladder benchmarks: both ladders measurement-backed, reusable script
items.body:
Closes #9

## Why

The D2 ladders were seeded as hypotheses. The eyes side was corrected by measurement in #28 (which removed a 121s-to-504 model). This closes the brain side and leaves a reusable script so re-measurement — free models churn monthly — is one command instead of ad-hoc probes.

## Measurements (live, run by the orchestrator)

| Rung | Model | Runs | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| brain 1 | `nemotron-3-ultra-550b-a55b:free` | 21.0, 16.1, 18.2, 10.4, 13.5, 9.9s | accurate every run; production verifier PASS every run |
| brain 2 | `nemotron-3-super-120b-a12b:free` | 16.7, 23.8s | accurate both runs |

**Current order confirmed — no config change.** Both inside the 45s ceiling. Full deep path end to end: **~16–27s** for a dense document. Zero invented numbers across 8 live brain calls.

## What ships

- `scripts/benchmark_ladders.py` — manual-only; model list derived from `load_registry()` so it **cannot drift from config**; request shapes reused byte-identical from the production nodes; brain replies scored with the production `_numbers_verified`, not ad-hoc string matching
- `tests/test_benchmark_script.py` — 8 offline tests; the drift guard fails if the script hardcodes models (mutation-proved: 4 tests fail)
- 291 tests total

## Why production-verifier scoring is load-bearing

My first ad-hoc probe marked a correct reply as a failure — the model had legitimately spelled amounts out ("forty-one dollars and twenty cents"), which literal string matching flagged. Benchmarks that misjudge models cause wrong ladder decisions; the script now scores exactly as production does.

## Honest notes

- That spelled-out style exposed a verifier leniency: `_numbers_verified` checks digit tokens only, so a spelled-out invented amount would bypass it. Accepted for now (zero hallucinations observed in all live runs; word-to-number parsing judged not worth it) — recorded in the decision log with a revisit trigger under #33.
- Red-first sequencing slip, disclosed by the implementer: the script was drafted before the red commit was staged, then the sequence was reconstructed honestly. The committed red artifact genuinely fails on checkout (verified independently); noting the slip rather than hiding it.
- No network at import (verified with a socket-level trip-wire); no client constructed outside `main()`.
