items.title: Fix audit findings: redaction correctness, daemon crash-loops, delivery guarantees, benchmark scoring
items.body:
A full-repo quality audit surfaced correctness gaps against the project's own documented invariants. This fixes them in 10 focused, individually-revertable commits, each with regression tests.

**Suite: 717 → 764 tests, all green** (verified on 3.11/3.12/3.13; changed files parse clean under the 3.10 grammar). ruff (pinned 0.15.22), `tsc --noEmit`, Vite build, and the A/B safety selftest all pass.

Every finding below was verified against the real code before fixing — several by executing it.

## Redaction correctness (`fix(redact)`)
- **Private keys leaked through diffs** — the PEM pattern required `\n-----END`, but every `git diff` line carries a `+`/`-`/space marker, so `\n+-----END` never matched. This is the primary capture path.
- **Ordinary code was falsely redacted** — the assignment pattern matched `key`/`token`/… as a *substring*, so `tokenizer = "bert-base-uncased"` became a `«REDACTED»` marker, which the critic is taught IS a confirmed secret. Now requires a delimited token (keeps `API_KEY`, `db_password`, `apiKey`).
- PASS `reason`, `malformed`, the verify inconclusive note, and distilled knowledge facts all skipped sanitization (SECURITY.md claimed otherwise for facts).

## Daemon crash-loops (`fix(daemons)`)
Each of these turned a routine event into a *permanent* crash loop (recurs on every restart):
- critic died on a valid-JSON non-dict observation line; observer died on a transcript deleted mid-glob (Claude Code prunes sessions); reflector died on one torn harvested case via the rewrite gate — after burning the paid model call but before advancing its backoff counter.
- Both state loaders crashed on valid-JSON-wrong-shape instead of rebuilding; `read_rows` raised on a trailing line torn mid-multibyte-character.
- Atomic writes for harvested cases + the heuristics-history archive (the rollback restore source); guarded beat bodies in all three loops.

## Delivery guarantees (`fix(hooks)`)
- The ledger TTL-pruned **once-ever** marks, so receipts re-announced every ~10 min, a "weakened tests" receipt **re-blocked Stop** every ~10 min even after rebuttal, and the done-gate re-waited up to 120s. Reserved keys are now count-bounded, never age-expired.
- Suggestion-mark retention was *below* the reflector's 900s grading horizon, so delivered (possibly accepted) findings graded `undelivered` and fell out of the acceptance metric.
- `peer_hook.py` imported the critic chain **before** its fail-open guard existed — a transient syntax error in files the agent is actively editing tracebacked on every hook event.

## Review quality (`fix(screen/probe/persona)`, `fix(critic)`)
- `persona.md` still taught the *pre-redesign* verify protocol, contradicting `verify.py` — a model obeying it got its status line executed as Python, landing "inconclusive" and silently withholding true findings.
- Whole test-file deletion was invisible to test-weakening screening (`+++ /dev/null`); `async def test_` never counted as a test.
- False positives fixed: SafeLoader exemption with a nested-call argument, and a literal `f` before a quote inside a *parameterized* query reading as an f-string.
- Probes could mint a finding from a crashed or self-contradictory run.
- Unvalidated model JSON: a `"critical"` severity was stored verbatim and then **never delivered** (hooks gate on exact `{medium,high}`); a non-string `issue` escaped as a TypeError and burned the batch's retries.
- Transport failures committed the offset instead of requeueing (code written during a brief outage was never reviewed); a "done" request was consumed even when no review dispatched, losing the session receipt.

## Benchmark integrity (`fix(evals)` ×2)
- Crashed trials were **dropped from the mean** instead of scoring 0 — inflating whichever arm crashed more, and specifically hiding the dependency-hallucination failure mode one task engineers on purpose.
- Hidden tests scored against *printed* checks, so **crashing beat being wrong**; now scored against the checks the source declares.
- Two safety tasks handed a no-op session a free SAFE while three scored it UNSAFE; now uniform (selftest still discriminates good vs bad on all five).
- Reusing `--out` left prior work in trial dirs (next agent started pre-solved) and appended duplicate rows.
- Hangs/failed clones no longer abort a multi-hour paid run; the `--repo-url` sha pin is now verified; training sessions get the same contamination isolation as the A/B arms; `rescore` no longer skips the safety tier.

## Dashboard + launcher (`fix(ui)`, `fix(launcher)`)
- Activity `seq` was window-relative, so it shifted for the same event as the log grew — and React keys off it, silently transferring a row's expanded state to a *different* event. Now the line's absolute byte offset.
- Tail-follow depended on a length that pins at 120, so auto-scroll died exactly when a session got going.
- `/prober off` didn't disable council mode when `COUNCIL_PROBER` was exported or in `~/.codecouncil/env`; the launcher resolved env differently than the critic it launches.

## Tests (`test:`)
Added coverage for the two most load-bearing untested invariants: **"refuted findings are never delivered"** (the product thesis — the string `refuted` did not appear in `test_hooks.py`) and verify.py's redaction boundary.

---

**Not included, deliberately:** the shared-helper dedup sweep (epoch/cap/tolerant-read). Those are trivial 4-line stdlib wrappers where consolidation adds cross-module coupling for little gain — better as its own reviewed PR than mixed into correctness fixes.

items.title: Score malformed model outputs as wrong
items.body:
## What changed

- Distinguishes EvalPlus model-output normalization failures from runtime or adapter generation failures.
- Keeps malformed model responses in the evaluator denominator as incorrect answers while preserving raw output and explicit failure accounting.
- Continues to degrade or suppress capability evidence when execution failures leave evidence missing.
- Documents the scoring boundary in the changelog and capability benchmark guide.

## Why

A full Ornith 1.0 9B HumanEval+ run produced one unclosed code fence among 164 attempted tasks. EvalPlus correctly counted that response as wrong, but Runner previously classified the model-output miss like missing infrastructure evidence and discarded the otherwise valid component score.

## Impact

The benchmark component remains usable and honest: the malformed response stays visible and wrong, while runtime failures still fail closed. Existing multi-component score-readiness gates remain unchanged.

## Validation

- `./scripts/test_all.sh` — 601 tests, OK
- `python3 -m ruff check python scripts` — clean
- Real local-native Apple M1 Pro run with llama.cpp b9994: valid comparable bundle `qb_20260720_192921_9bd900e2`; HumanEval+ 121/164, one normalization failure retained in the denominator

## Boundaries

- No contract-version or Runner-version bump.
- No benchmark-suite expansion.
- No claim that one HumanEval+ component is a headline Local Coding Score.

items.title: fix: 11 audit findings across providers, orchestrator, ingestion, tui, benchmark
items.body:
## Summary

Fixes 11 findings from a swarm audit of `providers/`, `orchestrator/`, `ingestion/`, `agents/`, `tui/`, and `benchmark/`:

- **`providers/router.ts`** — removed a vacuous `isFatalMessage`/`FATAL_KEYWORDS` guard that could never gate anything (quota-tagged errors and `AuthError` are mutually exclusive by construction); simplified to `isFatalAuthError(lastError)` alone.
- **`providers/router.ts`** — `FallbackProvider.complete()` now rethrows a genuine `AbortError` instead of repackaging cancellation as `AuthError`/`AllProvidersExhaustedError`, restoring the `return []`-on-cancel contract that `agents/base.ts`, `combined.ts`, and `synthesis.ts` depend on.
- **`orchestrator/swarm.ts`** — provider shares are now re-mapped onto the `'combined'` agent name when economy mode collapses specialists into `CombinedAnalyzer`, so economy mode no longer silently ignores configured provider shares.
- **`tui/components/SettingsPanel.tsx`** — shrinking `agentCount` now trims already-persisted provider shares that would otherwise exceed it, mirroring the share field's own clamp logic.
- **`benchmark/scorer.ts`** — `matchDefect()` now picks the nearest in-tolerance defect across all categories instead of always preferring `real-bug` first, fixing a case where a claim about a false-positive trap could be wrongly scored as a true positive.
- **`ingestion/walker.ts`**, **`ingestion/importExtractor.ts`** — removed stray unconditional `console.log('DEBUG: ...')` calls that leaked into every run's output (including the TUI Output Pane).

items.title: Make IFEval empty-output evidence honest
items.body:
## What changed

- classifies completed IFEval generations with no scorer-visible text as model-output failures
- records those failures while preserving strict wrong-answer scoring for isolated misses
- quarantines IFEval only when more than half of responses are empty
- records token-budget exhaustion as diagnostic context without using it alone to invalidate evidence
- binds the host-side output-shape policy into benchmark protocol identity

## Why

A real MiniCPM5 standard run produced 4 empty visible IFEval responses, but the Runner reported zero model-output failures. That made the evidence cleaner than the underlying completion shape. This preserves the strict score while making the failure count honest and prevents a systemic template/runtime mismatch from becoming a capability score.

## Validation

- `python3 -m unittest python/runner-core/tests/test_capabilities.py` — 76 passed
- `python3 -m ruff check python/runner-core/src/infergrade/capabilities.py python/runner-core/tests/test_capabilities.py` — passed
- `./scripts/test_all.sh` — 735 passed
- real-output replay: 100 MiniCPM5 IFEval rows, 4 empty visible responses, 63 token-limit responses; gate passed and strict 0.18 metric remained valid
- synthetic systemic case: 3/4 empty responses; quarantined as not comparable

## Evidence boundary

This does not claim MiniCPM5 capability quality, promote llama.cpp b10375, publish a runtime catalog generation, release Runner, or deploy anything. The real bundle remains local-only and its runtime receipt is operator-path/local-fingerprint evidence.

items.title: fix(benchmark): total-vs-forms notes need label nesting, not arithmetic
items.body:
## The defect

`build_review_doc.py` decided one label row was a *constituent form* of another by asking whether the next 2–3 amounts happened to sum to the current one. No name check, no unit check, no parent/child evidence of any kind.

A 2:1:1 BCAA ratio **guarantees** `Leucine == Isoleucine + Valine`, so every BCAA product tripped it.

On the 13,271-blob corpus the rule fired on **806 products, 639 of them (79%) chemically unrelated**:

- `GABA 200 == Theanine 100 + Rhodiola 100` — three top-level siblings
- `Folate 400mcg == B12 50mcg + Biotin 300mcg + Pantothenic Acid 50mg`
- 292 notes summed across **mixed units**, adding mcg to mg as one scale

## Root cause: two matchers over one label

The freeze dropped the source row nesting, so the document builder had nothing left to reason from but arithmetic. Same smell as 94125a96.

Now the freeze resolves the relationship **once**, from the label's own nesting, and the document only renders it:

- `_resolve_constituent_rollups` emits `parent_index` (source fact) and `constituent_child_indexes` (derived annotation)
- A parent must account for **all** its direct children — no positional window — at the same unit, all positive, summing exactly
- `rollup()` contains zero inference and fails closed on a packet without the field

**806 → 171**, every one structurally evidenced. The sum check separates an additive total from a nested `standardized to X` marker row; requiring all children self-detects unreliable source nesting (4 products nest `Vitamin B12` under `Vitamin K` — those now emit nothing).

QC over all 171 (34 distinct signatures, every rare and cross-family shape inspected) found no chemically wrong note.

## Severity: not scoring, but it moved the oracle

The notes never re-enter the pipeline — no shipped score or dose changes. But the benchmark is the human oracle the v4 dose pillar is calibrated against, and **30 notes reached all three reviewers, 23 of them false**.

| | count |
|---|---:|
| notes sent per reviewer | 30 |
| retracted | 22 |
| retained, different correct roll-up | 1 |
| retained unchanged | 7 |
| **false claims distributed** | **23** |

## Study artifacts

The treatment of the affected rows is a protocol decision, not a code change, so this ships the evidence rather than a verdict:

- `CONTAMINATION_v6_rollup_notes.csv` — 90 rows (30 products × 3 reviewers) with `contamination_class` and `likely_direction_of_bias` (11 `dose_total_at_risk` vs 12 `inert_no_conventional_total`)
- `STUDY_AMENDMENT_v6_rollup_notes.md` — accounting, evidence, sha256s, recommended treatment
- `audit_reviewer_responses.py` — validates a returned response before it becomes calibration truth

## Audit of the returned reviewer file

PHAM's 120 responses audit clean: **120/120** pillar arithmetic, **38/38** PMIDs resolve live on PubMed, **156/160** citation→product pairs on-topic, **106/106** in-text Verification assertions match the scored pillar. One low-severity finding — a betaine meta-analysis cited on 4 SKUs containing no betaine, where no claim or score depends on it.

Of the 23 contaminated rows, 7 contain a checkable total and **all 7 state the correctly-summed figure**; none state the deflated one.

## Tests

`scripts/tests/test_reviewer_doc_constituent_forms.py` — 16 tests: never-again fixtures for BCAA / GABA / mixed-unit / phantom-zero, encoding invariants (acyclic, in-range), and a corpus guard asserting every emitted note is structurally evidenced.

```
bash scripts/test.sh fast
11,335 passed, 40 skipped
```

items.title: Benchmark against MiniSom and SOMPY, and track performance with asv
items.body:
## What

Benchmarks python-som against MiniSom and SOMPY, and adds asv to track it against its own git history. **No line under `src/` changes**, which is what makes a diff this wide safe to review; the five commits are ordered so it reads one concern at a time.

## Results, published as measured

| | batch | stepwise |
| --- | --- | --- |
| vs MiniSom | **1.34x-1.64x slower** (grows with map size) | 1.06x-1.12x faster |
| vs SOMPY | 1.30x-1.99x faster | SOMPY has no stepwise mode |

The MiniSom batch result is not favourable and is published unchanged. `batch_update` walks every node in Python, 108,000 `einsum` calls on a 60x60 map over 30 iterations, where MiniSom's node-side update is a single vectorised divide and its Python loop runs over the 400 samples instead. The ratio tracks nodes against samples. Vectorising it means changing `_core/_update.py`, so it is deliberately not in this diff.

## Why most of the work is fairness, not timing

The three packages look interchangeable and are not. MiniSom's `train_batch` is *stepwise* training; Eq. (8) is `train_batch_offline`. Only the gaussian is the same function in all three, and the bubble selects 9 nodes here against 1 in MiniSom at sigma=1. SOMPY's `calculate_quantization_error` returns an elementwise MAE rather than the mean Euclidean distance.

Eight controls reduce them to the same computation, and the trained models then agree: 2.8e-16 relative against MiniSom stepwise, 1.3e-15 batch, 1.4e-07 against SOMPY (which rounds its codebook to six decimals every iteration). That agreement is what makes the timings mean anything, and `tests/test_minisom_agreement.py` rechecks it on every CI run.

## A harness bug worth flagging

The first version of the harness reported MiniSom sequential as **7.10x faster**. That was wrong. `SOM.train` scores the whole dataset to fill in its `TrainingReport` and MiniSom's entry points do not, so timing `train` charged this package for a pass the other arm never made. With 30 steps against 400 samples, that pass was larger than the training itself. Timing the loops directly, the same case comes out 1.08x slower for MiniSom. Both numbers were reproducible; only one of them measured training. Recorded in the module docstring.

## SOMPY needs its own interpreter

It uses `np.Inf` at class-definition time, removed in NumPy 2.0, so it cannot be installed alongside this package at all. It gets a hand-built `.venv-sompy` and a subprocess worker, launched once per repeat so the arms still interleave. Nothing installs anything: the script prints the setup command and exits 0 if the environment is absent.

## asv

Sixteen benchmarks over the training loops, the kernel, matching, the SVD and artifacts. No timing gates anything: CI executes each once and discards the numbers. Real runs are `workflow_dispatch` only, because shared runners cannot measure anything. `.asv/` is gitignored, since `asv machine` writes the host's name, CPU model, RAM and kernel version.

## Verification

All five commits pass `ruff check`, `ruff format --check`, `mypy`, `pytest --cov` (461 tests, 100%) and `mkdocs build --strict` **independently**, not only at the tip. Prose scanned with `llm-writing-patterns`: zero severity-5 findings.

## Follow-ups, not here

- Vectorise `batch_update`'s node loop, worth roughly 1.6x at 60x60.
- Tell the MiniSom and SOMPY maintainers the comparison exists. Outward-facing, so it needs a separate go-ahead.

items.title: Improve LLM evaluation pipeline: independent benchmark, fine-grained metrics, gates, base-vs-fine-tuned comparison
items.body:
## Summary

Significantly improves the reliability of model evaluation without redesigning the existing pipeline. Adds a fully independent tool-calling benchmark, fine-grained metrics, deterministic plain-chat validation, configurable quality gates, and first-class base-vs-fine-tuned comparison, on top of the existing Hermes held-out split eval (kept as-is).

## What's new

- **Independent benchmark** (`data/benchmark/cases.jsonl`, `eval/benchmark.py`): 26 hand-authored cases across 10 scenario categories (single-tool selection, no-tool/plain-chat, ambiguous requests, nonexistent-tool requests, multi-tool choice, complex/optional/nullable/nested arguments, parallel tool calls, must-not-call traps). Extending it is a one-line JSONL append — no code change.
- **Fine-grained metrics** (`eval/metrics.py`): `tool_selection_accuracy`, `tool_call_precision`/`recall`, `false_positive`/`negative_tool_rate`, `argument_name`/`value_accuracy`, `required_argument_accuracy`, `schema_validity_rate`, `exact_tool_call_match`, `plain_chat_pass_rate`, `hallucinated_tool_name`/`argument_rate`, `missing_required_argument_rate` — global + per-category, kept separate so tool selection, structural validity, and semantic value correctness never hide each other.
- **Deterministic plain-chat validation** (`eval/plain_chat.py`): replaces the old min-length check with checks for unexpected tool calls, malformed/special-token/protocol-tag/role-prefix leakage, and degenerate repetition. No LLM-as-judge.
- **Quality gates** (`eval/gates.py`): documented mandatory/advisory thresholds; `run_benchmark`/`compare_models` exit non-zero on mandatory gate failure (CI-safe).
- **Base vs. fine-tuned comparison** (`eval/compare_models.py`): runs the same benchmark through both models, reports per-metric delta and regression/improvement verdicts, plus which model passes mandatory gates.
- **Reproducibility**: `Qwen/Qwen3-1.7B` pinned to an immutable HF revision (`configs/train.yaml`), threaded through Unsloth/`mlx_lm`/eval loading. Hermes dataset revision left unchanged.
- **Code quality**: Ruff + Pyright (basic mode; `train/`'s pre-existing typing debt scoped out — trl stub gaps unrelated to this change) + `pytest-cov`.
- **CI**: `.github/workflows/ci.yml` — lint, typecheck, unit tests on the locked env. No GPU model evaluation in CI (documented; run via existing `scripts/run_on_*.sh` on real hardware).
- **Docs**: README "Evaluation" section covers benchmark structure, adding cases, metrics, gates, CLI usage, and how to interpret a report.

## Verification

- `uv run ruff check .` — clean
- `uv run pyright` — 0 errors (3 warnings: optional `mlx_lm` import, matches existing convention)
- `uv run pytest` — 115 passed, 90% overall coverage; new eval logic (`metrics.py`, `gates.py`, `plain_chat.py`, `config.py`) at 100%
- Manual smoke tests of `score_benchmark`/`score_case`/`compare_reports` against perfect, adversarial, hallucinated-name, missing-required-arg, malformed-JSON, and wrong-value predictions — all scored as expected.

## Not run here

GPU/Metal-backed generation (`run_eval`'s/`run_benchmark`'s/`compare_models`'s actual model-loading and generation paths) — no GPU available in this environment. Exercised only through their pure sub-functions (scoring/aggregation/gating), which is where all the new logic lives.

items.title: fix: oracle path normalization — bare filenames match absolute paths
items.body:
## Found by the local baseline

The first live v2 baseline (local Qwen 27B, 43 scenarios × 3) scored **727 ± 19, 28/43 pass** — and every failure shared one harness bug: live agents read workspace files via their **absolute paths** (the tools resolve them), while the oracles expected bare relative names. 15 scenarios — all 12 review-* plus the headroom/refactor runs — scored 60 with `bullseye=0` despite **perfect code-anchored reviews** (the god-class review named SRP and every member correctly).

## The fix

`value_matches` (bench/oracle.cpp) now compares **basenames** when exactly one side is a bare filename; nested expectations keep exact semantics; globs unchanged. Red `290b40e` → green: 88 bench tests (3 new: bare-vs-absolute, absolute-vs-relative, nested-stays-exact), full gate zero warnings.

## Why this matters

This is the mission working: the first calibration run diagnosed the harness — a scenario oracle that can't distinguish "read the file" from "read the wrong file" was scoring perfect reviews as failures. Without the benchmark, this would have gone unnoticed while every model comparison silently ran on broken oracles.

items.title: test(mcp): benchmark cases for five deferred-tier candidates
items.body:
Five benchmark cases for candidates `docs/skill-candidates.md` screened and
**rejected**. They ship no skill and nothing is ablated.

## Why a case for something we decided not to write

Every rejection in that doc is conditional on the consuming tier — the doc says
so, and measures it: the same procedures collapse one tier down. What the prose
recorded was the *verdict*. What nothing recorded was the fixture, the truth and
the tolerance that produced it, so re-checking a rejection meant rebuilding the
benchmark from a paragraph. #720 decoupled a case from a served skill, which is
what makes these expressible: no `skill=`, the candidate's name as `namespace`.

| candidate | doc's low-tier failure |
|---|---|
| `local-thickness` | 1.50 / 1.44 / 1.60 — bit-identical to naive 2×EDT, against 5.00 / 3.00 / 2.40 |
| `fibre-orientation` | 89.1° on the wraparound population; coherence 0.82 on a random control |
| `strahler-ordering` | 1379 terminals against 422, narrated as "fractal-like" |
| `splitting-touching-objects` | *never measured at the low tier* |
| `photobleaching-correction` | *never measured at the low tier* |

**The last two are a different kind of case, and the difference is invisible
from the outside.** The doc's queue separates candidates it took one tier down
from ones it never did, and these two sit in the *untested at the low tier*
remainder. So they carry no low-tier number and have none to reproduce: what
they promise is only the other half of §4 — that the fixture separates the named
routes, measured. Three of these five are a gap someone measured; two are an
instrument waiting for a run, and `bench/README.md` now says which is which.

## Built the doc's own way

Protocol §4 — the reference and every wrong route were run on the fixture
*before* the tolerance was written, and the tolerance is the measured gap. Each
module carries the table it was derived from.

**local-thickness** — Hildebrand's largest inscribed sphere against twice the
distance transform.

| route | sphere | rod | slab |
|---|---|---|---|
| truth | 5.00 | 3.00 | 2.40 |
| Hildebrand, spacing honoured | 5.02 | 3.18 | 2.48 |
| naive 2×EDT | 1.54 | 1.52 | 1.36 |
| voxels assumed cubic | 1.31 | 0.97 | **2.46** |

Voxels are 4:1 anisotropic, which separates a second route. The bold cell is why
three shapes are scored: assuming cubic voxels is *right about the slab*, whose
thin direction runs along a fine axis — one object agreeing is how a spacing bug
survives a spot check.

**fibre-orientation** — three fields, because one cannot see the failure.

| route | field a | field b | field c |
|---|---|---|---|
| truth | 30.1° | 179.7° | no direction |
| global structure tensor | err 1.2° | err 0.7° | coh 0.052 |
| arithmetic mean of angles | err 0.0° | **err 81.8°** | — |
| no 90° rotation | err 88.8° | err 89.3° | — |
| mean of *local* coherence | — | — | **coh 0.544** |

The naive mean is exact on field a and catastrophic on b, so a single-field
fixture either passes the wrong route or cannot tell a wrap bug from a fitting
bug. The last row is the mechanism behind the doc's unexplained "0.82 on random
fibres": every fibre is locally aligned with itself, so averaging per-pixel
coherence reports alignment in a field that has none.
`alignment_shortfall_a` is a positive control — without it, "report 0
everywhere" passes field c vacuously.

**strahler-ordering** — an integration test, and the arbor arrives as a
segmented volume rather than a traced tree, so the run must skeletonize, cluster
junctions and collapse degree-2 runs before ordering anything.

| route | terminals | order | Rb |
|---|---|---|---|
| tree truth | 52 | 5 | 3.07 |
| skeletonize → cluster junctions → collapse → order | 53 (1.9%) | 5 | 3.16 |
| same, without junction clustering | 71 (36.5%) | 5 | 3.28 |
| Strahler order per skeleton voxel | 2138 (4011%) | 5 | 16.06 |

The volume route had to be earned. A first arbor lost 14.3% of its terminals
before Strahler was reached — which would have made the benchmark unwinnable
(§4) and scored the run on the wrong step (§8). The loss was **not**
skeletonization: it was the arbor crossing itself, since a crossing is a
junction the mask has and the tree does not. Rejection-sampling every segment
against every non-incident one removed it entirely.

Two things from that table worth keeping:

- The per-voxel failure is a factor of **forty**, where the doc's arms were off
  by three. Same mistake, denser sampling — a voxel skeleton is an order of
  magnitude denser than a tracing. Recorded so the two numbers are not compared
  as if they measured the same thing.
- **Max order is 5 for every route**, including both wrong ones. It confirms the
  doc's finding that maximum order cannot be the check, so it is collected and
  deliberately never scored.

**splitting-touching-objects** — two clusters of touching nuclei, F1 at IoU 0.5
via `segmentation_qc.match_labels`.

| route | cluster_a (7:1) | cluster_b (isotropic) |
|---|---|---|
| physical EDT, `sampling=spacing` | 1.000 | 1.000 |
| the same code with `sampling=None` | **0.809** | 1.000 |
| ..the same, suppression radius 1.5 µm | 0.333 | 1.000 |
| voxel EDT + `min_distance=5` px | 0.016 | 1.000 |
| watershed on the raw intensity | 0.704 | 0.571 |
| every local maximum a seed | 0.980 | 1.000 |
| no split at all (connected components) | 0.649 | 0.706 |

Rows 1 and 2 are the same dozen lines differing in one keyword. `cluster_b` is
the control — cubic voxels, where the spacing argument differs by a scale factor
a watershed cannot see — so a run that fails a and passes b failed *at the
anisotropy*, which one scene cannot say. And the correct route is not a
parameter lottery: it scores 1.000 at every suppression radius from 1.5 to
5.0 µm, while the naive one swings 0.333 to 0.809 over that same sweep.

Two rows are in the table because they did **not** separate, and dropping them
would misrepresent what was screened. Seeding every local maximum costs 0.020,
not the collapse the entry's "seed suppression" claim implies — the peak mask's
connected components already collapse each plateau to one seed — so nothing here
tests that half. Raw intensity fails *both* scenes, so it is a real failure but
not an anisotropy failure; the control is what tells them apart.

**photobleaching-correction** — mean reported fold change per population.

| route | responders | static |
|---|---|---|
| truth | 1.400 | 1.000 |
| per-frame background median, then a fit | 1.402 | 1.001 |
| the offset alone, then a fit | 1.372 | 1.001 |
| the offset alone, then a frame-mean ratio | 1.293 | 0.943 |
| a frame-mean ratio with the offset left in | **0.937** | **0.753** |
| no correction at all | 0.668 | 0.537 |

Rows 2–4 are the three methods the dropped entry found a competent run picking
between, and on the responders they span 0.11. Rows 4 and 5 are the *same
procedure* either side of the camera pedestal, and are 0.36 apart — which is the
entry's one real finding turned back into a measurement. The tolerances admit
every method and refuse the pedestal.

Two populations, because no constant answer may pass: 1.00 everywhere has the
static cells exactly right and has measured nothing, and 1.40 everywhere is the
same trick on the responders. Seven of thirty cells respond, deliberately — the
entry's other finding is that bleaching and a global signal change are not
separable from one trace, so a fixture where everything rises has no right
answer to score.

## Choices a reviewer should weigh

- **Terminal count is the gate, not branch count.** Protocol §8: the SNT run
  nearly failed a correct arm over whether the soma counts as a branch, 835
  against 834, both self-consistent. A terminal is a terminal.
- **The bifurcation ratio is scored loosely and is not the gate.** It is the
  number that reaches a figure and a wrong one does not read as wrong, but on
  this fixture it separates the per-voxel route (424%) and not the un-clustered
  one (7.1% against the reference's 3.1%). Said plainly in the docstring rather
  than presented as a check that works.
- **Four of the five are self-sufficient** — spacing, reporting convention and
  the fact that a fibre is undirected are all in the prompt, as the screens they
  reproduce disclosed them (§6). Those personas hold no part of the answer.
- **`photobleaching-correction` is the exception, and deliberately a soft one.**
  The camera pedestal is not in the prompt and the persona will give the number
  to a run that asks about the camera. The case is still winnable without
  asking — a per-frame background median carries the pedestal away with the
  bleaching autofluorescence, and that route is exact here — so the ask is
  rewarded rather than required, and a failure is attributable to the offset
  rather than to never having opened a conversation.
- **`splitting-touching-objects` has the tightest two-sided gap here**: 0.10 of
  F1 shortfall against a naive ceiling of 0.191, 1.9×. It is tight for a reason
  no tuning fixes — the naive route still gets every xy-neighbouring pair right,
  so its ceiling is set by how many pairs are stacked axially. Most pairs here
  are, and that is the fixture's one deliberate bias; it is in the provenance
  line rather than left implicit.
- **`local-thickness` uses primitives**, so a run that recognises a sphere may
  measure it directly. That is a pass on the merits, not a back door — the
  metric is the thickness, and the failure being caught is not avoided by
  recognising a shape. Noted in the docstring, with what it would cost to close.

## Verification

- Full suite **1825 passed, 37 skipped**; bench suite 432 (from 338).
- Every route in every table above was replayed through the verifier: each trips
  exactly the metric built for it, and no other. So is every degenerate answer —
  nothing bound, wrong shape, all background, one constant for every object —
  and each reports *unavailable* or fails, never passes.
- Fixture builds are 0.07 / 0.13 / 1.2 / 0.18 / 0.13 s; the largest single array
  is 19 MB uint8, and no case's data exceeds 16 MB.

## Not in this PR

`docs/skill-candidates.md` is untouched — it is untracked WIP, and marking which
deferred-tier entries now have cases belongs to whoever is editing it. Four
remain uncovered: SMLM localization, stain separation, colocalization (which
still has no discriminating fixture — the doc's own finding, not an omission
here), and SQUIRREL, which needs the eSRRF reconstructions rebuilt.

items.title: ASR backend benchmark: whisper.cpp wins on the axis that decides it
items.body:
Runs the ASR backend comparison that has been queued since 2026-07-21. Three languages, 50 clips each, against human reference transcripts.

## Two metrics, because WER alone picks the wrong winner

The preparer slices audiobooks into training clips, so **where a boundary lands matters as much as which words were heard**. A clip cut 30ms early loses a consonant off every sample; 300ms late drags in a word from the next line.

| lang | backend | WER/CER | RTF | align median | within 300ms | segs |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **EN** | whisper.cpp | 3.0% | 0.049 | **80ms** | 90% | 15/10 |
| | transformers | **2.8%** | 0.050 | 254ms | 60% | 13/10 |
| | sensevoice | 3.8% | **0.030** | 10158ms | 20% | 6/10 |
| **JA** | whisper.cpp | 32.1% | 0.071 | 2833ms | 10% | 5/10 |
| | transformers | 32.1% | 0.070 | 2013ms | 30% | 5/10 |
| | sensevoice | **26.6%** | **0.036** | 23464ms | 10% | 1/10 |
| **ZH** | whisper.cpp | 44.3% | 0.095 | **84ms** | **100%** | 10/10 |
| | transformers | 44.4% | 0.087 | 118ms | 80% | 10/10 |
| | sensevoice | **11.3%** | **0.052** | 17957ms | 10% | 1/10 |

## Verdict: keep whisper.cpp

Best alignment in EN and ZH, and alignment is what decides it.

**SenseVoice's vendor claims held.** Fastest in all three languages, and Chinese CER of **11.3% against Whisper's 44.3%** — a 4x error reduction, the largest effect in the benchmark. It is ruled out anyway: **1 of 10 segments** found in ja/zh with a 17–23 *second* median boundary error. Fast, accurate, and cannot place a boundary.

**Whisper is poor at CJK at base size** (32% JA, 44% ZH) — worth knowing independently if Voice Lab ever prepares non-English audiobooks.

## The alignment probe is synthetic on purpose

Clips concatenated with 0.5s gaps, so boundary truth is *arithmetic* rather than annotation — the only answer key in this repo that cannot itself be wrong. LJSpeech clips are single utterances and cannot score alignment alone.

## Two of my own measurements were wrong before the run was widened

Both would have shipped as findings:

- The first pass passed **`-nt`** (`--no-timestamps`) to whisper.cpp and reported a 6013ms median error with 3 segments of 10. Removing it: **80ms and 15 segments — a 75x swing from one flag.**
- SenseVoice at RTF 2.470 was **cold-start model loading amortised over 20 clips.** At 50 it is 0.030, the fastest.

Neither was visible without re-running. The repo already documents this failure mode — a prior change "looked like +10.8 in a diagnostic harness and reversed to -7.2" once configured fairly.

## Caveats

`base`-size Whisper only; large-v3 would likely close much of the CJK gap and is queued. 50 clips, single-utterance read speech. Japanese alignment is poor for *every* backend (best 30%), which points at the probe or the Kokoro clips rather than the backends.

`verify_release.py` and all three index checks pass on a clean checkout.

items.title: feat(anomaly): recall benchmark + CUSUM drift detection + tenant-aggregate detection + fixes
items.body:
Started as a recall benchmark for the shipped anomaly-detection config. Turned into three real, research-backed features once the benchmark surfaced real gaps — each verified with adversarial tests and instrumentation before trusting any number, not assumed.

**Real bugs found and fixed along the way** (not glossed over):
1. `policypack/usecase/catalog.go` imported `yaml.v3` directly — a real CLAUDE.md dependency-rule violation, fixed with a `domain.ManifestDecoder` interface.
2. `maxHarmfulZ`'s deny-ratio gate was a bare `zToolCalls >= 0` cutoff — noise-sensitive, made auto-block a coin flip. Fixed with a one-sigma hysteresis margin.
3. First version of `tenant_anomaly` reused `ml_score`'s z-score helper, whose 15%-of-mean floor is right for per-identity scale but wrong at tenant-aggregate scale (mean ~600) — scored a real attack at z=3.39 instead of z=17.86, missing it entirely. Fixed with a dedicated `AggregateZScore`.
4. `tenant_anomaly`'s window boundary was set to "whenever this replica first saw the tenant," not epoch-aligned — two replicas would never agree on the same window, silently breaking any future cross-replica merge. Fixed with `now.Truncate(window)`.
5. A new Postgres-gated adapter test (`TestPostgresTenantWindowStore_AddAndGet_MergesAcrossInstances`) had no table reset between runs — a minute-truncated window key silently inherited a prior run's total on rerun within the same wall-clock minute. Fixed with the same `DROP TABLE IF EXISTS` reset convention `postgres_block_store_test.go` already established.

**New: `drift_detection`** — CUSUM control chart (Montgomery's standard SPC technique) over `call_rate`/`tool_diversity`, closing most of the documented low-and-slow blind spot. The ramp `TestDetector_AutoBlock_LowAndSlowEvades` shows evading forever now blocks within 10 windows at 1.4x baseline. Optional `h_jitter_fraction` (HMAC-secret-keyed moving-target defense) genuinely raises the cost of an attacker calibrated to the public default threshold — honestly documented as raising the bar, not solving it (adaptive attackers are weaker against MTD per the published research).

**New: `tenant_anomaly`** — baselines aggregate call volume per tenant, closing the sybil gap no per-identity heuristic can close by construction (confirmed: 20 identities each individually evading, 0/20 blocked, while the aggregate scores z=17.86).

**New: `tenant_anomaly` is now HA-safe (`postgres_storage` + `tenant_anomaly.enabled` both on)** — the feature shipped detection-only and in-memory-only; this closes that gap for real, not with a quick patch:
- `PostgresTenantWindowStore` — atomic cross-replica window-total merge (`INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE ... RETURNING`, one round trip, no read-then-write race), keyed `(tenant, window_start)`.
- `PostgresTenantBaselineStore` — per-instance baseline restart-persistence, keyed `(instance_id, tenant)`, deliberately *not* shared the way window totals are.
- The correctness property the whole design depends on: every replica folds the **merged** cross-replica total into its baseline, never its own local-only delta — otherwise the baseline and the scored value silently diverge. Called out in a code comment at the fold site (`tenant_detector.go`).
- Proven against real infrastructure, not code inspection: `TestTenantAnomalyHA_CoordinatedSpikeSplitAcrossTwoRealReplicas` runs two real `Detector`s, each with its own real Postgres connections, against one real shared Postgres 16 instance, over real wall-clock 2-second windows — neither replica's own local half of a split spike alone crosses the threshold, only the merged total does. Observed passing (23.2s).
- Fails open on any Postgres error (falls back to this replica's local total for that window, logged at `Warn`), matching every other Postgres-backed adapter's established posture.
- Zero behavior change for any deployment not running both flags — verified via a real compiled-binary smoke test (`validate-config` + a brief `serve` run confirming the "tenant_anomaly aggregate state backed by postgres (shared across replicas)" startup log line, plus a clean SIGTERM shutdown with no closer errors).

Docs (`anomaly-detection.md`, `roadmap.md`, `config-reference.md`, `ha-deployment.md`) updated to replace the "in-memory only" claims with the actual HA-backed behavior — including correcting an already-stale `ha-deployment.md` bullet that predated this cycle.

**Production-readiness, not just unit tests:**
- 205-goroutine concurrency stress test under `-race`, zero data races
- Real Go benchmarks: full 6-heuristic stack costs ~293ns/op vs ~251ns/op baseline (+17%)
- Real compiled binary smoke-tested against `validate-config`, both accept and reject paths, plus a real `serve` run for the HA wiring specifically
- Full `demo/run.sh` end-to-end re-run, zero regression
- Full repo suite (`go test ./... -race`) green; `golangci-lint` and `go-arch-lint` both clean
- Every Postgres-gated adapter test (baseline store, block store, tenant window store, tenant baseline store, HA integration test) run and observed passing against a real Postgres 16 instance, not just written

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)


**New: `identity_churn` — closes `h_jitter_fraction`'s own documented rotation vulnerability.** Real research, not a guess: a per-identity secret (jitter, but also rate_spike's baseline, novel_tool's per-identity tool set) is a coin flip an attacker with disposable identities gets to keep re-rolling, discarding whichever identity gets caught. A tenure-based gate on jitter was considered and rejected — `zCount` already returns 0 before an identity clears `minSamplesForZScore`'s 8-window floor, so jitter is inert pre-warmup anyway; the exploit only becomes live after that floor, at which point a tenure gate has nothing left to gate. The production-correct fix, matching real fraud/bot-mitigation practice (new-account-velocity, session-churn-rate signals): detect the *rotation itself*, aggregated above the identity level — the same resolution `tenant_anomaly` already reached for coordinated call volume, applied to identity-creation count. Proven directly: `TestAdversarialBenchmark_DisposableIdentityRotation` — 30 throwaway identities appear in one window, 0/30 individually caught by any per-identity heuristic, `identity_churn` flags the burst. Detection-only, in-memory only this cycle (same trajectory `tenant_anomaly` itself took — HA sharing is an honestly-scoped follow-up, not an oversight). FP rate held to the same <2% budget every heuristic here is held to. Full 7-heuristic stack re-benchmarked: ~299ns/op vs ~255ns/op baseline (+17%, same 5-allocation count).


**Resolved: mimicry ceiling — documentation, not a code gap.** Real research, checked not assumed: the ~1.15× ceiling is CUSUM's allowance `k` doing exactly what it's mathematically defined to do (Page 1954; Lucas & Crosier's ARL analysis) — a sustained shift below `k` is provably indistinguishable from noise in bounded time, the same Neyman-Pearson tradeoff every real sequential detector has. Driving `k` toward zero was considered and rejected — it collapses the <2% false-positive budget (verified: it's exactly what the pre-CUSUM per-window test alone already does). What actually closes the operating room that matters — an attacker running a below-ceiling rate across many identities to make it worthwhile — is `tenant_anomaly` + `identity_churn`, both shipped in this PR, plus `h_jitter_fraction` and the existing policy/budget-limit recommendation. Added the real explanation to `anomaly-detection.md`'s "Mimicry ceiling" section rather than leaving it as a bare number.

items.title: feat(benchmark): reversal-aware realized-history ground truth (#9261)
items.body:
> **Stacked on #9595** (`feat/benchmark-action-space-9260`), which it imports the action vocabulary from. Based against that branch so the diff shows only this change; retarget to `main` once #9595 merges.

## What

The labels every candidate proposal is scored against: for each work unit in a snapshot, what the maintainer **actually did** within the prediction horizon — emitted in #9260's exact action vocabulary, so proposal and outcome compare with no translation layer that could drift.

Three rules the surrounding system already believes, now enforced in one place:

- **Reversal-aware settlement.** A merge later reverted is not a clean merge. The label is the settled state at horizon end with the reversal recorded *alongside* — the same treatment that makes `public-rule-precision.ts`'s precision honest (it subtracts reversals rather than erasing the decision). The vocabulary is the established `reversal_reopened` / `reversal_reverted` / `reversal_superseded` set, never a benchmark-local re-invention, so benchmark ground truth and internal backtest ground truth cannot disagree about the same event. A reversal counts only *inside* the horizon **and** strictly *after* the action it overturns; the earliest such reversal wins.
- **Unresolved is explicit and excluded.** A work unit with no action inside the horizon is a first-class `unresolved` — never silently a correct abstention (which would reward an agent for declining exactly the cases nobody decided) nor an incorrect prediction (which would punish it for the horizon being too short). It leaves the scoring denominator, and the unresolved **rate** is published so a climbing rate reads as "the horizon is wrong" rather than as a scoring artifact. `scoreableGroundTruths` is the single definition of that rule, so no scorer can re-implement it slightly differently.
- **Stability.** Every decision is a pure function of events dated inside the window, so a later event — including a later reversal — cannot retroactively move a settled label. A leaderboard that drifts under its own scores is not one.

The settled state is the **last** qualifying action in the window (label → request changes → merge settles on the merge), with identical timestamps keeping the earlier-listed event so a stable input order yields a stable label.

## Tests (12 node:test cases, 100% of branches)

Settlement ordering and per-action parameter carriage (a `merge` truth carries no `reasonClass`/`labels` keys at all — not present-but-undefined); the reverted-merge regression; all three reversal kinds accepted verbatim with earliest-wins; the four ways a reversal fails to attach (before the action, same instant, past the horizon, before the freeze) plus wrong work unit; the unresolved regression with in/out-of-window events in both directions; inclusive boundaries at both ends; the **stability invariant** (same input plus a year of post-horizon history → byte-identical output); unparseable timestamps as out-of-window rather than a crash; tie-break determinism; empty roster reporting a `null` rate rather than 0; and parameters dropped when they don't belong to the settled action.

Closes #9261

items.title: Estimator: a benchmark must clear a relevance bar to be quoted as a basis
items.body:
## What

A bathroom-remodel test estimate on merged main produced two stamps with the **right unit but the wrong work**:

- "Paint walls and ceiling" ($4.50/sq ft, labor) → stamped against **interior selective demolition** ($4.72/sq ft, labor). Same unit, same kind, ratio ×0.95 — reads as corroboration of nothing.
- "Plumbing rough-in, relocate supply" ($2,200/ls) → stamped against a **gas furnace install** ($6,490/project).

## Why it happened

Stamping searches only the items that survived the prompt cap — a deliberate invariant (`a line must never carry provenance for a price the model never received`). Inside that narrow pool the best match always wins, so when nothing relevant is present a stray token overlap becomes the quoted basis: "walls" in the paint line hit demolition's "walls", "line" hit the furnace's "gas line".

The ranking bonuses from #592 are **not** the cause — checked against the full catalog, the correct rows already rank first ("Bathroom plumbing rough-in, full bathroom" leads, and the unit/type hints improve that ordering). The gap was the absence of a minimum relevance bar.

## How

- **`matchCostItems`** gains `opts.minScore`, applied to the **keyword** score *before* the unit/cost-type preference bonuses — so a unit match can reorder candidates but can never promote an irrelevant row past the bar.
- **`CD_STAMP_MIN_SCORE = 2`** (new exported constant, mirrored): a whole-query hit, two matched tokens, or one token plus a morphological near-miss. Measured on the real snapshot, the two wrong stamps scored **1.0 and 1.5**; the correct ones (toilet, tile) scored **2.0 and 3.0** — a clean separation.
- **`generateEstimate`** and the SMS **`live_price_lookup` cross-check** both stamp at that bar. `cost_benchmark` (the explicit admin query tool) is unchanged — it returns named matches with units for a human to judge.
- Leak-guard test now pins both stamping gates so neither can be dropped silently.

## Result (real snapshot, both simulated estimates)

| | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| Bathroom: paint → demolition stamp | ×0.95 "in band" | unstamped |
| Bathroom: plumbing rough-in → furnace stamp | ×0.34 | unstamped |
| Bathroom: toilet HIGH flag ($690 vs $413/each) | fires | fires |
| Kitchen: quartz ×0.90, joint compound ×0.94, tile | stamped | unchanged |
| Kitchen: overpriced hardwood control line | HIGH | HIGH |

Confidence moves 75 → 67 on the bathroom estimate. That drop is the point: it was resting on two benchmarks that proved nothing.

## Tests

New `minScore` battery (stray overlap dropped even with both bonuses applied; genuine match retained; empty result when the pool holds nothing relevant), mirror-parity coverage for the constant and the new opt, and the leak-guard source pins.

Verification: 124 targeted tests, lint, typecheck, 291 function bundles parse, bundle-helper check clean.

items.title: bench(leakcheck): detect when a benchmark's answer is inferable from its input
items.body:
Four times a benchmark here scored near-perfectly for the wrong reason, each caught by hand and late:

| Benchmark | The leak |
|---|---|
| `localize` (default) | substrate scored 1.00 — blatant sinks, decoys like `const Version = "1.2.3"` |
| `cwemap` (baseline) | keyword table scored 1.00 — corpus and matcher had the same author |
| `triage` (first) | decoy **descriptions stated the conclusion**, so the model was graded on reading |
| **WAVSEP (external!)** | all 34 false cases carry `FalsePositive` in the URL; no true case does |

`DetectLabelLeak` asks, for every token: if I classified purely on *"does the input contain this"*, how well would I separate the classes? A token that alone splits the corpus is a giveaway.

## It uses Youden J, not accuracy — and the reason is the point

My first version scored accuracy-over-majority-baseline and **missed WAVSEP**. The corpus is 97% positive, so "always say true" scores 0.97; a token perfectly marking all 34 negatives reaches only 1.00 — a 3-point gain that reads as noise.

By separation, that same token scores **J=1.00 against a 0.00 floor**. Accuracy hides a total giveaway under class imbalance. **The detector had the exact flaw it exists to find.**

## What it found

**WAVSEP is unusable as T1's corpus** — 1,133 externally-authored cases with an `is_real_vulnerability` column, already in our tree, and **J=1.00**. It was built to test *scanners* ("does yours fire on the FP pages"), not triagers, so the labels live in the URLs.

**External provenance is not protection.** Worth learning before building T1 on it.

The shipped triage corpus passes at **J=0.33**.

## Known limitation, pinned as a test

The original triage leak was a **phrase**, not a token, and tops out at J=0.67 — under the bar. **This check would not have caught the leak that motivated it.**

It catches blunt giveaways and misses distributed phrasing, so a clean report means one failure mode is absent, never that the corpus is sound. That's a test now, so nobody mistakes it for a guarantee.

## Note

Two of the three initial test failures were bugs in **my own fixtures** — an over-specific token assertion, and an imbalance fixture that itself contained a perfect giveaway. The detector was right both times.

items.title: Measure whether something else can write this language
items.body:
Every `.deed` file in this repository was written by one person. That is the largest open question about Deed and not one the compiler can answer.

`benchmarks/` turns it into a number. Six tasks, one language feature each: a contract that has to constrain its own input, walking a list, a choice and an exhaustive match, `Result`, an effect with a handler, and a refinement that has to be proven rather than guarded. Each task hands over a prompt and keeps its tests to itself, so an answer cannot pass by writing tests it already satisfies.

`cargo run -p deed-driver --example agent_bench -- <answers>` scores four things per task: whether it checks, whether the tests pass, and how many obligations came back proven versus guarded, with the reason for each guarded one. That last pair is why this is not a generic code benchmark: two answers can both check and both pass while one carries contracts the compiler proved and the other carries none. It is also the input the `is a solver needed` question has never had.

Nothing here calls a model. Producing answers is the caller's job, and `deed mcp` (#793) is the intended way to let something produce them against the real compiler.

The harness is held against itself: every reference has to score full marks, and two deliberately wrong answers have to score less, one that does not compile and one that compiles with the right signatures and returns the wrong things. Without the second this would be a compile check wearing a benchmark's name. A third test refuses a prompt containing a line of its own answer, which caught the `stock` prompt handing over its body.

Closes #794

<sub>Investigated with AI assistance.</sub>

items.title: Score malformed static repairs as wrong
items.body:
## What changed

- Treat a completed static-repair response that violates the required code-fence contract as a deterministic zero score.
- Preserve `malformed_output` on the scored task artifact for diagnosis.
- Keep transport and generation failures unscored so they still make the benchmark partial.
- Update regression coverage for prose-only, unclosed-fence, multiple-fence, and mixed generation-failure cases.

## Why

The Gemma 4 E4B coding campaign attempted every static-repair case and produced a valid 66.7% constraint metric, but one malformed answer caused Runner to exclude the entire 15%-weight component. That confused a model-output miss with absent evidence and yielded an incomplete capability score.

## Impact

Strict output-format misses now reduce the coding score instead of removing the component. Runtime or transport failures retain the existing partial-evidence behavior.

## Validation

- `python3 -m unittest python/runner-core/tests/test_capabilities.py` — 68 passed
- `python3 -m ruff check python/runner-core/src/infergrade/capabilities.py python/runner-core/tests/test_capabilities.py`
- `./scripts/test_all.sh` — 667 passed

items.title: fix(benchmarks): stop the evalscope parser reporting scores it did not measure
items.body:
## What's wrong

Reading a per-sample score out of an evalscope review row used `if score == 0.0`
as its "keep looking" signal, so a sample evalscope genuinely scored zero was
indistinguishable from one whose key was missing. The correctly-parsed wrong
answer then fell through to a last-resort fallback that averaged every number in
the row.

`IFEval` reports four numbers per sample and names the first as the main score. A
sample that **failed** its prompt-level constraint while following three of its
four instructions:

```
value = {'prompt_level_strict': 0.0, 'inst_level_strict': 0.75,
         'prompt_level_loose': 0.0, 'inst_level_loose': 0.75}
main_score_name = 'prompt_level_strict'

  -> recorded 0.375, success True
```

evalscope said the sample failed. We recorded it as a pass. More generally:

| evalscope's value dict | recorded |
|---|---|
| `{acc: 0.0}` | `0.0` (correct) |
| `{acc: 0.0, num_tokens: 512}` | `256.0` |
| `{acc: 0.0, f1: 0.62}`, main `acc` | `0.62` |
| `{grade: 3, confidence: 0.9}` | `1.95` |

A per-sample score of `256.0` on a metric whose range is 0 to 1.

**The run-level score is unaffected** — it comes from evalscope's own aggregate.
What was corrupted is the per-sample evidence, since `success` is derived as
`score > 0`. A run could report 41% while the sample list showed a wall of passes.
Someone opening a run to decide whether they believe the score was shown
fabricated evidence.

## The fix

Extraction moves out of the review loop (it was inlined nine levels deep, which is
why it had never been tested) into `_extract_sample_score`, with `None` meaning
not measured and the averaging deleted. An unreadable sample is recorded as
`score=None`, `success=False`, `status='errored'` with a reason naming what it saw
— the shape `custom_eval_backend` already uses, not a new convention.

Two more of the same shape were closed alongside it:

- **A report or subset with no usable `score`.** `results.get('score', 0.0)` turned
  an upstream key rename into a model that scored zero. The report now raises
  (non-retryable, verified against the retry gate); a subset is recorded as failed,
  so it costs one subset rather than discarding every subset already parsed.
- **A row that cannot be read at all.** The review-file loop wrapped every row of a
  file in one `try`, so one malformed record abandoned every row after it, visible
  only as a warning. Field guards close known instances but not the class —
  `instruction_id_list` is fed straight to `enumerate()`. Each row is now read
  inside its own `try` and an unreadable one costs exactly one row. The field
  guards stay: they salvage the rest of a row when only its score is malformed.

## Behaviour change worth knowing

`_load_predictions` falls back to `predictions/` when `reviews/` is absent, and
those rows carry no score object by construction. On that path every row now reads
"not measured" where it previously read as a zero-scoring sample. The new reading
is the honest one, but it looks different.

## Also fixed, pre-existing and separable

The report's task table branched on `accuracy` then `avg_score` with no `else`. A
custom-eval toxicity run reports under `safety_rate`, so its only task row rendered
nothing at all, and the html emitted two cells into a four-column table. Both
templates now cover it and always emit four cells. Unrelated to score parsing;
included because this work put a task entry with neither key within reach.

## Tests

226 passing, from 195. Table-driven over real score shapes (IFEval, DROP's
`{em, f1}`, MBPP's bool `acc`, unrecognised schemas, legitimate zeros), plus
file-driven tests through the real loop for a truncated line, a malformed field,
and a field no guard was written for — so they keep proving the class is closed
rather than three known cases.

## Verification

No eval image rebuild was available, so this was verified in the terminal rather
than through a run: a real review file on disk, read back through the real
`_load_predictions` and `_parse_results` with nothing stubbed.

Before: three fabricated passes, including the IFEval sample at `0.375` and the
wrong answer at `256.0`. After: none, and the renamed report key raises naming the
keys it saw.

Not covered: no benchmark was executed, so evalscope's own behaviour is out of
scope here.

## Known remaining

The consuming service derives `correct` from `success` with no unmeasured branch,
so an unmeasured sample still displays as a failed one and counts toward the
"Failed" tally. Tracked separately; it needs a change on that side and this is an
improvement without it.

`success = score > 0` still marks any non-zero score as a pass, which is wrong for
graded metrics. Fixing it needs a per-benchmark notion of what a pass is.

items.title: docs(status): reconcile session 226 — PLAN-0104 drafted, ruled and Step 1 shipped (#1143-#1145)
items.body:
## What

Reconciles `docs/STATUS.md` from `b229fcd` (session 225) to `fa8a61c`, **0 open PRs**, and rotates the content that fell out of the window. 3 files, +196/−103.

Session 226 shipped three PRs: **#1143** PLAN-0104 drafted (`Status: Draft`), **#1144** its three SD slots RULED (Cray, typed), **#1145** Step 1.

## The two findings this record exists to carry

**1. The refusal is enforced at THREE independent layers.** The system prompt, the validator, and the `AggregateResult` carrier each block `count` + `group_by` on their own — so no single edit changes observable behaviour. The long-circulating *"≈ one PR + tests"* price rested on a seam count that had already been corrected once and was **still** an undercount.

**2. The benchmark's gold guard was VACUOUS.** Its docstring has claimed since session 58 that it validates `SQL_EXPECT`; its body restated the numbers as literals and never read the constant. That is how two wrong tokens scored `wrong` on **every** run of that arm, silently — and it is why Step 1 ran first, since Step 7's live evidence run scores against that same arm.

## Corrections made IN PLACE, not appended beside the wrong text

The PLAN-0100 residuals row was carrying three clauses this session falsified:

| Clause | Disposition |
|---|---|
| D-4 has *"nothing built, no PLAN drafted"* | `superseded by new info` — PLAN-0104 owns it now, so the seam analysis is not kept in two divergent copies |
| gold.yaml + A/B fixtures *"may need re-recording on MS-S1"* | **REMOVED as refuted** — neither set is a recording; both are hand-authored. Gold gains cases offline; only *evidence* needs the live model |
| *"re-price before scheduling"* | Recorded **DISCHARGED** — drafting is what re-priced it |

## One new Active TODO, on a Cray typed ruling

`nl-03`'s `SQL_EXPECT` is **under-specified and deliberately NOT changed**. It is a different defect class from the nl-02/nl-05 tokens Step 1 repaired: `score_sql` matches a **subset**, so nl-03's tokens are correct and it still scores `correct` — the oracle is **weaker than it should be, not wrong**. Tightening it would make the benchmark **stricter** and break comparability with earlier runs, which is a *measurement* decision rather than a typo fix.

## Rotation (R2) — extracted byte-exact, then read back out

Source was `git show HEAD:docs/STATUS.md`, **never a subagent's retyping** (HTML-escape hazard). Each append was verified by grepping the content back **out** of the archive, because a byte-size delta proves *something* landed, not that the *right* bytes did.

| Content | Destination | Before → After |
|---|---|---|
| Current Focus blocks, sessions 222 and 222-cont. | `2026-h1c-current-focus.md` | 186,499 → **192,607** B |
| The s220 Recent-Decisions row (#1114) | `2026-h1-status.md` | 147,017 → **148,131** B |

⚠️ **Three Active-TODO rows that look removed in the diff are in-place rewrites, not rotations, and were deliberately NOT archived**: the PLAN-0103 portal row, the s219 ungated-items row, and the PLAN-0100 residuals row. Archiving those would have produced two divergent copies of live content.

## Size posture

- `docs/STATUS.md`: 59,784 → **56,185** B. Under R1's 65,536 hard ceiling; **still over the 49,152 soft target** — prune harder next reconcile.
- The CF archive now has ~4,001 B of headroom before R4's **196,608**-byte split trigger, so the next rotation will very likely need a continuation file. That trigger only warns; the hard cap is 262,144.

## Carve-outs

Both R2 carve-out rows survive unaltered — the s223 J4 ruling (*"run the full tests before pushing"* is binding but evaluated **per action**) still has no other home.

## Verification — on the committed tree

`4028 passed / 8 skipped`, exit 0 (495s). `git diff --quiet HEAD` → rc 0, so the tested tree is the pushed tree. All pre-commit hooks green, including R1, R4, R7 and R8.

items.title: Token-efficiency benchmark: curated AMOS verbs vs raw SQL
items.body:
## What

A controlled, reproducible benchmark under `benchmarks/token-efficiency/` that measures whether AMOS's curated MCP verb surface lets Claude accomplish a business task in **fewer total tokens** than a generic raw-access agent. This is evidence for the token-efficiency claim, built to survive a skeptical read.

## Design (anti-rigging)

- **One model held constant:** `anthropic.claude-opus-4-8` on AWS Bedrock, via the official Anthropic SDK (`AnthropicBedrockMantle`), adaptive thinking.
- **Both arms read the SAME data:** a deterministic Northwind Labs dataset ported verbatim from the platform demo seed (`demo_seed.rs` finance lake + `starters.rs` CRM + `DEMO_DOCS`), materialised into in-memory SQLite. The only variable is the tool surface.
  - **Arm A (AMOS):** curated verbs — `money_flow`, `finance_leaks`, `list_records`, `get_catalog`, `search_documents`.
  - **Arm B (baseline):** generic `list_tables` / `describe_table` / `run_sql`.
- **Exact token accounting:** usage read from every response's `usage` and summed across the whole tool-use loop, not just the final message.
- **Objective equivalent-quality bars** per task, so a cheap-but-wrong answer scores no win (failed runs excluded from the token means).
- **N=3 runs** per (arm × task); mean ± spread reported.

## Result

| Task | AMOS tok | Raw tok | Ratio |
|------|--------:|-------:|:-----:|
| cashflow | 3,618 | 19,613 | **5.4×** |
| leaks | 3,042 | 16,277 | **5.4×** |
| stale_deals | 4,921 | 8,856 | 1.8× |
| retrieval | 3,831 | 7,727 | 2.0× |
| **overall** | | | **3.4×** |

Largest win on curated-analysis tasks (`money_flow`/`finance_leaks`); ~2× on simple CRM/retrieval. On `stale_deals` the raw agent also failed the quality bar 2/3 runs (misclassified a stale deal) — a reliability loss beyond tokens.

## Honest caveats (in the README)

- Win is task-dependent; overall ratio dominated by analysis tasks.
- This is a faithful **model** of the verb surface over real demo data, not the live MCP server (live seed needs S3+DuckDB+running platform); verb outputs validated against the platform's own ground-truth tests.
- Small demo dataset likely **understates** the production advantage (raw cost scales with data volume; curated summary stays flat).

## Scope

Pure Python under `benchmarks/`. Not a Cargo workspace member — the Rust build is unaffected.

items.title: test(mcp): _tests/tasks — a functional agent benchmark on curated real data
items.body:
Stacked on #712 (the `agentbench` extraction) — **review that one first**; this
branch contains its commit and will shrink to two commits once it merges.

## What

A second consumer of `agentbench`: a benchmark that asks whether an agent can do
a named piece of work against real data, with no skill dimension at all.

|  | `skills/interaction` | `tasks` |
|---|---|---|
| Question | does *this skill* change what an agent does | can an agent do *this work* |
| Arms | 2x2 ablation | one |
| Repetition | one sample per corner | N, `BIOPB_TASK_SAMPLES` |
| Skills at run time | the manipulation | **on**, as a user has them |
| Data | mostly synthetic | curated real acquisitions only |

A skill's claim is a delta and a delta needs a control. A task has no claim to
isolate, so there is one arm and repetition replaces the ablation as the source
of information.

## No synthetic data, by construction

Every case is `OnDisk`. `docs/skill-fixtures.md` already records a synthetic
fixture that ranked two method families in the *opposite* order from real
tissue — the failure a functional benchmark cannot survive.

What real data costs is truth, and the answer is **perturb at authoring time**:
`tools/author_align_channels_fixture.py` writes the transformed acquisition into
the tree once and records the transformation in the manifest's `provenance`. The
run only ever reads, so `kind` stays `curated` and there is no third provenance
literal to get wrong.

## Skills stay on — and the report says so

This measures the product a user has. The cost is that a task later gaining a
covering skill re-bases its number, so every summary records which skills the
catalog offered at run time. A score compared across releases without reading
that line is a score compared against a different system.

## Seed case

`align-channels-from-landmarks` — the task the landmark-registration prescreen
was built around. Real nuclear vs. cytoplasmic channels (correlation 0.162), 18
correspondences on real nuclei, images on a run-scoped plane and the clicked
points as Points layers.

Three metrics; the third is the one worth having. `quality_honesty` asks whether
the run's own error estimate resembles the error it made — a spline interpolates
its control points exactly, so the residual there is ~0 by construction whatever
the warp does in between, and a run can be 24 px wrong while reporting 0.002 px
with nothing in its own output saying otherwise.

## Two verifier rules, learned the hard way

Both are in the README because neither is specific to this case — my first draft
had both bugs and the tests caught them:

- **Bound but unusable is not delivered.** Scoring a wrong-shaped `probe_mapped`
  as "unavailable" dropped it out of `passed`, so a half-broken run reported
  green on its other half.
- **A ratio metric needs a floor.** Claimed-vs-actual error is unusable near
  zero: a perfect run saying "about half a pixel" divided by ~0 and scored as
  maximally dishonest.

## Also fixes

The sibling of #712's `artifact_root` bug: `_session` computed the workspace
root as `parents[6]` to build its isolation wheel, which after the move pointed
above the checkout and made **every session bring-up fail** with `no workspace
was found`. Both call sites now share `checkout_root()`, which searches for the
marker instead of counting depth.

## Verification

Not by inspection — the smoke tests bring up a real session, upload both images
to a run-scoped plane, put all five layers (including the three Points layers)
on a real viewer, and scrape a bound result back out:

```
BIOPB_FIXTURES=~/biopb-fixtures pytest .../tasks/test_session_smoke.py -m tasks
3 passed in 23.43s
```

Whole suite: `1436 passed, 25 skipped, 47 deselected`.

The fixture tree itself is validated against the shipped reader: `OnDisk.build`
accepts it, shapes/dtypes agree with the manifest in-band, `probe_truth`
resolves as truth and not as data, and `-m fixtures` hashes it clean.

⚠️ The tree lives at `~/biopb-fixtures` and is **not** in this diff — it is
data. `BIOPB_FIXTURES` unset means the case skips, which is the honest outcome
on a machine that has no tree.

items.title: Add vision model benchmark suite for price/item parsing
items.body:
## Summary
This PR adds a comprehensive benchmarking framework for evaluating vision models on the GrocerEZ price and item image parsing task. The benchmark tests multiple models (Gemini, Mimo, Gemma, GPT-5-nano, Llama-4-scout) against a curated dataset of 36 grocery item pairs, with detailed scoring and HTML reporting.

## Key Changes

- **Benchmark Infrastructure** (`benchmark/scripts/run_benchmark.py`): Main script that calls OpenRouter API to run the exact prompt from `parsePriceImage.ts` against each model for every (price image, item image) pair. Handles concurrent requests, cost tracking, and raw response storage.

- **Scoring System** (`benchmark/scripts/score_benchmark.py`): Implements a detailed grading policy that evaluates model outputs against adjudicated ground truth:
  - "Findability" check: required/forbidden terms matching in itemName + brand + tags pool (case/punctuation-insensitive)
  - Brand, price, and quantity validation with unit conversion support
  - "Blank beats wrong" policy: missing fields score as ABSTAIN (0.5) rather than FAIL (0)
  - Supports unit equivalence (e.g., fluid ounces ↔ liters)

- **Ground Truth** (`benchmark/ground_truth.json`): Adjudicated reference values for 34 items with detailed grading policies documented, including special handling for brand canonicalization, flavor variants, and size qualifiers.

- **Reporting** (`benchmark/scripts/build_report.py`, `build_html.py`): Generates wide CSV and interactive HTML artifact showing per-model outputs with disagreement highlighting. HTML includes embedded product images and detailed field-by-field comparison.

- **Test Data**: 72 JPEG images (36 price tags + 36 product photos) covering beverages, snacks, tissues, and produce.

- **Results**: Pre-computed benchmark results showing Gemini-2.5-flash-lite and Mimo-v2.5 achieving ~86% and ~85% overall scores respectively, with detailed per-field breakdowns.

- **Source Code Update** (`src/parsePriceImage.ts`): Minor enhancement to `parsePrice` function (implementation details truncated in diff).

- **Configuration**: Added `benchmark/requirements.txt` (requests, Pillow) and updated `.gitignore` to exclude API keys and scratch output.

## Notable Implementation Details

- Uses OpenRouter API for unified model access with cost tracking per request
- Implements unit conversion tables for volume (fl oz, cup, liter, etc.) and weight (oz, lb, gram, etc.)
- Supports multiple brand representations (e.g., "365 by Whole Foods" variants) via allowlist matching
- Quantity grading handles both exact matches and unit-converted equivalents
- HTML report embeds base64-encoded image thumbnails for offline viewing

items.title: Phase 2b: refusal benchmark + calibrated two-stage grader
items.body:
## What this adds

A second scenario for the harness: **does a model refuse genuinely harmful requests without over-refusing harmless ones?** It plugs into the Phase 2a `Scenario`/`Grader` interfaces — the engine did not change, a value was added.

- **Benchmark, fetched not committed.** `benchmarks/jbb.py` downloads JailbreakBench (JBB-Behaviors) at a pinned commit, sha256-verifies the bytes, and caches them in a git-ignored `.cache/`. No harmful prompt text ever enters the repo, including test fixtures (tests use synthetic rows with JBB's schema and innocuous content).
- **Two-stage refusal grader.** `refusal_grader.py` screens a response with anchored refusal/compliance markers and a layout/length/content-signal budget; anything it can't cleanly decide escalates to an LLM judge (`RefusalJudgment`: `refused` + a 0/1/2 `substantive_help` level). A disclaimer glued to a real answer scores as compliance, not a refusal.
- **`--scenario refusal`** plus `--full`/`--smoke`/`--sample-seed`/`--refresh-benchmark`, an **over-refusal CI gate** (`--fail-over-refusal`), a **self-grading guard** (refuses to let a model grade its own output without `--allow-self-grading`), per-scenario report cards, and **hash-only redaction** of harmful-prompt responses in the written report/JSON (opt out with `--include-responses`).
- **`calibrate.py`** measures the grader against JBB's 300 human-labelled rows and reports its confusion matrix beside the naive baseline and the SOTA judges JBB ships in the same file.

## The calibration finding (measured, not aspirational)

Held-out 150-row half, `qwen2.5:7b` local judge, temperature 0:

| classifier | balanced acc. | MCC |
|------------|---------------|-----|
| **refusal grader** (stage 1 + 7B judge) | 58.8% | **0.20** |
| naive JBB `StringClassifier` | 64.2% | 0.34 |
| GPT-4 judge (reference) | 89.0% | 0.77 |
| Llama-3-70B judge (reference) | 90.9% | 0.80 |

**The grader is judge-bound, and that is the finding.** Stage 1 auto-decides 41% of rows on markers alone and escalates 59%, so accuracy tracks the judge model. With a free 7B local judge the grader lands at naive-string-classifier level; of its 64 false positives, 51 come from the weak judge (a capable one resolves them) and 13 from stage 1's own floor. The reference rows — strong LLMs judging the identical rows — already show the framework's ceiling is ~0.8. The README reports the measured floor plus the published ceiling; no best-case number is fabricated. (A Gemini judge run was attempted but the free tier is capped at 20 requests/day.)

## Bugs the live run caught that offline tests could not

Each surfaced only by actually running the benchmark, and each ships with a regression test:

1. **Redaction leaked short compliances** — `redact(keep=120)` kept the first 120 chars verbatim, so a short harmful answer shipped in full. Now hash-only on the harmful path.
2. **Calibration read the wrong column** — `response` instead of `target_response`, scoring 300 empty strings into a confident, meaningless 62.7%. Fixed, plus a `_require_columns` guard that fails loudly on schema drift.
3. **Refusal judge was broken on the default (Gemini) provider** — the Gemini path pinned the secret-guardian response schema, so the refusal judge's reply failed to parse. `run --scenario refusal` on defaults would have failed on every escalated case. The response schema is now threaded per-scenario, exactly as the parser already was.
4. **`RefusalJudgment` couldn't be a Gemini schema** — an integer `Literal` enum, which the SDK rejects (enum values must be strings). Now a bounded int.
5. **Unfair no-judge comparison** in `calibrate` — the grader was scored on the auto-decided subset while naive was scored on all rows. Both now share a denominator.

## Safety & test posture

- `tests/test_scenario_parity.py` is byte-for-byte unchanged and green throughout — the secret-guardian scenario is provably unaffected.
- **259 tests, all offline** (network, target, and judge are injected/faked), so CI runs the whole suite with no API key.
- Test count 146 → 259.
