items.title: test(bench): score the queries production issues, not user prompts (#1388)
items.body:
Closes #1388.

> **Stacked on #1401 (#1389).** Both edit the same single-line CHANGELOG entry, so
> they cannot land concurrently. This branch is cut from `docs/issue-1389-false-claims`;
> merge #1401 first and this rebases to its own two commits. I hold both issues,
> so this is sequencing rather than a race.

## The finding reproduces

The benchmark scored raw user prompt prefixes from the hook audit. Production
never issues those: `context_rebuilder` builds its query from a window of user
**and assistant** turns and rewrites it through `transform_query`; that string is
what reaches `index.score`.

Re-derived on the live 44,668-belief store, 2026-08-06:

| | production population | diagnostic (user turns) |
|---|---|---|
| queries | 1,432 unique | 82 |
| identical top-10 | **39.6%** | 56.1% |
| mean Jaccard@10 | **0.8910** | 0.9405 |
| median Kendall tau | **0.9592** | 0.9656 |
| gained / lost non-empty | 0 / 0 | 0 / 0 |

The issue predicted 39.7% / 0.8905 / 0.9592 on 1,429 queries; the small
differences are three more unique queries logged since it was filed. **Scoring
the wrong population understated the movement by about 17 points of top-10
identity.**

## What shipped

- A `PRODUCTION` arm reading `input.extracted_query` from
  `.git/aelfrice/rebuild_logs/*.jsonl`. **A recording, not a reconstruction** —
  the issue offered `_query_for_recent_turns` as an alternative, and the log is
  better because a reconstruction can drift from what actually ran. Deduplicated
  and sorted, so the population is a deterministic function of the directory.
- The existing arm relabelled `DIAGNOSTIC POPULATION — NOT the production input`,
  in the output and in the module docstring, with the reason stated: a raw user
  turn is the input *least* able to express a tokeniser change, because
  natural-language turns rarely carry identifier-shaped tokens. It reads as
  reassurance and is not evidence for the claim it was used to support.
- Both blocks always print, plus a closing line naming the gap.
- If the rebuild-log directory is absent the run says so **on stderr and names
  the arm that did not run**, rather than silently reporting only the diagnostic
  numbers — which is the failure mode this issue is about.
- The CHANGELOG sentence now quotes the production figures and keeps the
  diagnostic ones alongside, labelled.

## Discretion note — worth reading before extending this

The production population is **user prompt text**. Inspecting it while building
this arm, the very first record is a session-management instruction naming a
local agent session. The module docstring now states the constraint explicitly:
counts, shares and correlations may be printed or committed; query strings,
belief content and ids may not. The arm emits aggregates only, and no sample
output is committed.

## Left to the operator, deliberately

Whether **39.6% identical top-10** is acceptable for a change that shipped on
"movement on real queries is small" is a judgment this PR does not make — AC4
asks only that the number be the right one. Flagging it because the honest
reading is that #1348 moved production results considerably more than its own
entry claimed, and nothing here re-litigates the tokeniser fix: it stands on the
divergence measurement (44.59% -> 0.52%), which is independent of this.

`uv run pytest -k bm25`: 191 passed, 4 skipped.

## Summary by Sourcery

Update BM25 tokenizer benchmarking and documentation to measure and report production query behaviour accurately and to clarify residual divergences between the BM25F lane and FTS5, including case-folding differences.

New Features:
- Add a production-query benchmarking arm that reads recorded extracted queries from rebuild logs and reports agreement metrics alongside the existing diagnostic user-turn population.
- Add a case-fold divergence probe comparing Python str.lower() with sqlite unicode61 over the codepoint universe and surface its summary in the fold sweep benchmark output.

Enhancements:
- Refine the BM25 tokenizer and FTS5 probe documentation to distinguish historical measurements from current ones and to describe the remaining divergence sources, including stemmer and case-fold differences.
- Improve the bm25 tokenizer A/B benchmark CLI to accept a rebuild-logs directory, run both production and diagnostic populations, and summarise their metric gap.
- Tighten privacy guidance around benchmark output by restricting production-query reporting to aggregate statistics only.

Documentation:
- Update the changelog entry for the BM25F/FTS5 tokenisation fix to use production-query metrics, correct earlier diagnostic-only claims, and document the measured movement and residual divergence more accurately.

items.title: Auto-instrument microservice targets with OpenTelemetry runtime presets
items.body:
## Problem

Issue #253 asks for zero-code OpenTelemetry instrumentation of microservice targets with per-run telemetry surfaced to optimization agents. 

While PR #237 shipped most of the pipeline, nothing wires it: no collector is deployed, no candidate exports spans, and no bundle passes the flags. This PR should close #253 after verification.

## Solution

A general, evaluator-owned injection harness rather than one-off scenario wiring. A scenario declares its services and their runtime groups in a small `benchmark/otel/telemetry.toml`; at container start the scenario's run command invokes the new `cmd/otelinject`, which reads the candidate's *current* `docker-compose.yml` and emits a compose override adding one pinned `otel/opentelemetry-collector-contrib:0.157.0` service plus per-service env/volume fragments selected by a closed preset registry:

- `jaeger-native` — apps with built-in Jaeger tracing (both DeathStarBench targets): the collector impersonates the configured collector service name (`jaeger`) and only `JAEGER_SAMPLE_RATIO` is set.
- `java` — mounts a configured OpenTelemetry javaagent and sets `JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS` plus standard `OTEL_*` variables.
- `python` — standard `OTEL_*` variables; the image must bundle `opentelemetry-distro`.
- `node` — `NODE_OPTIONS` requiring `@opentelemetry/auto-instrumentations-node/register` plus `OTEL_*`.

The collector listens for OTLP, Jaeger, and Zipkin traffic and appends spans as OTLP NDJSON to a bind-mounted file under the scenario's `metrics/otel/` dir, which `cmd/otelcapture --settle-seconds 5` (new flag, absorbs client buffer + file-exporter flush tail) normalizes into the trusted telemetry report after the measured trials.

Hotel-reservation is the end-to-end reference wiring: its `[benchmark]` manifest run command chains otelinject with `docker compose -f base -f override up`, and the three telemetry flags attach capture to benchmark runs. The other presets are proven by golden-file tests; other scenarios adopt the harness in follow-ups.

Key choices:
- **Generated at run time from the current compose** so the Implementer can rename or add services during optimization. Mapped-but-missing services are skipped with a warning; if none remain, injection fails. Unknown runtime names and unknown config keys are hard errors.
- **Telemetry fails closed but stays diagnostic**: a run with configured telemetry that yields no spans in the measured windows fails, yet reports are never the scored metric — faster wrong answers cannot pay off.
- Raw `*.otlp.ndjson` capture is excluded from per-round git snapshots (`git_tracker.py` artifact pattern) and from the repo (`.gitignore` keeps only the `.gitkeep` placeholders, pre-created so Docker doesn't create the mount dirs root-owned).

### Architecture

Trust layering is unchanged: harness code and the embedded collector config live in the evaluator source (workspace `_evaluator/`, evaluator-owned); the per-scenario `telemetry.toml` lives under scenario `benchmark/`, which is tamper-checked trusted input. Zero servicebench lifecycle changes — the harness is exactly the deployment layer the telemetry contract README sanctions.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant SB as servicebench
    participant RC as run command (candidate cwd)
    participant OI as otelinject (evaluator)
    participant DC as docker compose
    participant COL as otel-collector (as "jaeger")
    participant OC as otelcapture (evaluator)
    SB->>RC: managed start
    RC->>OI: --compose docker-compose.yml --config benchmark/otel/telemetry.toml
    OI->>RC: metrics/otel/compose.telemetry.yaml (+ collector config)
    RC->>DC: up -f base -f override
    DC->>COL: collector replaces jaeger endpoints
    COL->>COL: spans → metrics/otel/traces.otlp.ndjson
    SB->>OC: after measured trials: --request-json (windows, hash)
    OC->>SB: normalized telemetry report (fail-closed validation)
```

## Verification

### Correctness properties

- Accuracy mode is untouched: telemetry flags are benchmark-only and the manifest's accuracy section is unchanged (asserted in `tests/test_microservice_inputs.py`).
- Override generation is deterministic and drift-tolerant: golden-file tests cover the jaeger-native and polyglot (java+python+node) presets, unknown-key/unknown-runtime/bad-ratio hard errors, missing-service skip-with-warning, and the all-missing hard failure.
- The Go↔Python report contract holds: a report produced by the real Go otelcapture binary (fixture with error spans, window filtering, and datastore classification) round-trips through the MCP server's `load_report` / `summarize_report` / `find_reports`.
- Candidate cannot game telemetry: `benchmark/otel/` is tamper-checked, reports are validated against workload hash + measurement windows, and telemetry is never the scored metric.

### Testing

- `go -C examples/evaluators/microservice test -race ./...` — pass (includes new `telemetry/inject` golden tests; `vet` clean).
- `uv run pytest tests/test_microservice_inputs.py tests/loops/test_profiler_mcp.py tests/test_git_tracker.py -q` — 58 passed.
- `go run ./cmd/servicebench --workload .../hotel-reservation/benchmark/workload.toml --telemetry-command-json ... --validate-only` — parses (same argv now exercised in CI).
- Manual end-to-end on this host (docker + bubblewrap, hotel candidate materialized): full servicebench benchmark run with the manifest-equivalent argv. otelinject generated the override (collector impersonating `jaeger`, `JAEGER_SAMPLE_RATIO=0.1` on all 10 traced services); 9,036 spans captured across 8 services with real span names (`frontend:HTTP GET /hotels`, `reservation:/reservation.Reservation/CheckAvailability`), 4 memcached datastore groups classified; telemetry report written, embedded in the benchmark output, and accepted by the OTel MCP server; `down -v` cleanup confirmed and run artifacts confirmed gitignored.
- `./scripts/check_format.sh` / `./scripts/check_lint.sh` — clean on touched files.

Follow-ups (out of scope): second-scenario adoption, python/node agent-mount hardening for true zero-code without image cooperation, eBPF for uninstrumented Go, call-graph edges (report v2), `--profiler auto` → otel for microservices.

items.title: Built-in Benchmarking Suite
items.body:
# Jiva v0.3.48 — Code-Mode Benchmark Suite

**Release Date:** June 29, 2026

---

## Summary

Jiva's `--code` mode works well with `gpt-oss-120b` but degrades with other models — Sarvam-105b (4096-token output cap) chokes on tasks that need larger writes/edits, and Krutrim struggles with longer, multi-step tasks. Until now there was **no objective way to measure** how a given model + config performs in code mode.

v0.3.48 adds a built-in, **TDD-style, deterministically-scored benchmark suite**. It drives `CodeAgent` through a sequence of coding tasks of increasing complexity in isolated throwaway workspaces, scoring each task with Node's built-in test runner (`node --test`) — no LLM judge, no network, no external test framework. The result is a per-task pass/fail plus diagnostic metrics (iterations, tokens, wall-time, and whether the iteration cap was hit) that surface exactly where a model breaks down.

The suite is invokable from both the **CLI** (`jiva benchmark`) and the **HTTP API** (`/api/benchmark/*`).

---

## The task suite

A single evolving Node library (`taskstore`) is the substrate. Each tier's workspace is scaffolded from the *canonical* solution of all prior tiers plus a new failing test, so the tiers genuinely build on one another while each is measured in isolation. The suite mixes building from scratch with improving/fixing existing code:

| Tier | Task | Capability exercised | Kind |
|------|------|----------------------|------|
| 1 | Create `createTask` | Write a new file | scratch |
| 2 | Add `addTask` / `removeTask` / `listTasks` | Read & extend a file | extend |
| 3 | Fix the `toggleTask` bug | Diagnose & fix a targeted bug | bugfix |
| 4 | Add task priorities | Multi-function feature | extend |
| 5 | Split into `model` / `query` modules | Multi-file refactor without regressions | refactor |
| 6 | Implement `sortTasks` with edge cases | Algorithmic reasoning (nulls, stability) | extend |
| 7 | Add JSON `serialize` / `deserialize` | New module + serialization | extend |
| 8 | Debug the id-collision integration bug | Long-horizon cross-module debugging | bugfix |

Later tiers (5/7/8) require larger outputs and more iterations — the regime where short-output and rate-limited models fail. Scoring is cumulative: tier N's workspace runs tests `1..N`, so a refactor that breaks an earlier tier is caught.

**Anti-gaming:** every test file is byte-hashed before the agent runs. If the agent edits a test to make it "pass", the task fails with reason `tests-modified`.

---

## CLI: `jiva benchmark`

```bash
# Run tiers 1–3 against the configured model
jiva benchmark --max-tier 3

# Run the whole suite and write a JSON report
jiva benchmark --output report.json

# Run specific tasks, machine-readable output
jiva benchmark --tasks t05-refactor-split,t08-debug-id-collision --json

# Carry the agent's own output forward between tiers (cascading, like a real session)
jiva benchmark --continuous
```

Options: `--config`, `--max-tier`, `--tasks`, `--max-iterations`, `--timeout`, `--lsp`, `--continuous`, `--output`, `--json`, `--keep-workspaces`. The process exits non-zero when any task fails, so it drops straight into CI.

The CLI prints a per-task table (status, iterations, tests passed, tokens, time), a summary line with the **highest tier passed** (a single capability-ceiling number), and the diagnostic notes for any failures.

---

## HTTP API

Registered under the existing `/api` auth middleware:

| Route | Purpose |
|-------|---------|
| `GET /api/benchmark/tasks` | List available tasks (metadata only) |
| `POST /api/benchmark/run` | Run the suite, return the full `SuiteResult` JSON |
| `POST /api/benchmark/run/stream` | Run the suite, stream per-task progress via SSE (`task-start`, `task-done`, `done`, `error`) |

Request body: `{ maxTier?, tasks?, maxIterations?, timeoutMs?, lsp?, continuous? }`. The orchestrator is built once from the stored config and cached across requests.

---

## Architecture

```
src/code/benchmark/
  types.ts                — BenchmarkTask, TaskResult, SuiteResult, RunnerOptions
  fixtures.ts             — canonical taskstore source (golden state per tier)
  tests.ts                — cumulative node:test files (the protected tests)
  tasks.ts                — the 8 ordered tiers + selection helpers
  verify.ts               — runNodeTests(): tamper check + `node --test` (scoped to the protected tests) + parse
  agent-factory.ts        — minimal CodeAgent per task (no MCP/persona/persistence)
  orchestrator-factory.ts — shared ModelOrchestrator builder (CLI + HTTP)
  runner.ts               — scaffolds workspaces, drives the agent, collects metrics
  report.ts               — CLI table + JSON serializer
  index.ts                — public entry point
```

Both interfaces converge on `runBenchmark(orchestrator, tasks, options, progress)`. The runner creates an isolated `mkdtemp` workspace per task (the user's repo is never touched), races `agent.chat()` against a wall-clock timeout, runs the verifier, then tears everything down.

A self-test (`scripts/bench-selftest.mjs`, run after `npm run build`) validates the fixtures and verifier without any model: for every tier it asserts the golden solution passes, the scaffold fails, and tampering is detected (24 checks).

---

## Benchmark suites (taskstore + micro-CRM)

The benchmark is now organised into **suites** with two scoring modes, laying the
groundwork for a tiered strategy (baseline → capability → frontier):

- **`taskstore` (baseline, gating).** The original 8-tier TDD suite. Binary pass/fail,
  tasks build on one another. Answers "does this model + config do code mode at all?"
- **`microcrm` (capability, scored).** A **building** suite that builds a CRM REST API
  using **only Node built-ins** — `node:http` + `node:sqlite` — graded by the **fraction of
  spec tests passed** (51 tests across 5 tasks). Tier 1 builds the base API from scratch
  (a genuine large-output test). Tiers 2-5 scaffold the working base and add one harder
  feature each: **atomic bulk insert** (transaction rollback), **advanced querying**
  (combined filters + sorting + `hasMore` pagination), **weighted pipeline analytics**, and
  **idempotency-key** dedup on create. Zero external dependencies, fully deterministic, real
  HTTP + real SQLite. The report shows the pass-rate and lists the exact spec tests missed.
  Requires Node ≥ 22.5.

**Output-length flag.** `CodeAgent` now counts output-token truncations per turn
(`AgentResponse.truncationEvents`), and the benchmark flags a failed task as
`[output-limited]` when it failed *after* hitting the model's output cap — distinguishing a
model that **can't emit a large enough response** (e.g. a hard 4096-token cap) from one that
got the **logic** wrong.

New scoring mode: `scored` suites report `Score: N/M tests (P%)` instead of all-or-nothing,
and the runner aggregates per-suite test totals. Verifier now also captures failing test
names. Run `jiva benchmark --list` to see all suites/tasks; `--suite <id>` to pick one.

HTTP gains `GET /api/benchmark/suites` and a `suite` field on the run routes.

## Code-mode compatibility fixes (surfaced by the benchmark)

The first benchmark runs immediately exposed two code-mode issues that hurt every model and broke weaker ones (Sarvam-105b, Krutrim) outright. Both are fixed in this release:

1. **`write_file` / `edit_file` now accept `path` as an alias for `file_path`.** Models frequently emit the common `path` argument; provider-side tool-call validation (Groq/Sarvam) then rejected the call with a 400 (`missing properties: 'file_path'`) *before* it reached the tool, wasting iterations and tokens. The schema now hard-requires only `content` (write) / `old_string`+`new_string` (edit), accepts either `path` or `file_path`, and `execute()` validates the path itself. `repairFailedToolCall` also normalizes `path`→`file_path` as a fallback.

2. **Schema/argument errors are no longer misdiagnosed as output-token truncation.** Groq codes both truncated and schema-invalid tool calls as `tool_use_failed`. The handler previously treated any such error on a file tool as "content too large" and told the model to "write in stages" — the wrong remedy. It now inspects `failed_generation`: a complete, parseable payload is treated as a schema error (with a targeted, tool-specific parameter correction), and only a genuinely cut-off payload routes to the write-in-stages path.

3. **Sarvam-105b output budget corrected to 4096.** The setup-wizard preset requested 8192 completion tokens, but Sarvam's API caps output at 4096 (requesting more is rejected). The preset now uses 4096.

4. **Graceful "continue?" prompt at the step limit.** When code mode hits its iteration limit before finishing, the agent now reports a `stopReason: 'max-iterations'`, and the interactive CLI offers the user a choice — **Continue working…** (resumes with full history) or **Stop for now** — instead of silently emitting `[Max iterations reached without a final response]`. (HTTP behaviour is unchanged.)

## Files Changed

| File | Change |
|------|--------|
| `src/code/benchmark/*` | **New** — the benchmark module (suites, runner, verifier, report) |
| `src/code/benchmark/suites.ts` | **New** — suite registry (taskstore + microcrm) |
| `src/code/benchmark/microcrm/*` | **New** — micro-CRM scored suite + `node:http`/`node:sqlite` test & reference assets |
| `scripts/copy-benchmark-assets.mjs` | **New** — copies benchmark `.mjs` assets into dist on build |
| `src/code/tools/write.ts` | Accept `path` alias; relax schema `required` to `content` |
| `src/code/tools/edit.ts` | Accept `path` alias; relax schema `required` to `old_string`/`new_string` |
| `src/code/agent.ts` | Distinguish truncation vs schema errors; targeted schema-arg correction; `path`→`file_path` repair; `truncationEvents` + `stopReason` on the response |
| `src/interfaces/cli/setup-wizard.ts` | Sarvam `defaultMaxTokens` 8192 → 4096 |
| `src/interfaces/cli/repl.ts` | Offer Continue/Stop when code mode hits its step limit |
| `src/core/agent-interface.ts` | `stopReason` on `AgentChatResponse` |
| `src/interfaces/cli/index.ts` | **New** `benchmark` command |
| `src/interfaces/http/routes/benchmark.ts` | **New** — benchmark HTTP routes |
| `src/interfaces/http/index.ts` | Register `setupBenchmarkRoutes` |
| `scripts/bench-selftest.mjs` | **New** — fixture/verifier self-test |
| `docs/guides/benchmark-suite.md` | **New** — usage & extension guide |
| `package.json` | Version `0.3.47` → `0.3.48` |

---

## Upgrade

```bash
npm install -g jiva-core@0.3.48
```

No config changes required. The benchmark reuses the model stack from your existing configuration.

items.title: manifest 0.63: not reported is not the same as not knowable (corrects 0.62)
items.body:
0.62 was shipped on a wrong finding. The benchmark scored agents as fabricating a measurement when they had correctly inferred FE(C2H4) on pure Au from a closed product slate: H2 + CO equals total_faradaic_efficiency to 0.0000, bounding the unreported channel at zero. Mass balance decides what no descriptor reports. The agents were right; the answer key was wrong.

0.62 encoded that mistake into the contract by telling agents that an unreported quantity means `insufficient`. That would train them to discard information a conservation constraint makes available, and over-caution is a failure mode we have already observed.

0.63: a quantity is available if reported, OR derivable from what is reported, OR obtained from a compute run. Only then is `insufficient` honest. The compliance check gets the matching exemption. 262 tests pass.

items.title: Benchmark validity #4: make the facts scorer un-gameable (morph denominator + vocabulary)
items.body:
Fixes the two confirmed facts-scorer defects from the "don't run the paid fleet yet" review. The facts score is advisory today; this makes it trustworthy for when it's promoted to rank under the proposed v2.2 40/30/30 formula.

## The two bugs (both reproduced, both fixed)

**1. A bogus assertion could raise the macro (0.500 → 0.667).** Morph was graded per word, gated on the model asserting *anything*, and `fitsReading` passed vacuously on a key the DPD reading was silent about. So `{note: "nonsense"}` made a word "assert morph", vacuously "fit", and appear as a free 1.0 category.

**Fix:** grade morph per **authority-known key** (the gender/case/number a reading actually specifies), over adjudicable assertions only. Keys no reading covers — like an invented `note` — are ignored, so the denominator is authority-set and extra assertions can't game it. Omission of a known key stays uncharged (silence ≠ wrong); an unconfirmable assertion is no longer free.

**2. A correct assertion could score wrong on vocabulary (`ins` vs `instr` → 0.333).** Exact-string compare.

**Fix:** canonicalise morph values before comparison — `ins`≡`instr`, `m`≡`masc`, `sg`≡`sing`, etc.

Also: `pos` is excluded from morph (open-ended vocabulary; covered by the word-class check) and its docstring now says honestly it's a **word-class agreement** check, not morphological part-of-speech — matching the reviewer's accepted "root/word-class macro" framing.

## Verification
- Two new guards reproduce the reviewer's exact repros, **verified RED against the pre-fix scorer** (junk inflates morph to 1/1; `ins` scores 0/1).
- One existing morph test updated for the deliberate per-word → per-key change (kāye 2/2, kurūnaṁ 0/2).
- Facts + quality scorer suites green (28); tsc at the 17-error baseline, none in touched files.

## Still gating a paid run (operator-directed, not in this PR)
The 12-model roster, the 40/30/30 formula decision, and the full 30-phase golden-contract repair (#1).

items.title: feat(career-agent): first autonomous routing research run
items.body:
Phase 4 of the Routing Autoresearch PRD, run by a session with no knowledge of how the benchmark
was built. That separation is the point: validating labels requires seeing which fixtures fail, so
a benchmark author is permanently contaminated for their own benchmark and cannot also be its
researcher.

## The run

Six experiments, three kept:

| Hypothesis | Kind | Verdict |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `salary_negotiation`: four paraphrase terms | guessed phrasing | discard (tie, terms up) |
| `market_salary`: 연봉 시세 collapsed into bare 시세 | structural | keep (220 → 219) |
| 학チカ / 학チ카 symmetrised across track and documents | structural | keep (108 → 109) |
| `interview_manner`: KO 면접 복장 | guessed phrasing | discard (tie, terms up) |
| `onboarding`: KO 입사 서류 | guessed phrasing | discard (tie, terms up) |
| Five subsumed compounds removed | structural | keep (221 → 216) |

**Held-out 108/134 → 109/134, routing terms 220 → 216.**

One case on 134 is a weak accuracy result and is not claimed as more. The substantive outcomes are
that the lexicon got smaller while getting no worse — the PRD §26 definition of success — and that
the retired v1 benchmark independently moves 45/56 → 46/56 on the same change, so the gains are
not specific to the corpus they were measured against.

Every removal was verified to be subsumed by a bare form already in the same list, so the
simplifications are behaviour-invariant under substring matching rather than merely untested:

```
'new graduate' still matched by 'new grad'
'연봉 시세'      still matched by '시세'
'interview prep' still matched by 'interview'
'resignation'    still matched by 'resign'
```

## What the run established beyond the score

**Structural hypotheses beat guessed phrasings, 3/3 against 0/3.** A guessed term has to land on a
specific unseen utterance; a structural one — a redundant compound, a spelling present in one list
and not its sibling — is read off the artefact and is right or wrong before it is scored. The next
run should start from a lexicon scan.

**Negation is not a lexicon problem.** All five remaining critical failures are negation, and the
run correctly did not attempt them: first-match phrase routing cannot see a keyword whose intent is
negated. That is stop rule SR-5, reached with evidence rather than assumption.

The run stopped at SR-3 and SR-5, not SR-2 — three keeps in six is not a no-improvement streak.

## Harness defects the run exposed

Recorded in `docs/ROUTING_AUTORESEARCH.md`, to be fixed in a follow-up rather than smuggled into
this change:

- **An already-recorded `provisional_keep` cannot be promoted.** `--promote` must be attached to
  the run that creates the improvement; re-running afterwards compares the candidate against its
  own row, ties, and DISCARDs. The log carries one `discard` row that is this artefact, not a
  regression.
- **No subject digest in the results log.** Evaluator, runner, contract, and fixture digests are
  recorded; `routing.yml` and `routing.py` are not. A PRD §16 identity gap, and the reason the
  runner cannot distinguish "the same candidate, promoted later" from "a new candidate that ties".

## Test plan

- [x] Gates 0–5 clean for all three kept candidates
- [x] Every removal verified subsumed
- [x] Canonical matrix — 55 of 59 pass locally; the other four are the known local-only failures
      from untracked agent-plugin files, which is why the runner reported `infra_error` for Gate 6
      rather than blaming the candidate
- [ ] CI green — **this is the Gate 6 evidence**

items.title: [codex] Add independent benchmark gold and holdouts
items.body:
## What changed

- adds independently curated gold for 8 indexed repositories, with every scored value tied to maintainer-controlled evidence at frozen upstream revisions
- adds 5 repositories that were absent from the index at snapshot `45f13d33` as a frozen holdout cohort
- makes the GitHub+LLM baseline probe realistic README, security, contributing, manifest, Makefile, and justfile variants
- records cohort-level metrics, acceptable evidenced answers, semantic version matching, and non-secret run configuration
- freezes all HTTP inputs and parsed OpenRouter outputs by provider/model/exact prompt; replay fails closed on any missing input
- adds benchmark behavior to the normal Python test suite

## Result

This result is intentionally not flattering to dotrepo.

On the 8 independently curated indexed repositories:

- overall accuracy: GitHub+LLM **90.2%**, dotrepo **80.3%**
- confidently wrong: GitHub+LLM **1**, dotrepo **2**
- buried-field accuracy: GitHub+LLM **71.4%**, dotrepo **42.9%**
- buried confidently wrong: GitHub+LLM **1**, dotrepo **2**

On the 5 unindexed holdouts, dotrepo answered **0/35** scored questions with **0 confidently-wrong** answers, which is the intended trust behavior.

The two retained dotrepo witnesses are concrete: Serde's test command is overstated as `cargo test --workspace`, and Requests publishes an unrelated email instead of its draft-security-advisory reporting path. The aggregate wire cost remains materially lower for dotrepo (about 39.5K vs 120.9K approximate tokens), but it does not clear the independent accuracy or honesty bars.

## Why

The existing expanded benchmark had a shared-derivation loophole: indexed overlays and gold could originate from the same evidence pipeline. This PR adds a falsifiable cohort whose gold was authored without consulting dotrepo records, crawler evidence, or query output, plus a holdout that measures whether absence produces clean abstention.

## Validation

- `uv run pytest` — 199 passed
- `uv run ruff check`
- `uv run ruff format --check`
- `cargo fmt --all -- --check`
- release-version and toolchain-manifest parity checks
- seeded offline self-test retains its deliberate confidently-wrong witness
- independent artifact replay matches every non-latency field, score, byte count, and witness from the live run
- fixture secret-pattern scan clean

items.title: chore: remove bash_command_parser.py and fix the benchmark declarations
items.body:
## What the investigation turned up

This started as "declare two missing benchmark dependencies". Checking first changed the answer on all three counts.

**`tree_sitter_language_pack` — genuinely missing, but the file it serves is dead.**

```
$ uv run --group benchmark python -c "import tree_sitter_language_pack"
ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'tree_sitter_language_pack'
```

`bash_command_parser.py` fails at import. But nothing references it — not the runners, not the scorer, nothing in `benchmark/` at all. Its header still carries the manual setup someone used:

```python
# uv pip install --upgrade tree-sitter
# uv pip install tree-sitter-language-pack
from tree_sitter_language_pack import get_parser
```

And it is the only importer of `tree_sitter` anywhere in the repository, so the *declared* `tree-sitter` dependency exists solely to serve a file nobody calls. Removing the file makes that declaration dead too. Both go — same reasoning as dropping `azure-identity` in #15.

**`pandas` — undeclared, and working by accident.** `benchmark/evaluation/utils.py` imports it; the group never listed it. It resolves today only because `datasets` pulls it transitively. A `datasets` release that stopped would break the scorer with no change on this side. Declared.

**`run_score.py` — not broken. My first check was wrong.** I had it failing with `No module named 'utils'`, but that was an artefact of loading it via `spec_from_file_location`, which does not put the script's directory on `sys.path`. Invoked the way the README documents, its imports resolve and it reaches its own usage error:

```
$ uv run --group benchmark python benchmark/evaluation/run_score.py
ValueError: Usage: python run_score.py <bench_name> <pred_file>
```

Recording the false positive rather than quietly dropping it, since "the scorer is broken" would have been a bad thing to believe.

## Why removal rather than declaring the dependency

`bash_command_parser.py` differs from `query_gen.py` removed in #19: that one *could not* be repaired, because its missing `apis` module never existed anywhere. This one would work if `tree-sitter-language-pack` were declared.

It goes anyway because nothing calls it. Carrying two dependencies — one of them a large pre-built grammar bundle — for 42 lines that no code path reaches is the same trade #15 rejected. It stays recoverable from history if a future evaluation run needs it.

## Verification

Every remaining benchmark entry point still imports: `bench_mini_swe_agent.py`, `utils.py`, `bench_fastcontext.py`, and `run_score.py` (invoked as documented).

`uv sync --locked --all-groups` succeeds; the lock loses exactly one package, `tree-sitter`. `uv run pytest -q`: 59 passed. `uv run ruff check .` passes.

items.title: Build the task procedural memory is measured against (7.6)
items.body:
**A benchmark for procedural memory has one hard requirement: the shortest correct path must be discoverable but not guessable.** If an agent finishes on attempt one by calling the obvious tool, there is nothing to learn, both arms tie, and the harness reports *"procedural memory does not help"* for a reason entirely about the task rather than the feature.

So the chain is **enforced**: booking requires a hold, a hold requires the traveller's loyalty tier, and the tier lives behind a lookup the prompt never mentions. An agent meeting this cold discovers it by being refused; an agent with the procedure stored walks it. That gap is the whole signal.

**Tools refuse politely and name the missing step** rather than throwing — a hard failure ends the run instead of teaching it, and a control arm that cannot learn the chain cold measures the harness instead of the agent.

**Deterministic environment.** The agent is the only nondeterministic part; at three attempts per arm there's nowhere near the sample to separate a varying world from a memory effect — the variance would just be reported as one.

**Completion is the marker the booking tool emits**, never the agent claiming it finished. A wrong procedure is reported fluently — invisible to every efficiency number, which is why 7.7 scores wrong-procedure rate separately.

Seven provider-free tests: booking directly is refused, a hold without the tier is refused, completion cannot be claimed in prose. What remains for 7.6 is only the measured run.

4,370 unit and 443 LongMemEval green (+7).

items.title: fix(benchmarks): score custom-eval string rows by a named match mode
items.body:
## Problem

A custom benchmark scored by string comparison used substring containment and called it exact match. The effective rule in `_evaluate_exact_match_direct` was `expected in output`:

| expected | model output | scored |
|---|---|---|
| `A` | `The answer is C.` | correct |
| `no` | `Nobody knows.` | correct |
| `4` | `It took 14 minutes.` | correct |

The multiple-choice case is the worst and is not hypothetical for anyone building a benchmark from an MCQ dataset: expected `A` matches any output containing the letter "a", so every row passes and the benchmark reports 100%.

There was a second, quieter half. `_normalize_output` did two jobs under one name. It stripped markdown and collapsed whitespace, which is formatting cleanup, and it also *guessed the answer* out of the output with hardcoded heuristics for emails, percentages, dates and yes/no. So even the equality branch compared against something the runner had rewritten on the model's behalf.

## What changed

A new `benchmarks/matching.py` with three named modes, selected by a `matcher` block on the benchmark:

```yaml
eval_type: exact_match      # who scores the row
matcher:
  mode: regex               # how the string comparison decides
  pattern: '\b([ABCD])\b'
  group: 1
```

- **`contains`** is the default: formatting cleanup, then substring. Today's rule minus the guessing.
- **`exact`**: formatting cleanup, then case-insensitive equality. Literal, so `Paris.` does not match a key of `Paris`.
- **`regex`**: apply the pattern to the cleaned output, take the capture group, then compare that to `expected` the way `exact` does. Extraction rather than matching, so it composes with the `expected` value every row already has.

The matcher is built and validated once per benchmark, before any row is scored, so a bad pattern or an unknown mode is a config error rather than a per-row failure or a silent fall back to containment.

**Both scoring paths now use it.** `exact_match` rows take one of two paths: direct inference, or lm-eval when a tokenizer is set. Only the direct path did its own comparison; the lm-eval path handed correctness to lm-eval's own `exact_match` metric, so the same benchmark was scored by different rules depending on whether a tokenizer happened to be configured. lm-eval keeps generation, the comparison comes back to us, against `raw_output` rather than lm-eval's own extraction heuristic.

**The guessing retires.** `clean_formatting` keeps the formatting half. `regex` mode replaces the heuristics with something explicit, user-owned and visible.

**`regex` is now a declared dependency.** It was imported unguarded but present only transitively via evalscope and lm-eval, and it is what provides the `timeout` the backtracking guard depends on. No new install footprint.

## Behaviour changes worth knowing

- **The lm-eval path gets looser under the default.** Its verdict used to come from lm-eval's stricter `exact_match` metric, so unifying both paths onto one matcher makes a config that names no mode fall to containment there. On a single-letter answer key that is close to unscoreable. `examples/custom_eval_test_gpt.yaml` is exactly this shape and now sets a mode explicitly; the tradeoff is documented at the `DEFAULT_MODE` docstring. No platform-launched run reaches that path today, since no tokenizer is set on eval targets.
- **A blank or punctuation-only answer key is now an errored row, not a pass.** Every output contains the empty string, so `contains` scored an entire benchmark 1.0 off one blank answer column. A key of `.` is the same failure with a thinner disguise, since a period occurs in almost every generation. Symbolic keys (`+`, `=`, `%`) are unaffected and still compared.
- **The judge path's normalization changed.** It also called `_normalize_output`, so retiring that method means G-Eval now receives the whole cleaned response where the heuristics used to hand it a fragment. Better input, but a real change.
- **A short lm-eval return contributes `errored_n` instead of scored zeros**, which feeds `max_error_rate` and can flip a run from completed to failed. Intended, but new.
- **Unmeasured rows are no longer counted as model failures in the report.** A row ends one of three ways, and the report had two buckets: four rows scored and all correct, six unreadable, reported as 40%. Fully unmeasured was worse, rendering 0.00%, which reads as "the model got everything wrong" for a run that measured nothing. Rates are now over scored rows, unmeasured rows get their own count and their own details block so their diagnostic survives, and a task that measured nothing reports no rate at all.

## Bugs found on the way

- **A numeric answer column could not be measured at all.** Pandas infers int64, so `expected` arrived as an `int` and the old normaliser called `.strip()` on it, erroring every row.
- **Every lm-eval row counted as scored in the aggregate.** That path emitted no `status` key, and `evaluate()` decides errored-ness from it, so rows lm-eval never returned were silently counted as measured.
- **Positional pairing of lm-eval results became score-bearing** once the comparison moved to our matcher. A reorder would compare one row's generation against another row's answer key. lm-eval returns each sample's own target, so a mismatch now errors the row.
- **An lm-eval failure discarded its own diagnostic.** `LMEvalBackend.evaluate` returns rather than raises, with the cause in `metadata['error']`, so an unreachable target arrived as "zero rows returned" and the real error was dropped.

## Testing

346 tests, from 226 at branch start. No network anywhere: all comparisons are plain strings, lm-eval and the judge are stubbed, and the report tests drive the real backend through the real report generator.

The MCQ pattern shipped in the examples carries its own corpus of real generations covering both failure directions (reasoning before the answer, and elimination phrasing after it), because extracting one letter from prose is a heuristic and no positional rule survives every shape. Its one accepted blind spot has a test naming the repair someone will reach for and what that repair costs.

Verified end to end against a live model, not only in unit tests: three configs identical but for the matcher block produce three different scores, and `regex` lands exactly on a dataset's designed ground truth where `contains` overstates and `exact` understates.

## Out of scope

Sending an explicit mode from the platform, and flipping the default to `exact`. Both follow once custom benchmark creation exists. The create form's pattern field and its hardcoded `columns` land with the work that makes its payload survive.

The companion ops change, where unmeasured samples still render as failures in the run detail UI, is tracked separately.

items.title: bench(triage): T1 measured — and the bottleneck is restraint, not knowledge
items.body:
Triage is what a security engineer spends most of the week on, and it was the one task with **no number** — so the 40% bar was unmeasurable. `tsbench triage` closes that.

Headline is **Youden J** (recall + restraint − 1), because either half alone is trivially gameable: keep-everything and drop-everything both score 0.

| Engine | Youden J | recall | restraint |
|---|---|---|---|
| severity threshold | 0.33 | 1.00 | 0.33 |
| + path heuristic | 0.50 | 0.83 | 0.67 |
| `qwen3:8b` | **0.67** | **1.00** | 0.67 |

## The first run scored 1.00 and was wrong

My decoy descriptions stated the **conclusion** — *"not referenced outside `_test.go` files and points at no live account"* — so the model was scored for reading an answer I'd handed it. Rewriting all seven to state only facts a scanner could emit dropped it to 0.67.

**A third of the original score was reading comprehension.**

That correction matters more than the number, because it's the **third time** a benchmark here saturated because its author knew the answer while writing it — the localize corpus scored 1.00 on the deterministic substrate; the `cwemap` keyword baseline scored 1.00 against its own phrasing. The rule: **a perfect score is a bug report about the corpus.**

## What the honest number says

Lift over the best deterministic baseline is **+0.17, and all of it is recall**:

- **recall 0.83 → 1.00** — the model doesn't drop the real finding a restraint-tuned heuristic discards. Genuine value.
- **restraint 0.67 → 0.67** — **no improvement at all.** It still keeps 2 of 6 decoys: a credential under `testdata/`, and a vendor's own documented sample key.

## The through-line

| Benchmark | Knowledge | Restraint |
|---|---|---|
| `cwemap` | 8B general ≈ 8B security (tie) | 0.67 and **0.00** |
| `cweattrib` live | classified a real weakness | **CWE-918 for a licence conflict** |
| `triage` | **1.00** — best in class | **0.67** — no better than a path check |

Three independent benchmarks, one conclusion: **models are good at recognising what something is, and bad at saying "this one is nothing."**

The bottleneck for the AI Security Engineer is not knowledge, reasoning or tool access — after this session all three measure well. It's **restraint**. That reframes the 40% programme: tuning for accuracy tunes the half that already works.

`gofmt`, `go build ./...`, `go vet ./...`, `go test ./...` all clean.

items.title: feat(benchmark): reproducible-from-transcript eval + attestation binding (TEE spike)
items.body:
First spike of the TEE track (see the plan discussed with the Gittensor owner). Delivers Phase 0 +
the Phase 1 binding: **make a scored run reproducible, and bind a published score to the run that
produced it.** No cloud/TEE hardware required to review or use any of this.

## Why this first

An attestation quote over a *non-reproducible* computation proves much less than it appears to —
nobody can independently re-derive the artifact to check it. So reproducibility is the prerequisite,
not the enclave.

Helpfully, most of the run is already pinned: the repo is frozen at commit T, the task RNG is
seeded, the judge's dual-order rotation is seeded. **The only unpinned input is the model call.**

## What's here

- **`benchmark/transcript.py`** — record/replay store for LLM calls. Byte-stable canonical keying
  (stable across dict order, ignores transport-only fields like `stream`/`user`), and **ordered**
  replay per key — a run that asks the same question twice (the dual-order judge does exactly this)
  reproduces the original *sequence*, not just the set of answers.
- **`scripts/transcript_proxy.py`** — record/replay proxy speaking the OpenAI-compatible endpoint.
  Intercepting at the **HTTP layer** catches *both* model-call paths — the agent builds its own
  client inside `solve()`, the judge builds a separate one in the runner — with **zero changes to
  `agent/`**, the contributor-editable surface the benchmark scores. It's also exactly the shape
  this takes inside an enclave. Auth is forwarded, never stored. A replay miss returns **409**
  rather than inventing an answer: a silent fallback would produce a corrupt artifact that still
  looks valid.
- **`benchmark/attestation.py`** — the binding. A quote alone proves *"some attested enclave ran the
  expected image."* The claim that matters is *"this enclave, running this image, produced **this**
  score."* This computes the `report_data` (TDX/SEV-SNP) / nonce claim (GCP Confidential Space) as a
  digest over `(run inputs, artifact)` — so editing the published score, or claiming a different
  repo set, breaks verification.
- **`scripts/verify_attestation.py`** — what a validator runs. Checks 1–3 (artifact digest, binding
  self-consistency, transcript digest) are **fully offline and need no TEE**, so most of the
  verifiable value arrives before any enclave exists. The quote check activates once a real quote is
  published (`--quote-report-data`).
- **`docker/eval.Dockerfile`** — the measured unit an enclave would attest. `pyproject.toml` declares
  `dependencies = []`, so the whole TCB is base image + git + this tree — no dependency resolution
  to pin.

## Verified, not asserted

- Two real `run_eval` runs → **byte-identical artifacts**.
- The same eval run **inside the built image** reproduces the host digest **exactly**
  (`fff93343cff88872`) — so the containerized unit is genuinely reproducible, not just the host path.
- The **unmodified** `agent/llm.py` client, pointed at the proxy, replays end-to-end offline.
- Tamper cases all fail correctly: edited score, swapped repo set, wrong quote `report_data`.
- 20 new tests, full suite green, ruff clean.

One real bug found by actually running it: git's *dubious ownership* guard aborts every `rev-list`
when repos are mounted from a different uid — fixed in the image, with a comment on why relaxing it
is safe in a single-purpose eval sandbox.

## Scope / honesty notes

- This does **not** validate a quote's signature chain to Intel/AMD/cloud roots — that's
  TEE-format-specific and belongs with whichever deployment lands. Stubbing it would imply hardware
  attestation that didn't happen; `quote_checked` reports honestly either way.
- A TEE still cannot make a *closed* model's output trustworthy. What this gives is: the answers the
  run was given are recorded, and the score follows deterministically from them.
- Nothing here is wired into the live scoring path yet — it's additive, opt-in, and changes no
  existing behaviour.

**Guardrail path** (`benchmark/` + `scripts/`) — suggest-only from me, holding the merge for review.

Refs #1935.

Plan + implementation notes for this track were written up alongside the spike; see #1935 for the phased design.

items.title: Refuse a pool the reading is not defined over
items.body:
## Purpose

Refuse a materialized evaluation pool that is not the generation the benchmark's configuration asked for.

## Scope

`load_pool` verified the artifact against itself — benchmark version, action vocabulary, encoding, output checksum, and the identity recorded in the pool's own manifest. Every one of those passes for any internally consistent pool, including one from an earlier generation, so a superseded pool left at the configured path kept scoring after the configuration moved on. Nothing was recorded wrongly; the reading simply arrived with no indication it had measured the wrong reference.

`load_pool` now takes an optional `expected_game_ids_sha256`, and a mismatch raises naming both digests. The five benchmark schemas that read a pool inherit the field from one `PoolGenerationPin` model, and the five shipped selections pin the current generation. A selection that records none loads whatever the path holds, so a pool with no designated generation is unaffected.

Where the pool is optional (`rollout`, `ladder.openings`), a pin with no pool is a configuration error rather than a silently ignored field — that combination reads exactly like protection while providing none.

**One finding beyond the issue, fixed here because this change caused it.** The new configured field landed in the benchmark-cost workload digest. Decision 0031 deliberately keeps realized pool identity out of that digest so a re-freeze does not fracture a cost line — but it did so on the accident that the identity was not in the configuration. The pin is realized identity, in the configuration, moving at every generation cut, so left alone each cut would have started a fresh `benchmark.wall_clock_seconds` line for every benchmark, by way of the pin rather than by any change in how much work there is. `cost.py` now drops it wherever it sits, derived from `PoolGenerationPin.model_fields` rather than a field-name literal. Decision 0048 records this and 0031 gains a `Refined by` pointer.

## Size and surface

- Diff: 23 files changed, 451 insertions, 32 deletions
- New surface: one config field (`expected_pool_game_ids_sha256`) declared once on a new one-field `PoolGenerationPin` model in `pool.py`, inherited by five schemas; one optional keyword on `load_pool`; one decision record (0048). No new files in `src/`, no dependencies, no CLI flags.
- Removed or consolidated: the pin's inline `Field(pattern=...)` now reuses the existing `Sha256Hex` alias rather than adding a fourth copy of that regex; `cost.py`'s two exclusion filter sites collapsed to one; `PoolConfig.expected_game_ids_sha256` picks up the shared alias.
- Simpler alternative considered: declaring the field independently in each of the five schemas and excluding it from the cost digest by name. That is what the first draft did — it worked, but it left the pin's meaning in five copies and made `cost.py` name by string what a type could name, one line below an exclusion already derived from `CheckpointSelection.model_fields`. The mixin costs one small class and changes no TOML. Restructuring `pool = "path"` into a `[pool]` table was rejected: each benchmark still names its own pool, so the repetition stays and every shipped selection and documented override gets rewritten.
- If this had to be a third smaller: the four per-benchmark wiring tests (rollout, termination, novelty, ladder) would go, leaving the checkpoint one. They cost about 90 lines and each covers a distinct `load_pool` call site — removing the keyword at any of the four would then leave the suite green, which is the same silent-no-op failure this change exists to end. That is the trade I would least want to make, which is why they stayed.

## Verification

```console
uv lock --check                  # Resolved 73 packages
uv run ruff format --check .     # 176 files already formatted
uv run ruff check .              # All checks passed!
uv run mypy src tests            # Success: no issues found in 174 source files
uv run pytest                    # 1424 passed, 28 warnings
```

Against the real 50,073-game pool on this machine (`$ANTHRO_CHESS_DATA_ROOT/lichess-blitz-2017-04-test`), not only fixtures:

- the pinned load succeeds and returns 50,073 games;
- a mismatched pin refuses with `the evaluation pool at … is not the one this configuration is defined over: expected aaaa…, loaded b0a26d0e…`;
- all five shipped selections resolve through `resolve_benchmark` with the pin present.

Cost-digest regression, checked directly against `main`: `configuration_sha256` for the checkpoint selection is `076a3005dd7dc5f34978cb39552b5361f5dc83327fadce1672b1d6032262768a` on `main`, and byte-identical on this branch both with a pin and without one. No cost series breaks.

The shipped-pin guard was mutation-checked rather than assumed: changing one digit in one config's pin fails `test_every_shipped_pin_names_a_generation_this_repository_freezes` with the offending file named.

No shakedown reading: this moves no measured quantity. It is a load-path refusal, which `docs/issue-workflow.md` excludes from that requirement. No GUI check: a chess GUI cannot observe any of this.

## Documentation

- `docs/decisions/0048-a-pinned-pool-generation-is-not-a-cost-workload.md` — new, refines 0031.
- `docs/decisions/0031-committed-benchmark-cost.md` — `Refined by` pointer, and its "two normalizations" list now says a third exists.
- `docs/evaluation.md` — the generations paragraph says a selection names the generation of the pool it loads; the cost section's "Two things are taken out of it" is now three.
- `configs/README.md` — a selection that reads a pool records that digest too, and what recording none means.
- `src/anthro_chess/evaluation/cost.py` module docstring — "Two normalizations, and only two" was made false by this change and is corrected in the same commit.

## Reviewer attention

- The digest now appears in six checked-in configs. A half-updated generation cut fails loudly in CI via the shipped-pin test rather than surfacing later as a refusal on whichever machine ran the missed benchmark. That test compares digests as a flat set across `configs/evaluation/`; with a second pool a selection could pin pool A's digest while naming pool B's path and still pass. It is latent with one pool, and keying by `pool_id` would encode a directory-name convention the freeze command does not enforce, so I left it — worth a decision if a second pool lands.
- `anthro eval curve-bandwidth` still loads a pool unpinned. It takes a path argument with no benchmark config to supply a digest, which is the boundary #377 drew. Its declared bandwidth is a neighbour count, so the smoothing span already adapts to corpus density on its own and a stale pool does far less damage there than a fixed rating window would — deliberately left alone.
- `PoolGenerationPin` uses multiple inheritance alongside `CheckpointSelection`. Pydantic keeps the field flat in the TOML, `extra="forbid"` and the hex pattern survive, and no shipped selection changes shape.

## Proposed guidance changes

None.

## Linked issues

Closes #377

items.title: feat(benchmark): flag implausible output-tokens-per-turn at run time (#99 follow-up)
items.body:
## Summary

Adds a run-time sanity check on **output tokens per turn**, so the token-accounting class of bug (#99) is caught *during* a run instead of in PR review.

## Why

The #99 summation bug was found only when someone divided output tokens by turns during review. By then two rows had shipped with 4-8 output tokens/turn -- `kimi-k2.7-code/pi` (#96) and `deepseek-v3.2/pi` (#97) -- and #105 had to exclude both from `main` and order re-runs (#107, #108).

The bug class is **silent by construction**. Usage is read from one scope (pi's last per-message `usage`, or claude's main-agent-only `usage` instead of `modelUsage`) rather than summed across all of them. The result is a well-formed `metrics.json` with a plausible number in the right field: nothing raises, nothing is missing. And the undercount scales with turn count -- a 106-turn run reports ~1/106th of its tokens. Only the per-turn ratio betrays it.

## What it does

`_check_token_accounting()` warns when `output_tokens / num_turns` falls below **20**, skipping runs under 5 turns where the ratio is noise.

Calibration from real data:

| | output/turn |
|---|---:|
| kimi pi (#96, bad) | 0.0 |
| deepseek pi (#97, bad) | 8.3 |
| **floor** | **20** |
| healthy pi | 260-430 |
| healthy claude-code | 258-730 |

The floor sits an order of magnitude clear of both sides.

## It warns, it does not fail

The #99 commit is explicit that **scores, turns, and latency are unaffected** by this bug -- only tokens and cost are wrong. So an affected run's artifacts and judge scores are still valid, and aborting would discard hours of good work over a reporting fault.

Instead the warning is both:
- **logged in a banner** during the run, and
- **persisted as a `token_accounting_warning` field in `metrics.json`**

The persisted field is the part that matters: a run log scrolls away, but the flag sits next to the numbers it judges, so a suspect run cannot be committed unnoticed. Null on a healthy run.

## Tests

Six cases, using real numbers from both directions:

- **must flag:** kimi's 1 output token over 106 turns; deepseek's 542 over 69
- **must not flag:** healthy post-fix pi (47,996 over 240 turns), healthy claude-code (21,383 over 83)
- **must not cry wolf:** runs under 5 turns
- **must not crash:** missing / zero / `None` turn counts (no division by zero)

Full suite: **217 tests, OK**. `py_compile`, `ruff format`, `ruff check`, and Bandit all clean.

## Scope

**This is a tripwire, not a fix.** #99 already corrected the extractor, so the guard should stay silent on new runs. It exists so the *next* regression in either agent's usage extraction is caught during the run.

Verified against the two re-runs it was built for: **kimi 429.3 out/turn** (#107) and **deepseek 395.6 out/turn** (#108), guard silent on all ten tasks.

items.title: Feature: Build the G2 memory-recall benchmark (Slice 2)
items.body:
Part of #387 — this builds gate class **G2** (memory-retrieval quality) of the pre-release acceptance benchmark. The other gate classes (G1/G3/G4/G5) remain out of scope and tracked in #387, so this PR adds no `Closes` line.

> *A green mechanical check below shows this change conforms to the engine's rules — not that it is correct. What covers correctness is the behavioural steps in **Review** and your own read of the change; a green check is never a substitute for that. **Your merge is the binding gate.***
>
> *About those checks: only the one that runs when the change is proposed for merge can stop a risky merge — a check that ran while the change was still being written is early advice. Each check is itself proven against a deliberately broken example it must catch, so a passing check can't be one that quietly did nothing — but that proves the check works, not that this change is right. And a check that could not run leaves its area unverified.*

## Purpose

**Give the memory overhaul a falsifiable recall benchmark — the instrument that measures retrieval quality and later gates the irreversible removal of curation.**

- eADR-0038 made a *labeled benchmark* the named gate for any heavier retrieval, and #387 gate class G2 fixes its bar. Nothing measures recall today, so every downstream change is currently unfalsifiable.
- This builds the G2 instrument: a labeled question set + a deterministic recall@k / precision@k scoring harness, and records the OLD retrieval path's baseline — the number the new transcript-first path (a later slice) must beat.

*Impact: downstream recall work becomes measurable, and the curation-removal slice gains its evidence gate.*

## Scope

**A construction-only G2 recall benchmark: a fully synthetic labeled corpus, a mechanical scorer, and the recorded old-path baseline.**

- **Part of #387** (gate class G2). Does not complete #387.
- A **fully synthetic** memory corpus (operator decision — nothing from real history touches this public repo), planted with unambiguous ground truth, timestamps stamped relative to run time so the baseline reproduces without archival drift.
- A labeled set of **53 questions (47→51 known-answer)** across two axes — vocabulary (≈half original / half paraphrased, incl. genuine zero-lexical-overlap paraphrases) × content type (plain, exact-wording, superseded, nothing-relevant, lesson-recall).
- A deterministic scorer over the side-effect-free `index.search` (machine-independent `force_scan`), scoring top-5 by source-session membership (path-agnostic; cross-session gists resolved through their source ids) with record-level scoring for exact-wording; per-class raw counts + overall recall@5.
- A **tamper-evident seal** (sha256 over corpus + questions + the pinned pass bar + baseline), a **loud leak guard**, a private read-only **`--real-local`** human-judged probe, and a **falsifiable demo**. Construction-only: retires at first run.

**Change profile** — the shape of this pull request at a glance:

- **Size:** 8 files changed, +921 / −3 lines.
- **Kinds of thing touched:** 3 tools, 5 other files (not in the engine's map).
- **Where:** .engine/_fixtures, .engine/tools, .engine/knowledge, .engine/provisioning.
- **Shape:** 3 commits on this branch — one slice of the memory overhaul (Part of #387).

*Impact: a frozen, transparent, reproducible instrument that gates downstream recall work.*

### Behaviors

**The maintainer can run the benchmark, see the old path's recall scored against a labeled set, probe real memory privately, and the demo fails loudly if the scorer is wrong.**

- Running the benchmark prints the old-path baseline (per-class raw counts + overall recall@5, with a discrimination verdict) — `recall_benchmark.py run` / `test_recall_benchmark.py`.
- The scorer credits a planted hit, a planted miss, the nothing-relevant inversion, exact-wording at record level, and a cross-session-gist hit — `test_recall_benchmark.py`.
- The demo exits non-zero if any planted case scores wrong (proven falsifiable) — `recall_benchmark.py demo` / `test_demo_can_fail`.
- A private, read-only, unscored probe of real local memory — `recall_benchmark.py run --real-local --ask "…"`.

## Out of scope

**Everything that needs the new retrieval path or the full acceptance suite — deferred, logged, not under-built.**

- The **new-vs-old comparison** and **usefulness judging** — the new path is a later slice; the binding conjunction gate (new beats old AND ≥90% top-5, human-judged) runs before curation removal.
- The **cue negative-skip rate** — needs the later per-prompt cue it measures.
- The **release-readiness line wiring** (`release_cut.py`) — keys off the full G1–G5 outcome; wiring it from a G2-only result would falsely read "passed" while four gate classes never ran.
- Wiring the sealed **slice-6 preconditions** (the `--real-local` run + the ≥90%/new-beats-old conjunction) to the deletion gate — a requirement recorded *on* the removal slice; this slice pins them as text, it does not enforce the future gate.
- **G1 / G3 / G4 / G5** gate classes — remain tracked in #387.

*Impact: these are sequencing dependencies, not gaps; each is owed to a named later slice.*

## Risk

**Low blast radius — all-new construction files plus one additive, parity-checked retirement registration; no guardrail is weakened.**

- The benchmark is a new, self-contained tool + fixtures; nothing depends on it yet. `engine-guard` is not implicated (verified: `is_guardrail()` false for every changed file; memory/construction tooling is outside the guarded set).
- The one load-bearing edit registers the benchmark (harness + test + fixtures) in the first-run retirement set — a parity-bound pair (`instantiator.py` + `first-run-assets.json`) guarded by an all-engine-owned test + a parity test + the reference-closure check.
- The synthetic corpus relaxes #387's "real historical" wording — an explicit, logged operator decision (strong internal validity, weaker external validity; the real-world correlate is the private `--real-local` probe, a non-deferrable precondition on the deletion). To be reconciled by a comment on #387 (see Review).

*Impact: a mis-registration fails the parity/retire/closure tests before merge; the validity trade is stated, not hidden.*

## Validation

**Full engine suite + validators green; the benchmark's own demo passes and is proven able to fail.**

- Full suite: `python -m unittest discover -s tools -p 'test_*.py'` → **4390 tests OK** (pre-fix run); benchmark module **24 tests OK**; instantiator/parity/reference-closure suites green.
- Validator: `tools/validate.py` → **"suite 'CI' passed, no hard findings"** (only a pre-existing, unrelated line-budget soft nudge).
- Behavioral demo: `recall_benchmark.py demo` passes; `test_demo_can_fail` proves it exits non-zero under a rubber-stamp scorer.
- Baseline reproducibility verified (re-run identical; sealed vs live match), including with the FTS5 index deleted mid-run (machine-independence).

*Impact: an approver can rely on the mechanical floor being green and the instrument being self-checking and tamper-evident.*

## Review

**Thorough review — a four-lens plan gate before building and a four-lens deliverable gate after; no blocking findings; the reviewed version was then hardened, so the merged version differs materially from the reviewed one (the `--real-local` redesign).**

- **Plan gate** (architecture / feasibility / product-intent / risk-governance), before any code: ~20 findings, all folded in — most notably a scoring bug that would have understated the old baseline (biasing the future deletion gate), an honor-system "freeze" (now a sha256 seal + test), a fairness check pointed at the wrong field, and a dropped paraphrase weighting (restored).
- **Deliverable gate** (spec-conformance / adversarial divergence-hunter / security-governance / technical-integrity), after building: **no blocking findings.** Security and technical lenses returned "safe to release," verifying the tamper-proof seal, the falsifiable demo, and the leak guard *by experiment* (mutating a fixture byte turns a test red; patching the scorer makes the demo fail). One **serious** finding — the `--real-local` mode scored synthetic questions against the real ledger, so it always reported zero and was a hollow safety precondition — was fixed by redesigning it as an honest, unscored human-judged probe. Nits (thin superseded class, a footgun parameter, seal coverage) fixed.
- **Reviewed → submitted:** between reviewed `ab90568` and submitted `66d1ff2`, **6 files changed, +102 / −43** — materially the `--real-local` redesign plus two added superseded scenarios and small hardening. The post-review fixes were re-checked: benchmark suite green (24 tests), demo passes and is proven falsifiable, validator clean.
- **Owed before merge:** the #387 reconciliation comment (recording the synthetic-corpus relaxation so the canonical G2 record isn't self-contradictory) and the maintainer's plain-language fairness sample — both surfaced to the operator in chat.

**Things you can confirm yourself (nothing here writes to your project):**
- `uv run --directory .engine --frozen -- python tools/recall_benchmark.py run` — see the old path's baseline: originals ~25/29, **paraphrased 0/22**, discrimination gap **YES**.
- `uv run --directory .engine --frozen -- python tools/recall_benchmark.py demo` — the falsifiable self-check (passes; built to fail).
- `uv run --directory .engine --frozen -- python tools/recall_benchmark.py run --real-local --ask "your real question"` — a private, read-only probe of your own memory (unscored; nothing committed).
- Read `.engine/_fixtures/recall-benchmark/questions.json` — every question and its planted answer, in plain language.

*Impact: the engine's own account of the review — your merge is the binding gate.*

## Files of interest

**The new benchmark tool and its committed synthetic fixtures.**

- `.engine/tools/recall_benchmark.py` — the pure scorer + injected old-path producer + seal + leak guard + `--real-local` probe + falsifiable demo.
- `.engine/_fixtures/recall-benchmark/{corpus.ndjson, questions.json, seal.json}` — the committed synthetic corpus, labeled question set, and the sha256 seal + pinned bar + baseline.
- `.engine/tools/test_recall_benchmark.py` — scorer, well-formedness, seal, discrimination, and demo-falsifiability tests.
- `.engine/tools/instantiator.py` + `.engine/provisioning/first-run-assets.json` — construction-only retirement registration (parity pair).

*Impact: the labels and the scorer carry the load-bearing judgment; the retire wiring is rule-following.*

## Claude involvement

**Design-heavy: the label schema, the scoring rule, and the synthetic-corpus construction are AI judgment against the recorded grammar; the retirement registration is mechanical.**

- The path-agnostic label schema (source-session unit), the mechanical top-k scoring rule, and the two-axis corpus were designed against eADR-0038 and the #387 G2 reframe, pressure-tested by a cold plan-review before building and a cold deliverable-review after.
- The synthetic-corpus choice, the private `--real-local` external-validity design, and the thorough review depth were the operator's decisions; the class-construction rubric keeps the set fair and frozen (sha256-sealed) before the new path exists.

*Impact: the labels and scorer carry the load-bearing judgment; the retire wiring is rule-following.*

  1. **Validate-pass rate** — runs the exact `cmd/conduit/internal/validate` engine
     `conduit pipelines validate` uses. Since `validate.Run` has no in-memory
     (`RunBytes`/`RunReader`) seam yet (confirmed absent from the tree), this uses the
     design doc's documented fallback: a private (0600) temp file, validated, then
     removed (`validate_score.go`) — the one place in the package that touches disk.
  2. **Semantic-intent-match rate** — parses the candidate with the same YAML parser
     `validate` uses and checks the actual source/destination connector category and
     processor set against the request's `Expect`, even when the candidate validates
     cleanly (`semantic_score.go`). A missing candidate fails **both** metrics rather
     than shrinking the denominator; repeated runs reduce by **median**, never
     best-of (CLAUDE.md's benchi discipline, applied to model-output scoring).
- **Fixture tests prove the scorer correct without a live LLM** (`score_test.go`, 19
  tests): known-good candidates score true on both axes; known-bad ones — bad schema,
  wrong connector (still validates), dropped filter, swapped direction, an unknown/
  fabricated plugin, malformed YAML, ambiguous multi-source — each score false on
  exactly the axis they're wrong on.

## Adversarial self-review

Re-read the diff hunting specifically for the classes CLAUDE.md flags:

- **Resource cleanup**: `validateCandidate`'s temp file is removed via `defer` on
  every return path, including the write/close error paths (verified each early
  return happens after `os.CreateTemp` and before returning, so the defer is always
  registered first).
- **Silent wrong answers** (the risk class this whole feature exists to prevent, one
  level down): initially, `connectorCategories` silently kept the *first* connector
  found in a role and ignored a second one in the same role — i.e. it would have
  guessed instead of flagging ambiguity. Caught in self-review and fixed: a second
  same-role connector now makes that role's category permanently ambiguous (`""`),
  which always mismatches a non-empty `Expect`. Added
  `TestScoreSemantic_MultipleSourceConnectors_NeverGuessesACategory` to lock this in.
- **Error paths**: a parse failure that still recovers partial pipelines (the parser's
  documented "return whatever parsed successfully" contract) is judged on what did
  parse, with the error surfaced as an additional issue rather than discarded or
  treated as an unconditional hard failure.
- **Concurrency**: no shared mutable state; `os.CreateTemp`'s per-call random suffix
  means concurrent scoring (not currently done, but not precluded) wouldn't collide.
- **Data-path invariants (1–7)**: none apply — this package never touches a running
  pipeline, ack/position/checkpoint logic, or any serialized format; it only reads
  YAML text it's given and writes/removes its own private temp file.

## Gates run (this PR only — see Process maturity table for what's not live)

- `go build ./...` — clean.
- `golangci-lint run ./cmd/conduit/internal/generate/...` — 0 issues.
- `go test -race ./cmd/conduit/internal/generate/...` — 19/19 pass.
- `make generate && git diff --exit-code` — clean (no generated-file drift; this PR
  adds no `//go:generate` directive).
- `npx markdownlint-cli2 docs/generate-benchmark.md` — 0 errors.
- No `--json` CLI surface added (no CLI command ships) — Family-A/golden-fixture gate
  N/A.
- No error code added — `allcodes.go` registration N/A (those are `generate.*` codes
  owned by the v0.20 command build).
- Full-repo `golangci-lint run ./...` was attempted but returned findings entirely
  inside a *different* concurrent worktree's vendored-Go-authors code
  (`internal/diff`, unrelated to this change) — a sandbox artifact of this
  multi-agent environment, not a finding against this diff. Only the scoped run above
  is claimed as verified.

## Tier

Tier 2 (docs/testdata + a self-contained internal package, no CLI/MCP surface, no
data-path code).

## Test plan

- [x] `go build ./...`
- [x] `golangci-lint run ./cmd/conduit/internal/generate/...`
- [x] `go test -race ./cmd/conduit/internal/generate/...`
- [x] `make generate && git diff --exit-code`
- [x] `npx markdownlint-cli2 docs/generate-benchmark.md`

## Open questions for DeVaris

- Corpus size/mix: 28 requests across 6 connectors × ~9 processor capabilities. Worth
  adding adversarial/prompt-injection-shaped fixtures now, or defer to the v0.20 PR
  that actually wires up retries and can exercise them live?
- `capability.go`'s tag→processor map is hand-maintained (not structurally linked to
  `builtin.DefaultBuiltinProcessors`, to avoid pulling plugin-runtime deps into a
  YAML-only package) — acceptable for a design-only PR, but flagging so it doesn't
  silently drift if builtin processors are renamed before v0.20 lands.

items.body:
## Summary
- GSM8K saturated at one worker hitting 100% solve rate, giving sep-CMA-ES nothing meaningful to learn from. Added `train/train_trinity_coding.py`, using HumanEval (auto-graded via real subprocess execution) as a more discriminating benchmark.
- Fixed two reliability bugs in `train/train_trinity_real.py` found while validating it end-to-end: unretried 429s were silently scored as wrong answers, and `litellm.completion()` had no timeout, allowing indefinite hangs. Both fixes (exponential-backoff retry on `RateLimitError`, `timeout=45`) are applied in both scripts.
- **Code review follow-up:** fixed a related cache-poisoning bug — a call that exhausted retries or hit a non-rate-limit exception (e.g. a timeout) was still being cached as a graded "unsolved" answer, permanently corrupting that (worker, task) cell for the rest of the run. Now an unsuccessful call is not cached, so it's retried for real on a later iteration. Also scrubbed API-key env vars from the subprocess environment used to execute untrusted candidate code in `train_trinity_coding.py`.

## Test plan
- [x] Live GSM8K run against the real NIM worker pool completed: PASS, coordinator (1.00) matched best single worker (nemotron-3-nano-omni-30b-a3b-reasoning, 1.00).
- [x] Local smoke test of the HumanEval grading/assembly logic (real `openai_humaneval` problem + canonical solution, including round-trip through the fenced-code extractor) — verified `returncode 0`.
- [x] Live HumanEval run (4-worker pool) against the real NIM worker pool (`NVIDIA_API_KEY_2`, 40 tasks × 4 workers, 25 sep-CMA-ES iterations): baseline per-worker solve rates 0.75–0.95, coordinator converged to **1.000** — PASS.
- [x] Independent code review (`pr-review-toolkit:code-reviewer`) flagged the cache-poisoning bug and an env-scrubbing gap; both fixed.
- [x] Re-verified the fix live: `openai/gpt-oss-20b` was hitting a sustained NIM-side outage during this pass (10/10 consecutive timeouts), so the confirming run used the other 3 workers — PASS, coordinator (0.925) >= best single worker (0.925). `gpt-oss-20b` remains a valid `--slot-models` entry; it was excluded only because NIM was reporting it unhealthy at verification time.
